explanationEn: By housing giant chillers at distant utility plants and circulating chilled water through subterranean tunnels, Al-Masjid al-Haram remains quiet, clean, and cool.

questionEn: What happens if a pilgrim performing Sa'i forgets which lap they are on, and a trustworthy companion walking beside them the whole time is 100% certain of the exact lap count?
optionsEn: They must ignore their companion and do 14 laps
They may rely upon their trustworthy companion's certain count as they walked together step for step
Both must cancel their Umrah
They must pay a penalty
explanationEn: Jurists state that while a lone doubting pilgrim takes the lower count, a pilgrim walking together with an attentive, reliable companion may rely on that companion's certain count.

questionEn: What did the Prophet ﷺ teach by beginning his Sa'i at Safa after reciting 'Inna as-Safa wal-Marwata min sha'a'irillah'?
optionsEn: That Marwah is optional
That alphabetical order is used
That the sequence mentioned by Allah in the Qur'an (Safa first, then Marwah) determines the mandatory starting point of the rite
That only one hill is needed
explanationEn: Imam al-Shafi'i and jurists cite 'Abda'u bima bada'Allahu bihi' ('I begin with what Allah began with') as a key proof that Qur'anic sequence here establishes legal order (tartib).

questionEn: Why do scholars say a pilgrim should NOT make the gesture of 'Istilam' (pointing with the right hand and saying Allahu Akbar as at the Black Stone) toward the rocks of Safa and Marwah?
optionsEn: Because hands must be kept in pockets
Because pointing is only for Rukn al-Iraqi
Because dua is forbidden on Safa
Because at Safa and Marwah the Sunnah is to face the Kaaba and raise BOTH hands in open-palm supplication (dua)—not to point at the hill rocks or kiss them
explanationEn: Pointing (istilam) belongs strictly to Al-Hajar al-Aswad during Tawaf; atop Safa and Marwah, one faces the Kaaba and raises both hands in ordinary dua posture.

questionEn: Which two women in sacred history are most famously remembered whenever a believer drinks Zamzam and walks between Safa and Marwah?
optionsEn: Hajar (RA) (whose trust and striving brought forth Zamzam and Sa'i) and Aishah (RA) (who preserved the Prophetic rulings of Sa'i and Zamzam in Hadith)
Cleopatra and Zenobia
Bilqis and Asiyah
Hind and Umm Jamil
explanationEn: Hajar (RA) lived the original miracle of Zamzam and Safa-Marwah, while Mother of the Believers Aishah (RA) transmitted the authoritative Prophetic explanations of 2:158 and carrying Zamzam.

questionEn: What did Ibn Abbas (RA) narrate in Sahih al-Bukhari (3364) that Prophet Ibrahim (AS) did on his third visit to Makkah when Ismail (AS) was sharpening arrows under a tree near Zamzam?
optionsEn: They traveled to Egypt together

Ismail rose to embrace his father as a son embraces a father, and Ibrahim said: 'O Ismail, Allah has commanded me with a matter'—to which Ismail replied: 'Do as your Lord has commanded you!'—and they raised the foundations of the Kaaba together
They closed the Zamzam well
They built a wall around Mount Marwah
explanationEn: Seated under the tree right beside Zamzam, Ismail (AS) immediately pledged help to his father Ibrahim (AS), and together they raised the foundations of the Sacred House.

questionEn: How does the story of Ismail (AS) helping his father Ibrahim (AS) near Zamzam echo his earlier response when tested with sacrifice in Surah As-Saffat (37:102)?
optionsEn: He asked Jurhum to decide
He hesitated for a year
In both trials—offering his life in youth and laboring in stone to build the Kaaba—Ismail (AS) immediately answered with unwavering submission to Allah's command
He went to Syria first
explanationEn: Surah Maryam (19:54) praises Ismail (AS) as 'true to his promise (sadiq al-wa'd)', demonstrated both in the trial of sacrifice and in building the Kaaba beside Zamzam.

questionEn: In Surah Maryam (19:54-55), what two virtues does Allah specifically praise Prophet Ismail (AS)—the first resident of Zamzam—for?
optionsEn: Writing books of astronomy
Building tall palaces and collecting gold
Conquering distant islands
Being true to his promise (sadiq al-wa'd) and commanding his family with prayer (Salah) and charity (Zakah)
explanationEn: Surah Maryam (19:54–55) honors Ismail (AS): 'Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet. And he used to enjoin on his people prayer and zakah and was pleasing to his Lord.'

questionEn: What is the 'Siqayat al-Hajj' mentioned in Surah At-Tawbah (9:19)?
optionsEn: Providing water (especially Zamzam) to pilgrims—an honorable deed which the verse clarifies still cannot equal true Iman in Allah and the Last Day and striving in His cause if done without faith
Building ships in Jeddah
Selling dates in Mina
Guarding Mount Thawr
explanationEn: When someone boasted of Siqayat al-Hajj (providing water to pilgrims) and Imarat al-Masjid al-Haram, Surah At-Tawbah (9:19) affirmed that while noble, faith (Iman) in Allah and striving in His path stand above all.

questionEn: Why was Surah At-Tawbah (9:19) revealed regarding 'providing water to pilgrims (Siqayat al-Hajj) and maintaining Al-Masjid al-Haram'?
optionsEn: To forbid giving water to pilgrims
To establish the hierarchy of deeds: outward service to the Kaaba and Zamzam only avails when rooted in sincere faith (Iman) in Allah and the Last Day
To close the Zamzam well
To abolish custody of the Kaaba
explanationEn: As Nu'man ibn Bashir (RA) narrated in Sahih Muslim (1879), this verse taught the companions that faith in Allah and striving for His religion are the foundation that gives value to all sanctuary services.

questionEn: When a pilgrim exits Al-Mas'a after finishing Lap 7 at Mount Marwah, which neighborhood/plaza of Al-Masjid al-Haram do the Marwah doors open onto?
optionsEn: The southern Ajyad tunnel
The western King Fahd Gate
The northern/northeastern Marwah plaza (Al-Qashashiyyah / Al-Mudda'a / Al-Shamiya side), where barber shops and open courtyards sit
Jabal Thawr
explanationEn: Mount Marwah sits at the northeastern corner of Al-Masjid al-Haram, opening onto the Marwah/Qashashiyyah courtyard where licensed barbers and transit links await pilgrims finishing Umrah.

questionEn: What was the historic 'Bab al-Mudda'a' near the northern Marwah end of Al-Mas'a famous for in Makkan history?
optionsEn: A fortress in Taif
A gate in Madinah
A port on the Red Sea
A historic gate and street near Marwah leading toward Jannat al-Mu'alla and upper Makkah
explanationEn: Located near Marwah on the northern side of Al-Mas'a, the historic Mudda'a quarter connected the sanctuary to upper Makkah and the Mu'alla cemetery.

questionEn: Why did the Prophet ﷺ enter Makkah from its upper northern pass (Kada' / Al-Mu'alla side) and exit from its lower southern pass (Kudai) when possible?
optionsEn: As a Sunnah of prophetic travel etiquette entering Makkah from the upper high pass (Thaniyyat Kada') facing the sanctuary and departing from the lower pass (Kudai)
Because the southern road was closed
Because horses could only walk downhill
To avoid Mount Safa
explanationEn: Ibn Umar (RA) narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari (1575) that the Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah from the upper pass (Thaniyyat al-Ulya at Kada'/Al-Hajun) and exited from the lower pass (Thaniyyat al-Sufla at Kudai).

questionEn: What is the spiritual connection between drinking Zamzam water and performing Sa'i between Safa and Marwah?
optionsEn: They occurred a thousand years apart
Both rites originate from the exact same historical event: Hajar's (RA) sevenfold striving between Safa and Marwah answered by Allah with the miraculous gushing of Zamzam
One happened in Madinah and one in Makkah
There is no connection between them
explanationEn: In the lived experience of every Umrah and Hajj pilgrim, drinking Zamzam and walking between Safa and Marwah reenact the unified story of Hajar and Ismail (AS)—showing that human effort (Sa'i) is met by divine grace (Zamzam).

questionEn: What profound life lesson do scholars draw from the fact that Zamzam gushed forth beneath infant Ismail's feet near the Kaaba RATHER than on top of Safa or Marwah where Hajar was searching?
optionsEn: That water only exists under trees
That searching on hills is useless
Allah requires believers to exert sincere effort (Sa'i), yet provision and relief come directly from Allah—often from a direction one did not expect ('min haythu la yahtasib', 65:3)
That one should never exert effort
explanationEn: Hajar (RA) fulfilled the command of striving between Safa and Marwah, while Allah granted the miracle of Zamzam right where her baby lay—teaching that we strive with the means while trusting the Creator of the means.

questionEn: When Hajar (RA) climbed Mount Marwah and looked down into the valley, why did she say to herself 'Sah!' ('Quiet—let me listen!') before spotting Angel Jibril (AS)?
optionsEn: She was reciting poetry
She was speaking to a passing merchant
She heard thunder from Yemen
She heard a mysterious sound near Ismail (AS), quieted herself to listen intently, and then called out asking the angel for help if he had good to offer
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari (3364), Ibn Abbas (RA) recounts Hajar's exact words atop Marwah: 'Sah!' (shushing herself to listen closely), then 'You have made yourself heard; help if you have any relief with you!'—whereupon she saw the angel at Zamzam.

questionEn: For how long did Hajar (RA) live beside the Kaaba and Zamzam raising Ismail (AS) before she passed away in Makkah?
optionsEn: Until Ismail (AS) grew into a young man, learned Arabic from Jurhum, and married among them
Only three days
She moved back to Palestine after a month
She moved to Yemen
explanationEn: Sahih al-Bukhari (3364) explicitly states: 'And the mother of Ismail passed away after Ismail had grown up and married a woman from Jurhum.'

questionEn: What did the Prophet ﷺ do when people asked him for water from his own bucket at the Zamzam well—why did pilgrims cherish drops from his vessel?
optionsEn: He forbade anyone from drinking after him
He drank from the bucket and rinsed/poured back into it, and the Companions cherished the Prophetic blessing while he taught them that Zamzam itself is blessed for all who drink it
He locked the well
He threw the bucket away
explanationEn: Narrations in Musnad Ahmad and Sunan Ibn Majah show the Prophet ﷺ drinking from Zamzam and confirming its universal blessing for every believer until the Day of Judgment.

questionEn: Can a pilgrim make dua in their own native language (such as English, Urdu, Malay, Turkish, or French) while drinking Zamzam or walking between Safa and Marwah?
optionsEn: Only Latin is allowed
No, dua in any language other than Arabic invalidates Sa'i
Yes—while prophetic Arabic adhkar are beloved, personal dua in any language one understands from the heart is completely valid and heard by Allah
One must remain completely silent if not fluent in Arabic
explanationEn: Allah knows every language and the secrets of every heart; scholars encourage memorizing the short prophetic adhkar while pouring out one's personal prayers in whatever language one speaks.

questionEn: What is the ruling on reading from the Mushaf (or a Qur'an app) while walking between Safa and Marwah during Sa'i?
optionsEn: Invalidates Sa'i
Strictly forbidden in Al-Mas'a
Required on all 7 laps
Permissible so long as it does not distract the pilgrim from watching where they walk or bumping into others, though heartfelt dua and dhikr are primary
explanationEn: Reciting Qur'an, making dhikr, and supplicating are all virtuous during Sa'i, provided one walks attentively and safely in the crowd.

questionEn: Why are there no fixed, mandatory separate 'Lap 1 Dua', 'Lap 2 Dua', ..., 'Lap 7 Dua' in authentic Hadith for Sa'i?
optionsEn: Because the Prophet ﷺ established only the opening verse (2:158), the dhikr/dua atop Safa & Marwah, and general remembrance/dua along the walk—leaving believers free to supplicate from the heart
Because the companions forgot to write them down
Because speaking is forbidden on Laps 2, 4, and 6
Because only Imams know the seven secret duas
explanationEn: Pamphlets assigning seven invented lap-specific duas have no origin in the Sunnah; authentic Prophetic practice combines the Safa/Marwah adhkar with sincere personal supplication throughout.

questionEn: What is the ruling if a pilgrim performs Tawaf around the Kaaba just before Isha, prays Isha in congregation, rests or eats dinner, and then performs Sa'i between Safa and Marwah an hour or two later?
optionsEn: Invalid—even a 5-minute pause voids Tawaf
Completely valid—while performing Sa'i immediately after Tawaf is Sunnah, a gap of a few hours for prayer, rest, or food does not invalidate the connection between Tawaf and Sa'i
They must pay a camel
They must repeat Tawaf
explanationEn: Jurists agree that immediate continuity between Tawaf and Sa'i is a Sunnah rather than a strict condition; resting or praying between them leaves Sa'i completely valid.

questionEn: What is the ruling if a pilgrim pauses in the middle of Sa'i (for example after Lap 4) due to sudden illness or exhaustion, rests in their hotel, and returns to complete Laps 5, 6, and 7?
optionsEn: They must sacrifice seven sheep
Their entire Umrah is permanently canceled
Valid when paused for a genuine excuse like illness or exhaustion (though restarting from Lap 1 is cautious if the break was very long without excuse)
They can skip the remaining 3 laps
explanationEn: Islamic law is built on ease when hardship strikes; an excused interruption due to sickness or severe fatigue allows resuming from where one stopped.

questionEn: Which two hills in Makkah stand as eternal monuments to a mother's love, reliance on Allah, and refusal to give up hope in a barren desert?
optionsEn: Mount Qasioun and Mount Lebanon
Mount Uhud and Mount Sila'
Mount Sinai and Mount Olives
Mount Safa and Mount Marwah
explanationEn: Every step between Safa and Marwah commemorates Hajar's (RA) active hope in Allah's mercy on behalf of her thirsty child Ismail (AS).

questionEn: According to the authentic hadith narrated by Jabir ibn Abdullah (RA), how much more rewarding is a single prayer offered in Al-Masjid al-Haram compared to a prayer in an ordinary mosque?
optionsEn: 100,000 prayers
1,000 prayers
10,000 prayers
500 prayers
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ stated: 'A prayer in my mosque is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere, except Al-Masjid al-Haram, and a prayer in Al-Masjid al-Haram is better than one hundred thousand prayers elsewhere.'

questionEn: In the hadith comparing the reward of prayers in the Sacred Mosques, how does a prayer in Al-Masjid al-Haram compare numerically to a single prayer in the Prophet's Mosque (Al-Masjid al-Nabawi)?
optionsEn: It is ten times more rewarding than a prayer in Al-Masjid al-Nabawi
It is one hundred times more rewarding than a prayer in Al-Masjid al-Nabawi
It is equal in reward to a prayer in Al-Masjid al-Nabawi
It is fifty times more rewarding than a prayer in Al-Masjid al-Nabawi
explanationEn: Since a prayer in Al-Masjid al-Nabawi equals 1,000 prayers elsewhere and a prayer in Al-Masjid al-Haram equals 100,000 prayers elsewhere, one prayer in Al-Masjid al-Haram equals 100 prayers in Al-Masjid al-Nabawi.

questionEn: According to the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (RA), toward which three mosques alone is a Muslim permitted to undertake a dedicated religious journey (shadd al-rihal)?
optionsEn: Al-Masjid al-Haram, Masjid Quba, and Al-Masjid al-Nabawi
Al-Masjid al-Haram, Masjid al-Khayf, and Al-Masjid al-Aqsa
Al-Masjid al-Haram, Al-Masjid al-Nabawi, and Al-Masjid al-Aqsa
Al-Masjid al-Haram, Masjid al-Qiblatayn, and Al-Masjid al-Nabawi
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Do not set out on a special journey (la tushaddu al-rihal) except to three mosques: Al-Masjid al-Haram, the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Al-Masjid al-Aqsa.'

questionEn: In Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh), what serves as the primary greeting of the mosque (Tahiyyat al-Masjid) for a person entering Al-Masjid al-Haram with the intention of performing Tawaf?
optionsEn: Praying four rak'ahs at Bab al-Salam before approaching the courtyard
Standing at the gate to recite Surah Al-Baqarah
Giving charity to seven needy residents before sitting
Performing Tawaf around the Kaaba
explanationEn: For one who enters Al-Masjid al-Haram intending Tawaf (such as a pilgrim arriving for Umrah or Hajj), beginning directly with Tawaf serves as the greeting of the Sacred Mosque, followed by two rak'ahs of Tawaf.
reference: Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 3/337; Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi 8/13

questionEn: If a person enters Al-Masjid al-Haram purely to attend the congregation or sit in the mosque without intending or being able to perform Tawaf at that time, what should they do before sitting?
optionsEn: Pray two rak'ahs of Tahiyyat al-Masjid as in other mosques
Sit down immediately without praying because rak'ahs are forbidden before Tawaf
Walk around the outer perimeter of the mosque gates once
Wait outside the gates until the Iqamah is called
explanationEn: Jurists explain that while Tawaf is the specific greeting for one intending Tawaf, anyone entering Al-Masjid al-Haram without performing Tawaf should pray two rak'ahs of Tahiyyat al-Masjid before sitting down.

questionEn: How are the congregational prayer rows (sufuf) uniquely arranged around the Kaaba inside the courtyard of Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Only behind the southern wall of the Kaaba facing north
In concentric circular rows surrounding the Kaaba from all four sides
In parallel straight lines running strictly from east to west across the Mataf
Only in the northern courtyard behind Maqam Ibrahim
explanationEn: Because the Kaaba itself sits at the center of Al-Masjid al-Haram as the Qiblah, worshippers in the Mataf and surrounding halls form concentric circular rows all facing inward toward the Sacred House.
reference: Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 2/23; Surah Al-Baqarah 2:144

questionEn: When praying in circular rows around the Kaaba inside Al-Masjid al-Haram, in what case is a follower's prayer considered invalid by the majority of jurists with respect to the Imam's position?
optionsEn: When the follower stands on one of the upper floors of the mosque
When the follower faces a different wall of the Kaaba than the wall the Imam faces
When the follower stands on the same side as the Imam and closer to the Kaaba than the Imam
When the follower stands behind Maqam Ibrahim while the Imam is near the Black Stone
explanationEn: According to the majority of scholars, standing closer to the Kaaba than the Imam on a different side is permissible because they face different directions toward the center, whereas standing ahead of the Imam on the very same side facing the same direction invalidates or dislikes the follower's position.
reference: Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 2/148; Bada'i al-Sana'i 1/215

questionEn: What is the ruling on facing the exact physical structure of the Kaaba ('ayn al-Ka'bah) for someone praying inside Al-Masjid al-Haram who can directly see the Kaaba?
optionsEn: Facing the general direction of Makkah (jihat al-Ka'bah) within 45 degrees is sufficient
They must face only the spout (Mizab) on the northern side
They may face any direction inside the Haram courtyard
They must face the actual physical structure of the Kaaba directly ('ayn al-Ka'bah)
explanationEn: Scholars agree that one who witnesses the Kaaba directly ('inda al-mu'ayanah) is obligated to face the physical edifice itself ('ayn al-Ka'bah), whereas those far away are required to face its general direction (jihat al-Ka'bah).
reference: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:144; Al-Ijma' by Ibn al-Mundhir p. 40

questionEn: On the Day of the Conquest of Makkah, when did the Prophet ﷺ declare that Allah first made Makkah a sacred sanctuary (Haram)?
optionsEn: On the very day Allah created the heavens and the earth
On the day the Prophet ﷺ conquered Makkah in 8 AH
When Qusayy ibn Kilab united the tribes of Quraysh
During the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah in 6 AH
explanationEn: In his famous sermon on the Day of the Conquest, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Indeed, Allah made this town sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, so it is sacred by the sanctity of Allah until the Day of Resurrection.'

questionEn: In the Conquest of Makkah sermon, for how long did the Prophet ﷺ state that fighting in Makkah was temporarily permitted for him alone before its inviolability returned forever?
optionsEn: For three complete days and nights
For only one hour (a brief portion) of one day
For the entire month of Ramadan in 8 AH
For nineteen days until he departed for Hunayn
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ declared: 'It was not permitted for anyone before me, and it was only made lawful for me for an hour of a day; it has now returned to its sanctity today just as it was sacred yesterday.'

questionEn: What did the Prophet ﷺ command regarding the wild game (sayd) living within the sacred boundaries of Makkah's Haram?
optionsEn: It may be hunted freely by residents of Makkah who are not in Ihram
It may be hunted at night provided a charity is paid
Its wild game must neither be hunted nor even frightened or driven from its resting place
Only birds may be caught while four-legged animals are protected
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ said regarding Makkah: 'Its game is not to be chased or frightened away (la yunaffaru sayduha).' Both pilgrims in Ihram and non-pilgrim residents are prohibited from hunting or disturbing wild land game inside the Haram.

questionEn: What is the ruling on the wild, naturally growing thorny trees and herbage (shawk and khala) of Makkah's Haram?
optionsEn: They may be cut down freely by anyone not wearing Ihram
They may be uprooted during the winter months for firewood
Only fruit-bearing orchard trees are protected from cutting
It is prohibited to cut, lop, or uproot naturally growing wild trees and herbage of the Haram
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ stated concerning Makkah: 'Its thorns are not to be cut (la yu'dadu shawkuha) and its fresh herbage is not to be uprooted (la yukhtala khalaha).' This applies to wild uncultivated vegetation native to the Haram.

questionEn: Which wild aromatic plant of Makkah was specifically exempted by the Prophet ﷺ from the prohibition of cutting Haram vegetation?
optionsEn: Al-Idhkhir (sweet rush / lemon-grass)
Al-Arak (the tooth-stick tree)
Al-Samur (wild acacia)
Al-Sidr (the lote tree)
explanationEn: When the Prophet ﷺ prohibited cutting the wild herbage and trees of Makkah, he granted a specific exception for Al-Idhkhir (Cymbopogon schoenanthus, an aromatic lemon-grass native to the Hijaz).

questionEn: Which companion requested the Prophet ﷺ to exempt Al-Idhkhir from the ban on cutting Haram plants, and for what practical uses did he mention it?
optionsEn: Abu Sufyan ibn Harb (RA), for feeding the trade camels of Quraysh
Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib (RA), for their blacksmiths/goldsmiths and for their houses and graves
Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA), for weaving mats inside Al-Masjid al-Haram
Bilal ibn Rabah (RA), for burning incense at the gates of the mosque
explanationEn: Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib (RA) said: 'Except Al-Idhkhir, O Messenger of Allah, for it is needed for our smiths (qaynihim) and for our roofs/houses (buyutihim)'—and in another narration 'for our graves'—whereupon the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Except Al-Idhkhir.'

questionEn: What do the majority of Islamic jurists hold regarding crops, vegetables, and trees that humans intentionally plant and cultivate in Makkah's Haram?
optionsEn: They can never be harvested once planted inside the Haram boundaries
They can only be harvested during the three days of Tashreeq
They may be harvested and cut by their owners because the prohibition applies to wild uncultivated Haram plants
They must be left solely for wild birds to eat
explanationEn: The majority of jurists (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali) permit harvesting and trimming vegetation cultivated by human labor in the Haram, restricting the prohibition to wild plants that grow naturally without human planting.
reference: Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 3/354; Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi 7/448

questionEn: How does the ruling on lost and found property (luqatah) inside Makkah's Haram differ from lost property found outside the Haram?
optionsEn: In Makkah's Haram, the finder becomes the owner after announcing it for three days
In Makkah's Haram, the finder becomes the owner after announcing it for one lunar year
In Makkah's Haram, half of the found item belongs to the finder immediately
In Makkah's Haram, lost property may only be picked up by one who announces it perpetually and never takes personal ownership of it
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ said concerning Makkah: 'Its fallen lost property (saqitatuha / luqatatuha) is not lawful to pick up except for a mu'arrif (one who announces it to return it to its owner).' Unlike outside the Haram, announcing it for a year does not transfer ownership to the finder.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1834; Sahih Muslim 1353; Sunan Abi Dawud 1717

questionEn: According to the hadith of Aishah and Ibn Umar (RA), how many harmful animals (al-fawasiq) did the Prophet ﷺ explicitly permit to be killed inside the Haram and while in Ihram?
optionsEn: Five harmful creatures (al-fawasiq al-khams)
Three harmful creatures
Seven harmful creatures
Ten harmful creatures
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Five animals are all fawasiq (harmful pests) and may be killed in the Haram (and while in Ihram): the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse/rat, and the rabid/biting dog.'

questionEn: Which of the following is the exact list of the five harmful pests (al-fawasiq al-khams) that are permissible to kill inside Makkah's Haram?
optionsEn: The wolf, the fox, the locust, the lizard, and the beetle
The crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse/rat, and the rabid/biting dog
The hoopoe, the frog, the ant, the honeybee, and the swallow
The gazelle, the ostrich, the wild hare, the pigeon, and the hyena
explanationEn: As narrated in both Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the five fawasiq permitted to be killed in Al-Hill and Al-Haram are the pied crow (al-ghurab al-abqa'), the kite (al-hida'ah), the scorpion (al-'aqrab), the mouse/rat (al-fa'rah), and the biting/predatory dog (al-kalb al-'aqur).

questionEn: What is the ruling on hunting or driving away the pigeons of Al-Masjid al-Haram and Makkah (hamam al-Haram)?
optionsEn: It is permissible for local residents to trap them for food
It is disliked only during the five days of Hajj
It is strictly forbidden to hunt, kill, or frighten them, and doing so requires compensation
It is permitted if they land outside the roofed porticos
explanationEn: Because the pigeons of Makkah are wild game residing in the Sacred Sanctuary, the Companions (including Umar, Uthman, Ibn Umar, and Ibn Abbas RA) ruled that killing a Haram pigeon is forbidden and requires expiation (a sheep or its equivalent for the poor).
reference: Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 5/175; Musannaf Ibn Abi Shaybah 14830

questionEn: According to the authentic hadith of Anas ibn Malik (RA), which two cities on earth will the False Messiah (Al-Masih al-Dajjal) be completely unable to enter?
optionsEn: Makkah and Damascus
Madinah and Kufa
Makkah and Sana'a
Makkah and Madinah
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ stated: 'There is no town that the Dajjal will not tread except Makkah and Madinah; there is no mountain pass (naqb) leading to them except that angels are standing in rows guarding it.'

questionEn: Besides the Dajjal, what affliction did the Prophet ﷺ state in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (RA) is prevented by angels at the mountain passes from entering Makkah and Madinah?
optionsEn: The plague (al-ta'un)
Drought and lack of rain
Flash floods in the valleys
Locust swarms
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ said that at the mountain passes of Madinah (and in Musnad Ahmad and Sahih texts, Makkah and Madinah) stand angels, and neither the plague (al-ta'un) nor the Dajjal shall enter them.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1880; Sahih Muslim 1379; Musnad Ahmad 7487

questionEn: Which Qur'anic verse revealed in the 9th year of Hijrah prohibited polytheists (al-mushrikun) from approaching Al-Masjid al-Haram after that pilgrimage season?
optionsEn: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:196
Surah At-Tawbah 9:28
Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:97
Surah Al-Hajj 22:29
explanationEn: Allah revealed in Surah At-Tawbah 9:28: 'O you who have believed, indeed the polytheists are impure, so let them not approach Al-Masjid al-Haram after this, their final year.'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hajj (22:25), how does the Qur'an uniquely warn against 'ilhad bi-zulm' (inclining toward wrongdoing or deviation) inside Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Wrongdoing in Makkah is only recorded if repeated three times
Only financial debts incurred in Makkah are subject to accountability
Whoever firmly intends wrongdoing therein out of injustice will be made to taste a painful punishment
Mistakes made out of forgetfulness in Makkah require leaving the city
explanationEn: Surah Al-Hajj 22:25 states: 'And whoever intends therein [a deed] of deviation by wrongdoing (wa-man yurid fihi bi-ilhadin bi-zulmin), We will make him taste of a painful punishment.' Ibn Mas'ud (RA) explained that in Makkah, even a firm resolution to commit a sin brings punishment.
reference: Surah Al-Hajj 22:25; Musnad Ahmad 4381; Tafsir Ibn Kathir

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hajj (22:25), what two groups of people does Allah declare equal in right regarding Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: The wealthy merchant and the tax collector
The horseman and the foot soldier
The scholar of law and the poet
The permanent resident therein (al-'akif fihi) and the visiting outsider/nomad (al-badi)
explanationEn: Allah describes Al-Masjid al-Haram as 'that which We have made for all mankind—equal therein is the resident (al-'akif fihi) and the visitor from outside (al-badi).' Hence no one may monopolize its prayer spaces.

questionEn: Which Qur'anic verse refers to the Sacred Mosque in Makkah using the name 'Bakkah' and describes it as the very first House of worship appointed for mankind?
optionsEn: Surah Al-Imran 3:96
Surah Ibrahim 14:37
Surah Al-Qasas 28:57
Surah Quraysh 106:1
explanationEn: Surah Al-Imran 3:96 states: 'Indeed, the first House [of worship] established for mankind was that at Bakkah—blessed and a guidance for the worlds.'

questionEn: By what title is Makkah addressed in Surah Al-An'am (6:92) and Surah Ash-Shura (42:7), signifying its status as the central mother of all settlements?
optionsEn: Madinat al-Salam (City of Peace)
Umm al-Qura (Mother of Cities/Settlements)
Dar al-Hijrah (Abode of Migration)
Qaryat al-Ansar (Town of the Helpers)
explanationEn: In Surah Al-An'am 6:92 and Surah Ash-Shura 42:7, Allah says: 'so that you may warn Umm al-Qura (Makkah) and those around it.'

questionEn: In Surah At-Tin (95:3), by what oath does Allah swear when referring to the sanctuary of Makkah?
optionsEn: Wa al-Bayt al-Ma'mur (And by the Much-Frequented House)
Wa al-Qaryat al-Mubarakah (And by the blessed village)
Wa hadha al-Balad al-Amin (And by this secure city)
Wa al-Wadi al-Muqaddas (And by the sacred valley)
explanationEn: After swearing by the fig, the olive, and Mount Sinai, Allah swears in Surah At-Tin 95:3: 'And by this secure city (wa hadha al-Balad al-Amin),' which exegetes unanimously identify as Makkah.

questionEn: When the Prophet ﷺ was forced to leave Makkah and stood looking back at it from Al-Hazwarah, how did he express Makkah's status in the sight of Allah and in his own heart?
optionsEn: He declared that he would never return to visit Makkah again
He prayed that Makkah's valleys would lose their trade caravans forever
He stated that Ta'if was dearer to him than Makkah
He declared that by Allah, Makkah is the best and most beloved of Allah's earth to Allah, and were he not driven out he would never have left
explanationEn: Narrated by Adi ibn Hatim / Abdullah ibn Adi ibn al-Hamra (RA): The Prophet ﷺ stood at Al-Hazwarah and said: 'By Allah, you are indeed the best of Allah's earth and the most beloved of Allah's earth to Allah; had I not been driven out from you, I would not have left you.'

questionEn: According to the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah (RA) in Sahih Muslim, what did the Prophet ﷺ prohibit carrying inside Makkah unless there is a genuine necessity?
optionsEn: Carrying weapons
Carrying leather waterskins
Carrying silver coins
Carrying walking staffs
explanationEn: Jabir (RA) narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'It is not lawful for anyone of you to carry weapons in Makkah.' This preserves the peace and security (amn) of the Sacred Sanctuary.

questionEn: What is the Sunnah etiquette when stepping across the threshold to enter Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Entering backward facing the street while reciting Surah Al-Ikhlas
Entering with the right foot first while invoking blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ and asking Allah to open the gates of His mercy
Jumping over the threshold with both feet together in silence
Touching the ground three times with the forehead at the outer gate
explanationEn: As with all mosques, and especially the Sacred Mosque, the Sunnah is to enter with the right foot first and say: 'Bismillah, was-salatu was-salamu 'ala Rasulillah, Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik' (O Allah, open for me the gates of Your mercy).

questionEn: What supplication is authentically reported from Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) upon seeing the Sacred House (the Kaaba) in Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Subhana alladhi sakhkhara lana hadha wa ma kunna lahu muqrinin
Allahumma barik lana fi Rajab wa Sha'ban wa ballighna Ramadan
Allahumma antas-salam wa minkas-salam, fahayyina Rabbana bis-salam (O Allah, You are Peace and from You is peace, so keep us alive, our Lord, in peace)
Alhamdulillah alladhi ahyana ba'da ma amatana wa ilayhin-nushur
explanationEn: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib reported that when Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) looked at the House, he said: 'Allahumma antas-salam wa minkas-salam, fahayyina Rabbana bis-salam.'
reference: Musannaf Ibn Abi Shaybah 13384; Sunan al-Bayhaqi 5/73

questionEn: How did classical jurists such as Ata ibn Abi Rabah and Ibn al-Zubayr treat the ruling on people walking in front of someone praying inside Al-Masjid al-Haram during intense crowding around the Mataf?
optionsEn: They ruled that the worshipper must physically strike anyone doing Tawaf in front of them
They ruled that voluntary prayers are completely forbidden inside the Mataf at all times
They ruled that a worshipper must restart their prayer from the first rak'ah whenever a pilgrim walks past
They granted a concession that circumambulators passing directly in front of a worshipper in crowded Al-Masjid al-Haram do not invalidate or incur sin
explanationEn: While placing a sutrah is the general Sunnah, authentic reports from Ibn al-Zubayr, Ata, and the jurists establish a concession in Al-Masjid al-Haram due to the unavoidable necessity of pilgrims performing Tawaf and moving through dense crowds.
reference: Musannaf Abd al-Razzaq 2300; Sunan Abi Dawud 2016; Al-Mughni 2/44

questionEn: According to the majority of scholars (including Ibn Abbas, Ata, and the four Sunni schools, with elaboration), does the 100,000-prayer reward apply only to the historic roofed portico around the Kaaba or to the expanded Al-Masjid al-Haram and the Sacred Sanctuary?
optionsEn: It encompasses the entire expanded mosque of Al-Masjid al-Haram (and according to many scholars, the entire Haram sanctuary of Makkah)
It applies only to a three-meter circle touching the Kaaba walls
It applies only to prayers offered inside the semi-circular Hijr Ismail
It ceased to apply to any area added after the era of the Umayyad Caliphate
explanationEn: Scholars agree that every expansion added to Al-Masjid al-Haram takes the full ruling and 100,000x reward of the Sacred Mosque, and a prominent position reported from Ata and major scholars extends the multiplication of prayer reward to the whole Haram boundary of Makkah.
reference: Tafsir al-Qurtubi 10/207; Majmu' Fatawa Ibn Taymiyyah 27/344; Fatawa Ibn Baz

questionEn: Are there any times of the day or night when performing Tawaf and its two rak'ahs of prayer—or voluntary prayers according to a well-known scholarly position—are permitted inside Al-Masjid al-Haram based on the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im (RA)?
optionsEn: No, Tawaf is strictly prohibited between Asr and Maghrib
Yes, at any hour of the night or day, nobody is to be prevented from circumambulating this House and praying
No, entering Al-Masjid al-Haram is forbidden between Fajr and sunrise
Only during the last ten nights of Ramadan is prayer after Fajr allowed
explanationEn: In the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im (RA), the Prophet ﷺ said: 'O Banu Abd Manaf, do not prevent anyone who circumambulates this House and prays at any hour he wishes of the night or day.'
reference: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 868; Sunan al-Nasa'i 2924; Sunan Abi Dawud 1894 (Sahih)

questionEn: Which clan did the Prophet ﷺ address in the hadith 'Do not prevent anyone who circumambulates this House and prays at any hour he wishes of the night or day'?
optionsEn: Banu Makhzum
Banu Sahm
Banu Abd Manaf
Banu Thaqif
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ addressed Banu Abd Manaf (who held authority and service roles over the sanctuary in Makkah): 'O Banu Abd Manaf, do not prevent anyone who circumambulates this House and prays at any hour he wishes of the night or day.'

questionEn: What is the ruling on praying on the upper floors or roof of Al-Masjid al-Haram when following the Imam leading prayer at the ground level of the Mataf?
optionsEn: It is invalid for obligatory prayers and valid only for Tarawih
It is valid only if the worshipper stands directly above the Black Stone corner
It is invalid because the Kaaba roof is lower than the upper floors
It is valid as long as the worshipper faces the air-column (hawa') of the Kaaba, hears or follows the Imam's transitions, and rows are connected
explanationEn: Jurists explain that the Qiblah extends from the earth of the Kaaba up to the heavens (hawa' al-Ka'bah); therefore praying on the upper floors and roof of Al-Masjid al-Haram facing the vertical plane of the Kaaba is completely valid.
reference: Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi 3/212; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 1/403

questionEn: How does Surah Al-Imran (3:97) describe the spiritual and legal security of the Sacred Sanctuary in the statement 'Wa man dakhalahu kana amina'?
optionsEn: Whoever enters it shall be safe (granted security from attack and aggression)
Whoever enters it is exempted from fasting in Ramadan
Whoever enters it becomes wealthy within a year
Whoever enters it does not need to perform ablution
explanationEn: Surah Al-Imran 3:97 declares: 'In it are clear signs [such as] the standing place of Ibrahim. And whoever enters it shall be safe (wa man dakhalahu kana amina).'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Qasas (28:57) and Surah Al-Ankabut (29:67), what blessing did Allah remind the Quraysh He had bestowed upon them in contrast to the people being snatched away around them?
optionsEn: That He gave them rivers flowing beneath their houses like Damascus
That He established for them a safe and secure Sacred Sanctuary (Haraman Aminan) to which fruits of all things are brought
That He built high stone fortresses around Makkah's borders
That He exempted them from death in this world
explanationEn: Allah says in Surah Al-Qasas 28:57: 'Have We not established for them a safe Sanctuary (Haraman Aminan) to which are brought the fruits of all things as provision from Us?'

questionEn: What is the ruling on performing the Funeral Prayer (Salat al-Janazah) inside Al-Masjid al-Haram after the obligatory prayers?
optionsEn: It is strictly forbidden because funerals must only be prayed in the desert outside the Haram
It is valid only on Fridays after Jumu'ah prayer
It is permissible and has been the continuous practice of Muslims in Al-Masjid al-Haram since the era of the Companions
It is valid only for people who died while wearing Ihram
explanationEn: In Sahih Muslim, Aishah (RA) noted that the Prophet ﷺ prayed the funeral prayer for Suhayl ibn Bayda inside the mosque, and praying Salat al-Janazah in Al-Masjid al-Haram after the five obligatory prayers is an established, continuous practice.
reference: Sahih Muslim 973; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 2/363

questionEn: In Surah Al-Qasas (28:85), when Allah promised the Prophet ﷺ during the Hijrah: 'Indeed, He who imposed upon you the Qur'an will surely take you back to a place of return (ila ma'ad),' what did Ibn Abbas (RA) explain 'ma'ad' to mean?
optionsEn: Bayt al-Maqdis in Jerusalem
The city of Ta'if
The land of Abyssinia
Makkah (returning him victoriously to his homeland of Makkah)
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA) explained that 'ladha raddaka ila ma'ad' in Surah Al-Qasas 28:85 means returning the Prophet ﷺ to Makkah, which was fulfilled at the Conquest of Makkah.

questionEn: If a person inside the Haram breaks a branch from a wild native tree or kills a wild animal of the Haram (even while not in Ihram), what do the majority of jurists require?
optionsEn: Repentance and paying the prescribed expiation/compensation (fidyah/jaza') distributed to the poor of the Haram
Leaving the religion and renewing their testimony of faith
Fasting for two consecutive months as in Zihar
Rebuilding a section of the Haram boundary stones
explanationEn: Because the sanctity of the Haram applies to both those in Ihram and non-pilgrims (halal), violating the wild game or wild trees of the Haram requires repentance and according to the majority of jurists (Hanafi, Shafi'i, Hanbali) compensation given to the poor of the Haram.
reference: Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 3/352; Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi 7/446

questionEn: What is the ruling on women attending congregational prayers and performing Tawaf in Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Women are only permitted to enter Al-Masjid al-Haram during the daytime
It is permissible and rewarding when observing Islamic modesty and avoiding crowding with men
Women may only perform Tawaf from the rooftop and never on the ground floor
Women are barred from entering Al-Masjid al-Haram outside the month of Dhul-Hijjah
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah' (Bukhari & Muslim), and the female Companions regularly performed Tawaf and prayed in Al-Masjid al-Haram while maintaining modesty and avoiding mingling with men.

questionEn: What did the Prophet ﷺ say in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr (RA) about the virtue of dying in one of the Two Sacred Cities (al-Haramayn)?
optionsEn: Whoever dies in Makkah is buried inside the Kaaba itself
Whoever dies in Makkah has his estate exempted from inheritance division
Whoever dies in one of the Two Harams, Allah will resurrect him among the secure (min al-aminin) on the Day of Resurrection
Whoever dies in Makkah does not need a funeral prayer
explanationEn: In Shu'ab al-Iman and other collections, early scholars and narrations highlight the great blessing of dying in Makkah or Madinah as dying in a sacred sanctuary of peace and faith, while the Prophet ﷺ himself asked for martyrdom and death in His Messenger's city.
reference: Shu'ab al-Iman by Al-Bayhaqi 3853; Sahih al-Bukhari 1890

questionEn: Why do scholars emphasize guarding one's tongue from arguments, backbiting, and foul speech inside Al-Masjid al-Haram and during residency in Makkah?
optionsEn: Because speaking any language other than Arabic inside the Haram invalidates ablution
Because speaking aloud in Makkah requires sacrificing a camel
Because any conversation inside the mosque cancels previous Umrahs
Because just as good deeds are magnified in honor in the Sacred Sanctuary, sins committed in the Haram are graver in weight due to the sanctity of the place
explanationEn: Companions such as Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Mas'ud (RA) warned that sins committed in the Sacred Sanctuary of Makkah are multiplied in gravity and severity—not in numerical count, as a sin is always recorded as one—because of violating the sanctity of Allah's sacred place (Surah Al-Hajj 22:25).
reference: Surah Al-Hajj 22:25; Zad al-Ma'ad by Ibn al-Qayyim 1/49; Majmu' Fatawa Ibn Baz

questionEn: What is the proper etiquette upon exiting Al-Masjid al-Haram after completing one's prayer or worship?
optionsEn: Stepping out with the left foot first and saying: 'Bismillah, was-salatu was-salamu 'ala Rasulillah, Allahumma inni as'aluka min fadlik'
Walking out backward from the gate so as never to turn one's back to the Kaaba
Stepping out with the right foot first while clapping three times
Running from the Mataf to the outer plaza without looking left or right
explanationEn: The Sunnah when leaving any mosque—including Al-Masjid al-Haram—is to exit with the left foot and ask Allah for His bounty ('Allahumma inni as'aluka min fadlik'). Jurists note that walking backward out of the Haram is an innovation (bid'ah) not practiced by the Prophet ﷺ or his Companions.
reference: Sahih Muslim 713; Zad al-Ma'ad by Ibn al-Qayyim 2/279

questionEn: How was the prayer space of Al-Masjid al-Haram structured during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ and the caliphate of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA)?
optionsEn: It was enclosed by a high marble portico with four minarets
It was an open courtyard around the Kaaba surrounded directly by the houses of Makkah without an enclosing perimeter wall
It was covered by fifty wooden domes built by Qusayy ibn Kilab
It was surrounded by a deep moat and iron gates
explanationEn: During the time of the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr (RA), Al-Masjid al-Haram had no outer boundary wall; the houses of Quraysh surrounded the open Mataf courtyard with narrow lanes between them serving as entrances.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/69; Wafa' al-Wafa

questionEn: Which Rashidun Caliph carried out the first expansion of Al-Masjid al-Haram in 17 AH (638 CE) by purchasing adjacent houses and building the first low enclosure wall around it?
optionsEn: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA)
Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA)
Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA)
Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan (RA)
explanationEn: In 17 AH (638 CE), as the number of Muslims grew rapidly, Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) purchased surrounding houses, demolished them to expand the courtyard, and built the first low perimeter wall (shadr) shorter than a man's height around Al-Masjid al-Haram.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/69; Tarikh al-Tabari

questionEn: When some house owners initially refused to sell their homes adjacent to the Kaaba during Umar ibn al-Khattab's (RA) 17 AH expansion, how did Umar resolve the matter justly?
optionsEn: He confiscated the houses without paying any compensation
He canceled the expansion on that side of the mosque permanently
He moved the Mataf outside the valley of Makkah
He assessed their fair value, placed their compensation money safely inside the Kaaba treasury until they later took it, and told them the Kaaba was their guest
explanationEn: Umar (RA) told them: 'You took up residence in the courtyard of the Kaaba; the Kaaba did not enter upon you!' He had their properties fairly appraised and deposited the compensation inside the Kaaba until they came and accepted their payment.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/69; Al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah

questionEn: What two additional infrastructure improvements did Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) introduce to Al-Masjid al-Haram during his 17 AH expansion?
optionsEn: Mounting oil lamps on the enclosure wall to illuminate the Mataf at night and constructing protective dams (al-radm) against flash floods
Building two tall stone minarets and digging an underground railway
Covering the entire Mataf with a dome and installing brass chandeliers from Spain
Paving the courtyard with green tiles and enclosing Mount Arafat
explanationEn: Following the violent 'Umm Nahshal' flash flood that swept through the Sacred Mosque, Umar (RA) built protective diversion dams in upper Makkah and placed lamps upon the new low perimeter wall so worshippers could perform Tawaf in the light.

questionEn: Which Rashidun Caliph expanded Al-Masjid al-Haram in 26 AH (646 CE) and was the very first to construct roofed porticos (arwiqah) around the courtyard to shade worshippers?
optionsEn: Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA)
Uthman ibn Affan (RA)
Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA)
Al-Hasan ibn Ali (RA)
explanationEn: In 26 AH (646 CE), Uthman ibn Affan (RA) bought additional neighboring houses to widen Al-Masjid al-Haram and was the first to build roofed arcades/porticos (arwiqah) around the mosque to shade worshippers from the intense sun.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/70; Tarikh Khalifah ibn Khayyat

questionEn: Who expanded Al-Masjid al-Haram in 65 AH (684 CE) after reconstructing the Kaaba on the foundations of Ibrahim (AS), enlarging the mosque area with marble columns?
optionsEn: Marwan ibn al-Hakam
Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan
Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr (RA)
Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf
explanationEn: In 65 AH, Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr (RA) purchased surrounding properties on the eastern, northern, and southern sides, substantially enlarging Al-Masjid al-Haram and roofing its porticos over marble columns.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/71; Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh

questionEn: Which Umayyad Caliph carried out a major architectural renovation and expansion of Al-Masjid al-Haram in 91 AH (709–710 CE), importing marble columns from Egypt and Syria and decorating the teakwood ceilings and capitals with gold?
optionsEn: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz
Mu'awiyah ibn Yazid
Marwan ibn Muhammad
Al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik
explanationEn: In 91 AH, the Umayyad Caliph Al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik demolished the old porticos and rebuilt them firmly with marble columns transported from Egypt and Syria, roofed with decorated teakwood (saj), and adorned the column capitals with gold leaf.

questionEn: Which Abbasid Caliph expanded the northern and western sides of Al-Masjid al-Haram between 137 and 140 AH (754–758 CE) and built the first documented minaret at Bab al-Umrah?
optionsEn: Abu Ja'far al-Mansur
Harun al-Rashid
Al-Ma'mun
Al-Mutawakkil
explanationEn: The Abbasid Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur expanded the northwestern section of Al-Masjid al-Haram (137–140 AH), paved Hijr Ismail with marble, and erected the first minaret above Bab al-Umrah.

questionEn: Which Abbasid Caliph carried out two massive expansions of Al-Masjid al-Haram in 160 AH and 164 AH (777 and 780 CE), relocating the flood channel of Wadi Ibrahim in order to place the Kaaba at the center of the mosque courtyard?
optionsEn: Al-Hadi
Muhammad al-Mahdi
Al-Amin
Al-Mu'tasim
explanationEn: During his pilgrimage in 160 AH, the Abbasid Caliph Muhammad al-Mahdi expanded the northern, eastern, and western sides, and when he saw in 164 AH that the Kaaba was not centered due to houses and the flood channel on the southern side, he ordered a second expansion that centered the Kaaba within Al-Masjid al-Haram.

questionEn: During the Abbasid caliphate of Al-Mu'tadid (281–284 AH) and Al-Muqtadir (306 AH), which two historical annexes were incorporated into the body of Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: The castle of Ajyad and the market of Dhu al-Majaz
The fortress of Qaitbay and the spring of Hunayn
The Dar al-Nadwah annex on the northern side and the Bab Ibrahim annex on the western side
The valley of Mina and the plain of Muzdalifah
explanationEn: Caliph Al-Mu'tadid annexed the historic site of Dar al-Nadwah on the northern side into the prayer halls of Al-Masjid al-Haram (284 AH), and Caliph Al-Muqtadir added the western Bab Ibrahim annex (306 AH), establishing the classical footprint that lasted for centuries.

questionEn: Which Mamluk Sultan reconstructed damaged parts of Al-Masjid al-Haram after the 802 AH fire and later built a famous madrasa and minaret alongside the mosque in 882–884 AH (1477–1479 CE)?
optionsEn: Sultan Baybars
Sultan Qalawun
Sultan Qansuh al-Ghuri
Sultan Al-Ashraf Qaitbay
explanationEn: Mamluk Sultan Al-Ashraf Qaitbay paid great attention to Al-Masjid al-Haram in the late 9th century AH (15th century CE), building the celebrated Madrasa al-Ashrafiyyah and the Qaitbay minaret.
reference: Ithaf al-Wara bi-Akhbar Umm al-Qura by Ibn Fahd 4/618

questionEn: Under which Ottoman Sultans (between 979 AH / 1571 CE and 984 AH / 1576 CE) were the flat wooden ceilings of Al-Masjid al-Haram replaced with fire-resistant multi-domed stone arcades known as Al-Riwaq al-Uthmani?
optionsEn: Sultan Selim II and completed under his son Sultan Murad III
Sultan Orhan and Sultan Murad I
Sultan Mehmed II and Sultan Bayezid II
Sultan Abdulhamid II and Sultan Mehmed V
explanationEn: When the wooden roofs of the Abbasid portico deteriorated, Sultan Selim II ordered a comprehensive reconstruction in 979 AH (1571 CE) replacing the flat wooden roof with small brick domes over marble and Shamsi stone columns; the project was completed under his son Sultan Murad III in 984 AH (1576 CE).
reference: Al-A'lam bi-A'lam Bayt Allah al-Haram by Al-Nahrawali p. 345-380

questionEn: Which renowned chief imperial architect of the Ottoman Empire designed the multi-domed Ottoman Portico (Al-Riwaq al-Uthmani) of Al-Masjid al-Haram in the 16th century CE?
optionsEn: Sedefkar Mehmed Agha
Mimar Sinan
Mimar Hayreddin
Davud Agha
explanationEn: The master Ottoman architect Mimar Sinan supervised the architectural plans for replacing the wooden roofs of Al-Masjid al-Haram with hundreds of fireproof domes resting on marble and yellow Shamsi stone columns.
reference: Al-A'lam bi-A'lam Bayt Allah al-Haram by Al-Nahrawali p. 350

questionEn: How many minarets stood at Al-Masjid al-Haram from the completion of the Ottoman renovation in the 10th century AH (16th century CE) until the First Saudi Expansion in the 20th century?
optionsEn: Two minarets
Four minarets
Seven minarets
Twelve minarets
explanationEn: Following the addition of the seventh minaret (the Suleimaniyyah minaret near Madrasa Suleimaniyyah) in the Ottoman era, Al-Masjid al-Haram was famous across the Islamic world for having seven minarets until the 20th-century Saudi expansions.
reference: Mir'at al-Haramayn by Ibrahim Rifat Pasha 1/246

questionEn: In what year did actual construction begin on the First Saudi Expansion of Al-Masjid al-Haram (ordered by King Abdulaziz and initiated under King Saud)?
explanationEn: Following King Abdulaziz's directive to expand the Two Holy Mosques, construction on the First Saudi Expansion of Al-Masjid al-Haram officially began in Rabi' al-Thani 1375 AH (November 1955 CE) under King Saud and continued in phases under King Faisal and King Khalid.
reference: Tarikh 'Imarat al-Masjid al-Haram by Husein Basalamah

questionEn: What major structural transformation did the First Saudi Expansion (begun 1375 AH / 1955 CE) accomplish regarding the Mas'a between Mount Safa and Mount Marwah?
optionsEn: It enclosed the Mas'a within a two-story roofed building directly integrated into Al-Masjid al-Haram and separated it from the city markets
It moved Mount Safa and Mount Marwah inside the circular Mataf
It left the Mas'a as an open-air dirt street shared with camel caravans
It replaced the Mas'a with an underground tunnel beneath the Kaaba
explanationEn: Before the First Saudi Expansion, the Mas'a between Safa and Marwah was an open street flanked by shops and homes; the expansion paved and enclosed it inside a two-story roofed gallery integrated directly with the eastern wall of the mosque.
reference: Imarat al-Masjid al-Haram wa al-Masjid al-Nabawi fi al-Ahd al-Sa'udi

questionEn: Why did the engineers of the First Saudi Expansion construct the large underground culvert known as Majra al-Sayl alongside Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: To channel seawater from the Red Sea at Jeddah into Makkah
To divert flash floods coming down Wadi Ibrahim away from the Mas'a and the Mataf courtyard
To serve as a subterranean horse track for pilgrims
To store olive oil for the mosque's historical lamps
explanationEn: Because Wadi Ibrahim naturally ran along the path of the Mas'a and repeatedly flooded the Mataf during heavy rains, the First Saudi Expansion diverted the floodwaters through a massive underground reinforced concrete culvert (Majra al-Sayl).
reference: Imarat al-Masjid al-Haram fi al-Ahd al-Sa'udi

questionEn: During the Second Saudi Expansion under King Fahd ibn Abdulaziz (1409–1413 AH / 1988–1992 CE), on which side of Al-Masjid al-Haram was the massive new wing and monumental gate constructed?
optionsEn: On the eastern side behind Mount Safa
Inside the valley of Mina
On the western side, between Bab al-Umrah and King Abdulaziz Gate
Directly north of Jannat al-Mu'alla
explanationEn: The King Fahd Extension added a huge three-story western wing (with a prepared rooftop prayer floor, three central domes, and escalators) between Bab al-Umrah and King Abdulaziz Gate, fronted by the monumental King Fahd Gate (Gate 79).
reference: Imarat al-Masjid al-Haram fi 'Ahd al-Malik Fahd

questionEn: With the addition of the two minarets flanking King Fahd Gate during the Second Saudi Expansion (1409–1413 AH), what became the total number of minarets of Al-Masjid al-Haram at that stage?
optionsEn: Five minarets
Seven minarets
Fifteen minarets
Nine minarets
explanationEn: The First Saudi Expansion had built seven modern minarets (three pairs of twin minarets at the three main gates plus one single minaret near Safa), and the King Fahd Extension added two more twin minarets at King Fahd Gate, bringing the total to nine.
reference: Imarat al-Masjid al-Haram fi 'Ahd al-Malik Fahd

questionEn: On which geographical side of Al-Masjid al-Haram was the massive Third Saudi Expansion—launched by King Abdullah ibn Abdulaziz in 1432 AH (2011 CE) and continued under King Salman—built?
optionsEn: On the northern and northwestern side (the Shamiyah district)
On the southern side over Jabal Thawr
On the eastern side over Jabal al-Noor
On the southwestern side in Kudai
explanationEn: The Third Saudi Expansion was constructed in the northern Shamiyah district overlooking Al-Masjid al-Haram, adding a multi-story northern prayer building, sprawling courtyards, service complexes, and the monumental King Abdullah Gate.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: What is the official gate number of the monumental King Abdullah Gate located at the center of the northern Third Saudi Expansion?
optionsEn: Gate 1
Gate 100
Gate 45
Gate 79
explanationEn: In the modern numbering system of Al-Masjid al-Haram's entrances, the grand portal of the northern Third Saudi Expansion is designated as King Abdullah Gate (Gate 100), flanked by two towering minarets.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: What is the official gate number of the monumental King Abdulaziz Gate on the southern side of Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Gate 25
Gate 62
Gate 1
Gate 100
explanationEn: King Abdulaziz Gate on the southern side of Al-Masjid al-Haram (facing the Ajyad / Clock Tower plaza) is the starting point of the mosque's perimeter numbering system and is designated as Gate 1.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: What is the official gate number of the monumental King Fahd Gate on the western side of Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Gate 11
Gate 45
Gate 100
Gate 79
explanationEn: King Fahd Gate, the main western entrance leading into the Second Saudi Expansion wing facing the Ibrahim al-Khalil / Jabal Omar plaza, is designated as Gate 79.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: Through which famous historical gate on the eastern/northeastern side of Al-Masjid al-Haram did the Prophet ﷺ commonly enter the Sacred Mosque, leading scholars to recommend entering from that direction when convenient?
optionsEn: Bab Bani Shaybah (and the adjacent Bab al-Salam)
Bab al-Wada'
Bab Ibrahim
Bab Ajyad
explanationEn: Historically, the Prophet ﷺ entered the Sacred Mosque through the gate of Banu Shaybah (Bab Bani Shaybah) facing the corner of the Black Stone; later pilgrims entering from the eastern side commonly entered through Bab al-Salam leading toward Bab Bani Shaybah.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1575 (chapter heading); Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi 8/11

questionEn: Why was 'Bab al-Salam' (the Gate of Peace) on the eastern side of Al-Masjid al-Haram near the Mas'a historically favored by pilgrims arriving in Makkah for the first time?
optionsEn: Because it was the only gate unlocked during the month of Dhul-Hijjah
Because entering through it brings the pilgrim toward the northeastern side facing the Black Stone corner, following the Prophet's ﷺ path of entry
Because entering through it exempted a pilgrim from Sa'i
Because it led directly into the interior chamber of the Kaaba
explanationEn: Classical manuals of Hajj and Umrah recommend entering via Bab al-Salam on the eastern side (when easy and uncrowded) because it aligns with the direction from which the Prophet ﷺ entered via Bab Bani Shaybah toward the Black Stone.

questionEn: Where is 'Bab al-Safa' located in relation to the layout of Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: On the far northwestern corner facing the road to Madinah
On the western wall of the King Fahd Extension
At the southern end of the Mas'a gallery directly adjacent to Mount Safa
At the northern end of the Shamiyah courtyard
explanationEn: Bab al-Safa (marked by a single minaret above it from the First Saudi Expansion) is located at the southern terminus of the Mas'a, providing direct access to Mount Safa where pilgrims begin Sa'i.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/91; Architecture of Al-Masjid al-Haram

questionEn: On which side of Al-Masjid al-Haram is the historic 'Bab al-Umrah' located, and with what prophetic event is it associated?
optionsEn: On the southeastern side facing Mina, associated with the Battle of Hunayn
On the southern side facing Yemen, associated with Abraha's army
On the eastern side behind Marwah, associated with the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
On the northwestern side facing the route to Al-Tan'eem and Madinah, associated with the Prophet's ﷺ entry for Umrah
explanationEn: Bab al-Umrah is one of the oldest and grandest gates on the northwestern side of Al-Masjid al-Haram; pilgrims returning from the Miqat of Tan'eem or arriving from the direction of Madinah historically entered through it for Umrah.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/97; Shifa' al-Gharam

questionEn: On which side of Al-Masjid al-Haram is 'Bab al-Fath' (the Gate of Conquest) located?
optionsEn: On the northern/northeastern side near Al-Marwah
On the southwestern corner facing Kudai
On the western facade of the King Fahd Extension
At the southern foot of Mount Safa
explanationEn: Bab al-Fath is one of the major historic and monumental twin-minaret gates on the northern/northeastern side of Al-Masjid al-Haram near the Marwah end of the Mas'a, commemorating the Prophet's ﷺ entry into Makkah from its upper northern side during the Conquest.
reference: Shifa' al-Gharam by Al-Fasi 1/240; Imarat al-Masjid al-Haram

questionEn: For what traditional purpose did pilgrims historically use 'Bab al-Wada'' (the Gate of Farewell) on the southwestern side of Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: For entering the mosque on the Day of Arafat
For exiting the Sacred Mosque after completing Tawaf al-Wada' (the Farewell Tawaf) when departing Makkah
For bringing sacrificial camels into the Mataf
For storing the Kiswah cloth during the year
explanationEn: Bab al-Wada' (originally known as Bab al-Hazwarah on the southwestern side toward the old road to Jeddah and Yemen) was named the Gate of Farewell because pilgrims traditionally exited through it after performing their Farewell Tawaf.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/95; Shifa' al-Gharam

questionEn: Why is 'Bab Ibrahim' on the western/southwestern side of Al-Masjid al-Haram NOT named directly after Prophet Ibrahim (AS), according to classical historians of Makkah such as Al-Azraqi and Al-Fasi?
optionsEn: It was named after Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt in the 19th century
It was named after an Abbasid general named Ibrahim ibn al-Ashtar
It was named after Ibrahim al-Khayyat, a pious tailor who lived by that gate in the early Islamic era
It was named after the city of Hebron (Al-Khalil) in Palestine
explanationEn: Makkan historians (including Al-Azraqi in Akhbar Makkah and Al-Fasi in Shifa' al-Gharam) explicitly clarify that Bab Ibrahim on the western side was named after a well-known tailor named Ibrahim al-Khayyat whose shop/house stood beside that entrance, not Prophet Ibrahim (AS).
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/96; Shifa' al-Gharam by Al-Fasi 1/250

questionEn: What special type of white marble is used to pave the open Mataf courtyard and outer plazas of Al-Masjid al-Haram so that the floor remains remarkably cool under bare feet even in scorching midday summer sun?
optionsEn: Black basalt stone quarried from Harrat Rahat
Red granite imported from Aswan in Upper Egypt
Yellow limestone quarried from the hills of Najd
White Thassos marble imported from the island of Thassos in Greece
explanationEn: The open Mataf and plazas of Al-Masjid al-Haram are paved with rare snow-white dolomitic Thassos marble from northern Greece, famous for its high crystal reflectivity and micro-pore properties that prevent heat absorption under intense desert sunlight.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: During the recent Mataf expansion project (2012–2015 CE), how was the historic Ottoman Portico (Al-Riwaq al-Uthmani) preserved while integrating it with the new multi-story Mataf rings?
optionsEn: Its original historic columns, capitals, and domes were painstakingly numbered, dismantled, restored by specialists, and reassembled in alignment with the expanded Mataf
It was permanently demolished and replaced with glass walls
It was relocated to a museum in Riyadh
It was buried intact beneath six meters of concrete
explanationEn: During the Mataf expansion, architectural conservation teams documented, numbered, and carefully restored the historical Abbasid and Ottoman columns, inscriptions, and domes of Al-Riwaq al-Uthmani, re-erecting them within the new Mataf structure.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: After the completion of the Mataf expansion project, approximately how many worshippers per hour can the multi-level Mataf structure accommodate for Tawaf?
optionsEn: Approximately 10,000 circumambulators per hour
Approximately 105,000 to 107,000 circumambulators per hour
Approximately 25,000 circumambulators per hour
Approximately 500,000 circumambulators per hour
explanationEn: The Mataf modernization and expansion increased total hourly Tawaf capacity across all floors from roughly 48,000 pilgrims per hour to approximately 107,000 pilgrims per hour.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: How many minarets stand on the main structure of Al-Masjid al-Haram following the addition of the two minarets of King Abdullah Gate and the two northern corner minarets in the Third Saudi Expansion?
optionsEn: 7 minarets
9 minarets
13 minarets
20 minarets
explanationEn: Adding the two minarets flanking King Abdullah Gate (Gate 100) and the two northern corner minarets of the Third Saudi Expansion to the previous 9 minarets brought the total count of Al-Masjid al-Haram's minarets to 13.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: Approximately how tall are the modern twin minarets of Al-Masjid al-Haram (such as those at King Abdulaziz, Bab al-Umrah, Bab al-Fath, and King Fahd Gates) from their base to the top of the crescent?
optionsEn: Approximately 25 meters tall
Approximately 250 meters tall
Approximately 400 meters tall
Approximately 89 to 98 meters tall
explanationEn: The minarets built during the First and Second Saudi Expansions stand roughly 89 to 92 meters high (with the newer Third Expansion minarets reaching around 98 to 135 meters), each topped by a gilded bronze crescent (hilal).
reference: Imarat al-Masjid al-Haram fi al-Ahd al-Sa'udi

questionEn: What architectural elements characterize the design of the modern Saudi-era minarets of Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: A square stone base transitioning into an octagonal shaft, two mu'adhdhin balconies with muqarnas corbels, and a bulbous finial crowned by a gold-plated crescent
A circular spiral ramp on the exterior modeled on the Great Mosque of Samarra
A flat-topped mud-brick pyramid modeled on West African mosques
A single cylindrical steel tower with no balconies
explanationEn: The minarets harmonize classical Hijazi/Mamluk heritage with modern engineering: a square base, an octagonal main shaft, two ornate balconies supported by muqarnas stalactite vaulting, and a slender turret topped by a gilded crescent spire.
reference: Imarat al-Masjid al-Haram fi al-Ahd al-Sa'udi

questionEn: How is the chilled-water air conditioning system of Al-Masjid al-Haram engineered so that massive noisy compressor machinery does not disturb worshippers inside the mosque?
optionsEn: Individual window air-conditioning units are mounted on every outer window of the portico
Central cooling plants located in Shamiyah and Ajyad/Kudai chill water and pump it through underground insulated tunnels to air-handling units inside the mosque
Blocks of ice are trucked into the Mataf every morning before Fajr
Cold air is piped directly from the summit of Mount Hira
explanationEn: To keep the Sacred Mosque serene and vibration-free, two massive district cooling stations (including the Shamiyah plant, one of the largest in the world) chill water and circulate it via subterranean pipes to heat exchangers across the mosque.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: How was the capacity of the Mas'a (between Safa and Marwah) expanded in the late 2000s to relieve severe congestion during peak Hajj and Ramadan seasons?
optionsEn: By digging five parallel tunnels connecting Safa to Jabal Thawr
By moving the starting point of Sa'i to Bab al-Umrah
By widening the Mas'a eastward and increasing its levels to four stories (plus basement and rooftop tracks), with dedicated lanes for wheelchairs and electric carts
By shortening the distance between Safa and Marwah to 100 meters
explanationEn: Without altering the sacred rock boundaries of Safa and Marwah, the Mas'a building was widened on the eastern side and raised to multiple levels (basement, ground, first, second, mezzanine for carts, and roof), more than doubling hourly Sa'i capacity to over 118,000 pilgrims per hour.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: What special facility is provided on the mezzanine levels and upper rings of the Mataf and Mas'a for elderly pilgrims and persons with disabilities?
optionsEn: Moving conveyor belts that carry standing pilgrims automatically
Cable cars suspended from the ceiling domes
Horse-drawn carriages operating on the roof
Dedicated smooth tracks and electric golf-style carts (and manual wheelchair lanes) separated from pedestrian crowds
explanationEn: Al-Masjid al-Haram features dedicated, barrier-free mezzanine rings and tracks where pilgrims with mobility impairments can safely perform Tawaf and Sa'i using manual wheelchairs or regulated electric carts without colliding with foot traffic.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: When and by whom was the historic library of the Grand Mosque officially named 'Maktabat al-Haram al-Makki al-Sharif' (Library of the Sacred Mosque in Makkah)?
optionsEn: In 1357 AH (1938 CE) by King Abdulaziz ibn Abd al-Rahman Al Saud
In 160 AH (777 CE) by Caliph Harun al-Rashid
In 984 AH (1576 CE) by Sultan Selim II
In 1432 AH (2011 CE) by King Abdullah
explanationEn: While book collections in the Haram trace their roots back to the Abbasid Caliph Al-Mahdi (160 AH), King Abdulaziz consolidated the endowments in 1357 AH (1938 CE) and officially named it Maktabat al-Haram al-Makki al-Sharif.
reference: Maktabat al-Haram al-Makki al-Sharif Official History

questionEn: What priceless cultural and religious treasures are preserved in Maktabat al-Haram al-Makki al-Sharif (the Library of Al-Masjid al-Haram)?
optionsEn: Ancient Greek statues and Roman military armor
Thousands of rare Islamic manuscripts, early Qur'anic folios, historical waqf endowments, and audio archives of Haram sermons and recitations
Original treaties signed between the Byzantines and Persians
The royal crowns of the Mamluk Sultans of Cairo
explanationEn: Maktabat al-Haram al-Makki al-Sharif houses over 7,000 original rare Arabic and Islamic manuscripts (alongside tens of thousands of digital/microfilm copies), rare printed books, and complete audio archives of the Imams and Khutbahs of Al-Masjid al-Haram.
reference: Maktabat al-Haram al-Makki al-Sharif Official History

questionEn: What historic landmark site in the eastern plaza of Al-Masjid al-Haram (in Suq al-Layl / Shi'b Ali) is occupied by the Makkah Library building near the Mas'a?
optionsEn: The site of the Cave of Thawr
The site where the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah was signed
The traditionally transmitted site of the house where Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born
The site of the well of Badr
explanationEn: In the eastern plaza opposite Mount Safa/Marwah (in Shi'b Banu Hashim / Suq al-Layl) stands the Makkah Library building erected in 1370 AH (1951 CE) by Sheikh Abbas Qattan with King Abdulaziz's approval on the traditionally transmitted birthplace of the Prophet ﷺ.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi; Tarikh Makkah by Ahmad al-Sibai

questionEn: Where is the main Imam's microphone and prayer station normally positioned during the daily congregational prayers in Al-Masjid al-Haram today?
optionsEn: Inside the semi-circular Hijr Ismail facing north
On top of the roof of the Kaaba itself
Outside King Abdullah Gate in the northern courtyard
On the eastern side of the Kaaba facing the Multazam/door side and Maqam Ibrahim (or in the southern/eastern portico during peak Mataf crowding)
explanationEn: The Imam of Al-Masjid al-Haram typically leads the obligatory prayers facing the eastern side of the Kaaba between the Black Stone corner, the Kaaba door, and Maqam Ibrahim, supported by a redundant multi-microphone acoustic system.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: How does the modern acoustic sound system of Al-Masjid al-Haram ensure that worshippers in distant halls and outer courtyards hear the Imam's recitation clearly without echo distortion?
optionsEn: Through thousands of directional speakers synchronized with digital time-delay processing so sound waves arrive in phase with the live voice
By having a chain of 500 mu'adhdhins shout each verse one after another across the courtyards
By broadcasting the prayer only over FM radio headsets
By closing all outer doors during the recitation of Surah Al-Fatihah
explanationEn: Al-Masjid al-Haram utilizes one of the world's largest precision audio networks—featuring over 7,000 speakers, dual-redundant microphones, and digital acoustic delay zones—so worshippers inside the halls and across the plazas hear crisp, echo-free recitation.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: How are the outer marble courtyards surrounding Al-Masjid al-Haram cooled for worshippers praying outside during hot summer afternoons?
optionsEn: By flooding the courtyards ankle-deep with water during prayer times
Through heat-reflective Thassos marble paving combined with column-mounted water misting fans (radhadh al-ma') and shading canopies
By covering the floors with black rubber mats
By spraying liquid nitrogen from the minarets
explanationEn: In addition to the cool Thassos marble floors and shading umbrellas in the northern courtyard, hundreds of high-pressure water misting fans mounted on light poles atomize purified water to reduce ambient courtyard temperatures by several degrees Celsius.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: In the geography of Hajj and Umrah jurisprudence, what are the three concentric territorial zones surrounding the Kaaba?
optionsEn: Al-Mataf, Al-Mas'a, and Al-Marwah
Mina, Muzdalifah, and Jamarat
Al-Haram (the Sacred Sanctuary), Al-Hill (the intermediate region between the Haram border and the Miqats), and Al-Afaq (the lands beyond the Miqats)
Najd, Tihamah, and Hijaz
explanationEn: Islamic jurists divide the earth in relation to Makkah into three zones: (1) Al-Haram (inside the sanctuary boundary markers), (2) Al-Hill (between the Haram boundaries and the spatial Miqats), and (3) Al-Afaq (all regions outside the ring of the five spatial Miqats).
reference: Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 3/245; Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi 7/148

questionEn: What does the term 'Al-Hill' mean in the context of the sacred geography of Makkah?
optionsEn: The interior courtyard directly beneath the roof of Al-Masjid al-Haram
The elevated plateau of Mount Hira
The underground channel of Ain Zubaydah
The land outside the sacred Haram boundaries where ordinary permissible acts (like hunting when not in Ihram) are lawful, specifically between the Haram border and the Miqats
explanationEn: Al-Hill literally means 'the place where things are lawful (halal),' contrasting with Al-Haram ('the Sanctuary where certain acts are forbidden'). In fiqh, Al-Hill especially refers to the belt surrounding the Haram up to the Miqats (such as Tan'eem, Ji'ranah, Hudaybiyyah, Arafat, and Jeddah).

questionEn: Who is referred to as an 'Afaqi' in the jurisprudence of Hajj and Umrah?
optionsEn: A person coming from beyond the five spatial Miqats (from Al-Afaq, the distant horizons)
A person who lives permanently adjacent to Al-Masjid al-Haram
A custodian who holds the key to the Kaaba door
A pilgrim who performs Tawaf only at night
explanationEn: An Afaqi is anyone residing outside the boundary circle of the five spatial Miqats; when traveling to Makkah intending Hajj or Umrah, an Afaqi is obligated to enter Ihram at or before passing their respective Miqat.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1524; Radd al-Muhtar by Ibn Abidin 2/475

questionEn: According to authentic prophetic traditions and Makkan histories, who originally set up the boundary markers (A'lam al-Haram / Ansab al-Haram) of Makkah's Sacred Sanctuary, and under whose guidance?
optionsEn: King Solomon (AS) with the assistance of the Jinn
Prophet Ibrahim (AS) under the direct guidance of the Angel Jibril (AS)
Alexander the Great during his journey to the East
The Abbasid Caliph Harun al-Rashid in the second century AH
explanationEn: Historical and hadith sources record that Angel Jibril (AS) showed Prophet Ibrahim (AS) the exact divinely ordained boundaries of the Haram, and Ibrahim (AS) erected the first stone boundary markers (Ansab al-Haram).
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/129; Al-Isabah by Ibn Hajar 1/490

questionEn: In the Year of the Conquest of Makkah (8 AH), which Companion did the Prophet ﷺ commission to renew and restore the boundary stones (A'lam al-Haram) of Makkah?
optionsEn: Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA)
Mu'adh ibn Jabal (RA)
