Tamim ibn Asad al-Khuza'i (RA)
Zayd ibn Thabit (RA)
explanationEn: In the Year of the Conquest (8 AH), the Prophet ﷺ appointed Tamim ibn Asad al-Khuza'i (RA) to renew the boundary markers (Ansab al-Haram) of Makkah's Sacred Sanctuary.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/130; Usd al-Ghabah 1/450; Al-Isabah 1/490

questionEn: Why do the distances from the Kaaba to the Haram boundary markers vary significantly depending on the direction (ranging from about 7.5 km in the north to 22 km in the west and northeast)?
optionsEn: Because medieval rulers moved the western stones outward every century
Because the boundaries simply follow the shoreline of the Red Sea
Because only areas with date-palm oases were included
Because the Haram boundaries are divinely revealed (tawqifiyyah) as shown by Jibril (AS) to Ibrahim (AS), rather than a uniform geometric circle
explanationEn: The boundaries of the Haram are tawqifiyyah (fixed by divine revelation through Angel Jibril to Ibrahim AS and confirmed by Prophet Muhammad ﷺ), following specific valleys and mountain passes rather than an equidistant radius.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/129; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 3/350

questionEn: Which Haram boundary point is the closest point of Al-Hill to the Kaaba, located approximately 7.5 km north of Al-Masjid al-Haram along the road to Madinah?
optionsEn: Al-Tan'eem (the site of Masjid Aishah)
Al-Ji'ranah
Al-Hudaybiyyah (Al-Shumaysi)
Adat Libn
explanationEn: Al-Tan'eem, located roughly 7.5 km north of the Kaaba, is the closest boundary point between Al-Haram and Al-Hill, which is why residents of Makkah and pilgrims inside Makkah most commonly go there to enter Ihram for a new Umrah.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/131; Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi 7/180

questionEn: Why is the famous mosque at the Haram boundary of Al-Tan'eem known as 'Masjid Aishah'?
optionsEn: Because Aishah (RA) was born in the village of Al-Tan'eem before the Hijrah
Because the Prophet ﷺ instructed Aishah's brother Abd al-Rahman (RA) to take her to Al-Tan'eem so she could enter Ihram for Umrah from there after the Farewell Hajj
Because Aishah (RA) lived there permanently after the passing of the Prophet ﷺ
Because Aishah (RA) led the Muslim army from that mosque during the Conquest of Makkah
explanationEn: During the Farewell Pilgrimage (10 AH), Aishah (RA) wished to perform an independent Umrah after completing the rites of Hajj; the Prophet ﷺ told her brother Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr (RA) to take her out of the Haram to Al-Tan'eem so she could enter Ihram for Umrah.

questionEn: Which Haram boundary point lies approximately 22 km northeast of Al-Masjid al-Haram, from which the Prophet ﷺ himself entered Ihram for Umrah in the night of Dhul-Qa'dah 8 AH after dividing the spoils of Hunayn?
optionsEn: Al-Tan'eem
Adat Libn
Al-Ji'ranah
Yalamlam
explanationEn: After the Battle of Hunayn and the Siege of Ta'if in 8 AH, the Prophet ﷺ stayed at Al-Ji'ranah (just outside the northeastern Haram boundary, ~22 km from the Kaaba), distributed the war spoils, and entered Ihram for Umrah from there by night.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 4358; Sahih Muslim 1180; Zad al-Ma'ad 3/425

questionEn: Because the Prophet ﷺ entered Ihram from Al-Ji'ranah, what did jurists of the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools conclude regarding the best place in Al-Hill for a person in Makkah to enter Ihram for Umrah?
optionsEn: Al-Tan'eem is the only valid place and entering Ihram at Al-Ji'ranah is invalid
Arafat is the only valid place in Al-Hill for Umrah
Jeddah is superior to both Al-Ji'ranah and Al-Tan'eem
Al-Ji'ranah is the most virtuous place in Al-Hill for Umrah Ihram, followed by Al-Tan'eem, and then Al-Hudaybiyyah
explanationEn: Many classical jurists (such as in the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools) stated that the most virtuous boundary point in Al-Hill from which to initiate Umrah is Al-Ji'ranah (because the Prophet ﷺ personally entered Ihram from there), followed by Al-Tan'eem (which he commanded for Aishah RA), and then Al-Hudaybiyyah.
reference: Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi 7/180; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 3/251

questionEn: Which historical site on the western boundary of the Haram (approximately 22 km west of the Kaaba along the old road to Jeddah) is known today as Al-Shumaysi?
optionsEn: Al-Hudaybiyyah
Dhat Irq
Qarn al-Manazil
Wadi Nakhlah
explanationEn: Al-Hudaybiyyah, famous for the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah and Bay'at al-Ridwan in 6 AH, is known in modern times as Al-Shumaysi and sits on the western boundary of the Haram (~22 km from the Kaaba), part of it in Al-Hill and part in Al-Haram.

questionEn: Approximately how far from the Kaaba is the southern Haram boundary marker at Adat Libn (Al-Akishiyyah) on the road toward Yemen?
optionsEn: Approximately 2 km south of the Kaaba
Approximately 16 km south of the Kaaba
Approximately 75 km south of the Kaaba
Approximately 450 km south of the Kaaba
explanationEn: On the southern Yemen road via Adat Libn (in the Al-Akishiyyah / Al-Kakiyyah direction), the Haram boundary marker stands approximately 16 km from the Kaaba.

questionEn: Approximately how far from the Kaaba is the Haram boundary marker in the direction of Wadi Nakhlah (the old Iraq road to the northeast)?
optionsEn: Approximately 1 km northeast of the Kaaba
Approximately 95 km northeast of the Kaaba
Approximately 13 to 14 km northeast of the Kaaba
Approximately 200 km northeast of the Kaaba
explanationEn: At the pass of al-Maqta' in the direction of Wadi Nakhlah to the northeast, the boundary of the Haram lies approximately 13 to 14 km from the Kaaba.

questionEn: Where does a resident of Makkah (or a pilgrim already staying inside Makkah during Tamattu') enter Ihram when intending to perform Hajj on the 8th of Dhul-Hijjah?
optionsEn: They must travel 450 km north to Dhul-Hulayfah (Abyar Ali)
They must go outside the Haram to Al-Tan'eem just as for Umrah
They must wait until they reach the plain of Arafat on the 9th of Dhul-Hijjah
From inside Makkah itself (from their own home or lodging inside the Haram), without going out to Al-Tan'eem or any Miqat
explanationEn: In the hadith of Ibn Abbas (RA) on the Miqats, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'And whoever is closer than that, then from where he starts, until even the people of Makkah enter Ihram [for Hajj] from Makkah.'

questionEn: Why must someone currently inside Makkah's Haram go outside the Haram boundary into Al-Hill (such as Al-Tan'eem or Al-Ji'ranah) to enter Ihram for an Umrah, whereas for Hajj they enter Ihram from inside Makkah?
optionsEn: So that every pilgrimage rite combines both Al-Hill (outside the Haram) and Al-Haram; Hajj already includes standing at Arafat in Al-Hill, whereas Umrah's rites (Tawaf and Sa'i) are entirely inside the Haram
Because the gates of Al-Masjid al-Haram are locked to anyone wearing Ihram inside the city
Because Umrah is only valid if started at night outside the city walls
Because Talbiyah cannot be recited inside a house in Makkah
explanationEn: Scholars explain that in Hajj, a pilgrim who enters Ihram inside Makkah still travels out to Arafat (which is in Al-Hill), thus combining Al-Hill and Al-Haram; in Umrah, since Tawaf and Sa'i are both inside the Haram, one goes out to Al-Hill to enter Ihram so the Umrah likewise combines Al-Hill and Al-Haram.
reference: Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi 7/179; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 3/250

questionEn: What is the exact status of the three major Hajj sites—Mina, Muzdalifah, and Arafat—with respect to the sacred boundaries of Makkah's Haram (Hudud al-Haram)?
optionsEn: All three—Mina, Muzdalifah, and Arafat—are completely inside the Haram boundaries
Mina and Muzdalifah are both inside the Haram boundaries, whereas Arafat is outside the Haram boundaries in Al-Hill
All three are outside the Haram boundaries in Al-Hill
Arafat is inside the Haram, whereas Mina and Muzdalifah are outside the Haram
explanationEn: Mina and Muzdalifah lie within the sacred sanctuary (Al-Haram)—which is why Muzdalifah holds the title Al-Mash'ar al-Haram—whereas the plain of Arafat lies just outside the eastern Haram boundary in Al-Hill.
reference: Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 3/350; Zad al-Ma'ad 2/235

questionEn: Which valley separates the eastern boundary of the Haram from the valid standing area of Arafat, and what did the Prophet ﷺ warn pilgrims regarding this valley on the Day of Arafat?
optionsEn: Wadi Muhassir; the Prophet ﷺ told pilgrims to spend the entire afternoon there
Wadi Fatima; the Prophet ﷺ declared it the center of Arafat
Wadi 'Uranah; the Prophet ﷺ instructed pilgrims: 'All of Arafat is a standing place, and move away from the valley of 'Uranah'
Wadi Badr; the Prophet ﷺ told pilgrims to collect pebbles there
explanationEn: Wadi 'Uranah runs along the western edge of Arafat between the Haram boundary and Arafat. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'All of Arafat is a place of standing (mawqif), and keep away from the belly of 'Uranah (warfa'u 'an batn 'Uranah).'
reference: Sunan Abi Dawud 1937; Sunan Ibn Majah 3012; Musnad Ahmad 16750 (Sahih)

questionEn: What important geographical detail should pilgrims praying Dhuhr and Asr inside Masjid Namirah on the Day of Arafat know about the layout of that mosque?
optionsEn: The entire Masjid Namirah is located inside Mina, 15 km away from Arafat
Masjid Namirah is built on top of the summit of Jabal al-Rahmah
Masjid Namirah is located at the Miqat of Qarn al-Manazil
The front (western) part of Masjid Namirah lies inside Wadi 'Uranah outside Arafat, while the rear (eastern) section of the mosque lies inside the boundary of Arafat
explanationEn: Clear signboards inside Masjid Namirah mark the boundary line: the western/front portion of the expanded mosque falls within Wadi 'Uranah (outside Arafat), while the eastern/rear portion lies within the valid plain of Arafat.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/131; Fatawa al-Lajnah al-Da'imah 11/208

questionEn: In the foundational hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA) in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, how many spatial Miqats (Mawaqit Makaniyyah) were designated for pilgrims coming from the horizons toward Makkah?
optionsEn: Five spatial Miqats (four explicitly named in Ibn Abbas's report plus Dhat 'Irq in the reports of Aishah, Jabir, and Umar RA)
Two spatial Miqats (one in the north and one in the south)
Seven spatial Miqats matching the seven minarets
Twelve spatial Miqats matching the twelve lunar months
explanationEn: Ibn Abbas (RA) narrated the four Miqats of Dhul-Hulayfah, Al-Juhfah, Qarn al-Manazil, and Yalamlam, while Aishah (RA), Jabir (RA), and Umar (RA) transmitted the fifth Miqat, Dhat 'Irq, for the people of Iraq, making five spatial Miqats agreed upon by consensus.

questionEn: Which spatial Miqat did the Prophet ﷺ designate for the people of Madinah, and what is its modern name?
optionsEn: Qarn al-Manazil, known today as Al-Sayl al-Kabir
Dhul-Hulayfah, known today as Abyar Ali
Yalamlam, known today as Al-Sa'diyyah
Al-Juhfah, known today as Rabigh
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ designated Dhul-Hulayfah (called Abyar Ali or Masjid al-Shajarah today), located just southwest of Madinah, as the Miqat for the people of Madinah and all who pass by it.

questionEn: Which of the five spatial Miqats is the farthest in distance from Makkah (located approximately 420–450 km north of Makkah and about 10 km from Al-Masjid al-Nabawi)?
optionsEn: Qarn al-Manazil (Al-Sayl al-Kabir)
Dhat 'Irq
Dhul-Hulayfah (Abyar Ali)
Yalamlam (Al-Sa'diyyah)
explanationEn: Dhul-Hulayfah (Abyar Ali) lies right outside Madinah—roughly 420 to 450 km north of Makkah—making it by far the most distant of the five spatial Miqats from the Kaaba, giving pilgrims from Madinah the longest journey in Ihram.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1524; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 3/246

questionEn: Why is the mosque at the Miqat of Dhul-Hulayfah also historically called 'Masjid al-Shajarah' (the Mosque of the Tree)?
optionsEn: Because the treaty of Bay'at al-Ridwan was signed at Dhul-Hulayfah
Because it was the only place in the Hijaz with palm trees
Because its roof was constructed from cedar wood from Lebanon
Because the Prophet ﷺ used to alight, pray, and enter Ihram under a Samurah (acacia) tree at that spot in Dhul-Hulayfah
explanationEn: Abdullah ibn Umar (RA) narrated that the Prophet ﷺ used to pray at the site of the Samurah tree in Dhul-Hulayfah when setting out for Hajj or Umrah, so the mosque built over that spot became known as Masjid al-Shajarah.

questionEn: Which spatial Miqat did the Prophet ﷺ appoint for the people of Al-Sham (the Levant/Syria), and by extension those coming from Egypt and North Africa along the northwestern route?
optionsEn: Al-Juhfah (near modern Rabigh)
Yalamlam (Al-Sa'diyyah)
Qarn al-Manazil (Al-Sayl al-Kabir)
Dhat 'Irq
explanationEn: In the hadith of Ibn Abbas (RA), the Prophet ﷺ appointed Al-Juhfah—located in the northwest near the Red Sea coast, roughly 180–204 km from Makkah—as the Miqat for the people of Al-Sham (and those coming via Egypt and North Africa).

questionEn: Why do pilgrims traveling from the northwest (Al-Sham, Egypt, and coastal highways) since the classical era commonly enter Ihram at the town of Rabigh?
optionsEn: Because Rabigh is closer to the Kaaba than Al-Tan'eem
Because the historical village of Al-Juhfah became deserted and ruined, and Rabigh lies just before Al-Juhfah on the route to Makkah
Because Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab abolished Al-Juhfah
Because Rabigh lies inside the sacred Haram boundary
explanationEn: When the village of Al-Juhfah fell into ruin after epidemics and floods in the medieval era, pilgrims began entering Ihram at the coastal town of Rabigh located slightly north/before Al-Juhfah as a precaution, while the restored mosque at Al-Juhfah itself also remains accessible today.
reference: Radd al-Muhtar by Ibn Abidin 2/476; Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi 7/152

questionEn: Which spatial Miqat did the Prophet ﷺ designate for the people of Najd (central Arabia), and what is its contemporary name?
optionsEn: Dhul-Hulayfah, known today as Abyar Ali
Yalamlam, known today as Al-Sa'diyyah
Qarn al-Manazil, known today as Al-Sayl al-Kabir
Al-Juhfah, known today as Rabigh
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ designated Qarn al-Manazil (also called Qarn al-Tha'alib in some hadiths, and known today as Al-Sayl al-Kabir, located ~75–80 km east of Makkah) as the Miqat for the people of Najd.

questionEn: What is 'Wadi Muhram' (Al-Hada) on the upper mountain highway connecting Ta'if to Makkah in relation to the five spatial Miqats?
optionsEn: It is the southern Miqat for pilgrims coming from Aden in Yemen
It is the valley between Muzdalifah and Mina where Abraha's elephant stopped
It is the northern Haram boundary marker next to Al-Tan'eem
It is the high-altitude alignment (muhadhah) of the Miqat of Qarn al-Manazil for pilgrims descending via the Ta'if–Al-Hada mountain road
explanationEn: Qarn al-Manazil encompasses a broad valley corridor: its lower northern branch on the Riyadh–Makkah highway is Al-Sayl al-Kabir, while its upper southern alignment on the Ta'if–Al-Hada mountain road is Wadi Muhram (~75 km east of Makkah).
reference: Majmu' Fatawa Ibn Baz 16/71; Mu'jam Ma'alim al-Hijaz

questionEn: Which spatial Miqat did the Prophet ﷺ designate for the people of Yemen and all pilgrims arriving from the south, and what is its contemporary name?
optionsEn: Yalamlam, known today as Al-Sa'diyyah
Dhat 'Irq, known today as Al-Daribah
Dhul-Hulayfah, known today as Abyar Ali
Qarn al-Manazil, known today as Al-Sayl al-Kabir
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ appointed Yalamlam—a valley on the southern Tihamah coastal route roughly 90–100 km south of Makkah, where the modern Miqat mosque stands at Al-Sa'diyyah—for the people of Yemen and everyone coming from the south.

questionEn: Which spatial Miqat is designated for the people of Iraq and those traveling overland from the northeast?
optionsEn: Al-Juhfah
Dhat 'Irq
Dhul-Hulayfah
Yalamlam
explanationEn: Dhat 'Irq (located roughly 94 km northeast of Makkah near Al-Daribah) is the Miqat for the people of Iraq and the eastern lands, reported from the Prophet ﷺ by Aishah and Jabir (RA) and independently confirmed by Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA).
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1531; Sahih Muslim 1183; Sunan Abi Dawud 1739

questionEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari (1531), when the people of Kufa and Basra told Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) that Qarn al-Manazil was out of their way across a gulf/mountain ridge, how did Umar instruct them to determine their Miqat at Dhat 'Irq?
optionsEn: He told them they were exempted from wearing Ihram until they saw the Kaaba
He ordered them to travel through Yemen and enter Ihram at Yalamlam
He told them: 'Look for a place on your route that is directly parallel/aligned (hadhwa) with Qarn al-Manazil,' and he fixed Dhat 'Irq for them
He told them to enter Ihram inside their homes in Baghdad before setting out
explanationEn: Ibn Umar (RA) narrated that when the two Iraqi garrisons (Basra and Kufa) were conquered, their delegation told Umar (RA) that Qarn was off their direct path. Umar told them: 'Find a spot on your road parallel (hadhwa) to Qarn,' and fixed Dhat 'Irq for them—which perfectly matched the Prophet's ﷺ earlier designation.

questionEn: What foundational legal principle did Umar ibn al-Khattab's (RA) statement 'Look for a place on your route parallel (hadhwa) to Qarn' establish for pilgrims traveling by routes—including modern air or sea routes—that do not pass directly through a Miqat town?
optionsEn: The principle that air travelers do not need to wear Ihram until landing in Jeddah
The principle that sea travelers can only perform Hajj, never Umrah
The principle that only people traveling on camels must observe the Miqats
The principle of Muhadhah (entering Ihram when coming into parallel alignment with the nearest spatial Miqat along one's path)
explanationEn: Classical and contemporary jurists base the rule of 'Muhadhah al-Miqat' (entering Ihram when passing parallel to the nearest Miqat by land, sea, or air) directly on Umar ibn al-Khattab's (RA) ruling in Sahih al-Bukhari 1531.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1531; Fath al-Bari by Ibn Hajar 3/389; Al-Mughni 3/249

questionEn: In the hadith of Ibn Abbas (RA), what rule did the Prophet ﷺ establish by saying: 'Hunna lahunna wa-liman ata 'alayhinna min ghayri ahlihinna mimman arada al-hajja wal-'umrah'?
optionsEn: Each Miqat is for its designated region's people AND for anyone from another region who passes by that Miqat while intending Hajj or Umrah
A pilgrim from Syria is forbidden from ever passing through Madinah's Miqat
Only citizens born in Madinah may enter Ihram at Dhul-Hulayfah
A pilgrim must return to their country of birth to enter Ihram
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ stated: 'These [Miqats] are for them (their people), and for whoever comes upon them from other than their people among those who intend Hajj and Umrah.' For example, an Iraqi or Egyptian who visits Madinah first and then travels to Makkah enters Ihram at Dhul-Hulayfah (Abyar Ali).

questionEn: If an Afaqi pilgrim from Egypt, Pakistan, or Indonesia travels to Madinah first to visit Al-Masjid al-Nabawi and then sets out from Madinah to Makkah for Umrah or Hajj, from which Miqat must they enter Ihram?
optionsEn: They must fly back to Al-Juhfah or Yalamlam first
From Dhul-Hulayfah (Abyar Ali), the Miqat of Madinah through which they pass
They may travel without Ihram to Jeddah and enter Ihram at the airport
They may travel without Ihram all the way to Al-Tan'eem in Makkah
explanationEn: Because they are traveling from Madinah to Makkah and passing directly by Dhul-Hulayfah (Abyar Ali), the prophetic rule 'and for whoever comes upon them from other than their people' requires them to enter Ihram at Dhul-Hulayfah.

questionEn: According to the hadith of Ibn Abbas (RA) ('Wa man kana duna dhalika fa-min haythu ansha'a'), where does a person who permanently resides in Al-Hill (closer to Makkah than the five spatial Miqats, such as a resident of Jeddah or Bahrah) enter Ihram for Hajj or Umrah?
optionsEn: They must travel backward away from Makkah to Rabigh or Al-Sayl al-Kabir
They must enter Makkah first and then go to Al-Tan'eem
From their own place of residence (min ahlihi / min haythu ansha'a) in Jeddah or Bahrah
They are exempted from wearing Ihram garments altogether
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'And whoever lives closer than that (duna dhalika, i.e., inside the Miqat circle in Al-Hill), then his place of entering Ihram is from where he initiates (min haythu ansha'a / min ahlihi).' Thus residents of Jeddah enter Ihram from their homes in Jeddah.

questionEn: Why is an international pilgrim flying from abroad (an Afaqi) intending Umrah or Hajj NOT permitted to wait until landing at King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah to enter Ihram?
optionsEn: Because Jeddah is inside the sacred Haram boundaries where hunting is forbidden
Because airplanes are not allowed to land while passengers are in Ihram
Because Jeddah is farther from Makkah than Dhul-Hulayfah
Because Jeddah lies inside the Miqat ring (approx. 75–80 km west of Makkah), so an Afaqi flying into Jeddah has already crossed the aerial alignment of their spatial Miqat before landing
explanationEn: Jeddah is a city in Al-Hill located closer to Makkah than the five spatial Miqats; therefore, only residents of Jeddah (or those who formed the intention for Umrah after arriving in Jeddah for unrelated work) enter Ihram from Jeddah, whereas Afaqis flying in for Umrah/Hajj must enter Ihram in the air when aligned with the Miqat (or before boarding).
reference: Qararat Majma' al-Fiqh al-Islami; Fatawa al-Lajnah al-Da'imah 11/130

questionEn: What is the ruling if a pilgrim intending Hajj or Umrah passes their spatial Miqat without entering Ihram?
optionsEn: They must return to the Miqat to enter Ihram; if they do not return and instead enter Ihram after passing the Miqat, their pilgrimage is valid but they must offer an expiatory sacrifice (dam) in Makkah
Their Hajj or Umrah is permanently invalid and can never be completed
There is no consequence at all because entering Ihram at the Miqat is merely optional
They only need to give a handful of dates in charity in their hometown
explanationEn: Entering Ihram from the Miqat is an obligatory duty (wajib) of Hajj and Umrah. One who crosses the Miqat without Ihram while intending Hajj/Umrah must return to the Miqat and enter Ihram there (whereupon no dam is due); if they enter Ihram past the Miqat without returning, they owe a dam (a sheep sacrificed in Makkah for the poor of the Haram).
reference: Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 3/254; Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi 7/168

questionEn: According to the majority of jurists (Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali), what is the ruling on a Muslim traveling to Makkah for trade, work, or visiting relatives without intending Hajj or Umrah when passing the Miqat?
optionsEn: They are punished with a mandatory sacrifice of seven camels
It is permissible for them to pass the Miqat and enter Makkah without Ihram, though entering in Ihram for Umrah is recommended
They are prohibited from praying inside Al-Masjid al-Haram during their stay
They must fast for thirty days before crossing the Haram boundary
explanationEn: In the hadith of Ibn Abbas (RA), the Prophet ﷺ specifically qualified the obligation of the Miqat with the words 'among those who intend Hajj and Umrah (mimman arada al-hajja wal-'umrah),' and the Prophet ﷺ himself entered Makkah at the Conquest wearing a helmet on his head without being in Ihram.

questionEn: In addition to the five spatial Miqats (Mawaqit Makaniyyah), what are the temporal Miqats (Al-Mawaqit al-Zamaniyyah)—the 'well-known months' (ashhurun ma'lumat) of Hajj mentioned in Surah Al-Baqarah 2:197?
optionsEn: Rajab, Sha'ban, and Ramadan
Muharram, Safar, and Rabi' al-Awwal
Shawwal, Dhul-Qa'dah, and the first ten days (or the whole month) of Dhul-Hijjah
Only the last three days of Dhul-Hijjah
explanationEn: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:197 states: 'Al-Hajju ashhurun ma'lumat (Hajj is in the well-known months),' which Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, and the Companions explained as Shawwal, Dhul-Qa'dah, and the ten days (or the entire month) of Dhul-Hijjah.
reference: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:197; Sahih al-Bukhari (mu'allaq before 1560); Al-Mughni 3/241

questionEn: How does the temporal Miqat (time) of Umrah differ from the specific months of Hajj?
optionsEn: Umrah is only valid during the month of Rajab
Umrah is prohibited during the months of Shawwal and Dhul-Qa'dah
Umrah can only be performed once every five years
Umrah has no restricted season and is valid throughout all months of the lunar year, with Ramadan being the most virtuous time
explanationEn: Unlike Hajj which is restricted to the months of Hajj, Umrah is permissible at any time of the year; the Prophet ﷺ performed all four of his Umrahs in Dhul-Qa'dah, and stated that an Umrah in Ramadan equals the reward of a Hajj with him.

questionEn: Why did the Prophet ﷺ perform all four of his Umrahs during the sacred month of Dhul-Qa'dah, as noted by Anas ibn Malik (RA) and explained by scholars like Ibn al-Qayyim?
optionsEn: To demonstrate the permissibility of Umrah during the months of Hajj and refute the pre-Islamic Jahiliyyah superstition that Umrah in the months of Hajj was the worst wickedness on earth
Because the gates of Makkah were snowed in during all other months
Because the well of Zamzam only flowed during Dhul-Qa'dah
Because the Quraysh banned travel in Ramadan
explanationEn: In pre-Islamic Jahiliyyah, the pagans considered performing Umrah during the months of Hajj (such as Dhul-Qa'dah) 'min afjar al-fujur' (the most wicked of sins). By performing all four of his Umrahs in Dhul-Qa'dah, the Prophet ﷺ abolished that superstition and established the Sunnah.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1564, 1778; Zad al-Ma'ad by Ibn al-Qayyim 2/90

questionEn: Which companion escorted Aishah (RA) on the back of his mount to Al-Tan'eem on the night after the Farewell Hajj so she could enter Ihram for Umrah?
optionsEn: Her nephew Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr (RA)
Her brother Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr (RA)
Her brother Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr (RA)
Bilal ibn Rabah (RA)
explanationEn: When Aishah (RA) wept because her companions had performed an independent Umrah before Hajj while she had combined her Umrah into Qiran after menstruating, the Prophet ﷺ instructed her brother Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr (RA) to take her to Al-Tan'eem to perform Umrah.

questionEn: What modern visual markers indicate the sacred boundary of the Haram (Hudud al-Haram) on the major highways leading into Makkah from Jeddah (Al-Shumaysi), Madinah (Al-Tan'eem), Ta'if (Al-Hada/Uranah), and Al-Layth?
optionsEn: Wooden fences painted blue and yellow
Deep water-filled moats with drawbridges
Monumental arched concrete portals spanning the highway together with multilingual guide signs marking the start and end of the Haram boundary
Red brick walls ten meters high with iron gates
explanationEn: Along the major highways entering Makkah (such as the Haramain Highway at Al-Shumaysi and the Al-Hada/Ta'if road), towering architectural arches shaped like open Qur'ans or Islamic portals and clear green/red road signs mark the exact Haram boundary line.
reference: General Presidency / Royal Commission for Makkah City and Holy Sites

questionEn: If a wild animal is hunted outside the Haram boundaries (in Al-Hill or Al-Afaq) by a person who is NOT in Ihram, and then brought inside the Haram, or if wild herbage cut in Al-Hill is brought into the Haram, what is the ruling?
optionsEn: It transforms into carrion immediately upon crossing the Haram arch
Anyone who eats it must fast for two consecutive months
It must be burned at the boundary stone of Al-Tan'eem
It is permissible according to the majority of jurists, because the prohibition applies to hunting the game of the Haram or cutting vegetation growing inside the Haram
explanationEn: The majority of jurists hold that vegetation cut in Al-Hill and game hunted lawfully in Al-Hill by a non-muhrim may be brought into the Haram and utilized, as the prophetic prohibition states 'its game is not chased and its thorns are not cut' (referring to what belongs to the Haram).
reference: Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi 7/448; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah 3/353

questionEn: Why is Muzdalifah called 'Al-Mash'ar al-Haram' (the Sacred Monument/Sanctuary) in contrast to Arafat?
optionsEn: Because Muzdalifah is a site of Hajj rites (mash'ar) that lies inside the sacred Haram boundary, whereas Arafat lies outside the Haram in Al-Hill
Because Muzdalifah is the only place where speaking is forbidden
Because Muzdalifah contains the well of Zamzam
Because Muzdalifah is located inside the courtyard of Al-Masjid al-Haram
explanationEn: Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, and the scholars explain that 'Al-Mash'ar' means a place of religious rites/signs, and it is described as 'al-Haram' (Sacred) because Muzdalifah lies within the inviolable Haram sanctuary of Makkah, unlike Arafat which is in Al-Hill.
reference: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:198; Tafsir Ibn Kathir 1/551; Sahih Muslim 1218

questionEn: Before Islam, why did the Quraysh (calling themselves 'Al-Hums') refuse to go out to stand at Arafat during Hajj, stopping instead inside Muzdalifah until the Qur'an corrected them in Surah Al-Baqarah 2:199?
optionsEn: Because they did not know where Mount Arafat was located

Out of pride as 'people of the Haram,' they claimed they should not leave the Haram boundary into Al-Hill (where Arafat lies), until Allah commanded: 'Then depart from the place from where all the people depart'
Because Arafat was flooded with seawater throughout Dhul-Hijjah
Because they thought Arafat belonged to the kingdom of Persia
explanationEn: Aishah (RA) narrated that the Quraysh and those who followed their creed (Al-Hums) used to stay inside the Haram at Muzdalifah saying 'We are the people of Allah's Haram, we will not leave the Haram,' whereas other Arabs stood at Arafat (in Al-Hill). When Islam came, Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ to go out to Arafat and depart from it with the people (Surah Al-Baqarah 2:199).
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1665, 4520; Sahih Muslim 1219; Surah Al-Baqarah 2:199

questionEn: Which companion was amazed during the pre-prophetic Hajj when he saw Prophet Muhammad ﷺ standing at Arafat alongside the rest of the people instead of remaining inside the Haram at Muzdalifah like the other Quraysh (Al-Hums)?
optionsEn: Salman al-Farisi (RA)
Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (RA)
Jubayr ibn Mut'im (RA)
Mu'adh ibn Jabal (RA)
explanationEn: Jubayr ibn Mut'im (RA) narrated that having lost his camel, he went looking for it in the valley of 'Aranah/Arafat and saw the Prophet ﷺ standing at Arafat with the people; Jubayr said to himself: 'By Allah, this man is from Al-Hums (Quraysh)—what brings him out here (into Al-Hill)?' That was a divine guidance (tawfiq) granted to the Prophet ﷺ even before revelation.

questionEn: In which direction and at what approximate distance from Al-Masjid al-Haram is Jabal al-Noor (the Mountain of Light), which houses Cave Hira?
optionsEn: Approximately 5 km south of Al-Masjid al-Haram on the road to Yemen
Approximately 22 km west of Al-Masjid al-Haram on the road to Jeddah
Directly inside the courtyard of Al-Masjid al-Haram next to Safa
Approximately 4 to 5 km northeast of Al-Masjid al-Haram
explanationEn: Jabal al-Noor (historically called Jabal Hira) stands roughly 4 to 5 km northeast of Al-Masjid al-Haram at an elevation of approximately 640 meters.
reference: Mu'jam al-Buldan by Yaqut al-Hamawi 2/238; Atlas al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah

questionEn: What Arabic term did Aishah (RA) use in Sahih al-Bukhari to describe the Prophet's ﷺ practice of spiritual seclusion and worship for multiple nights in Cave Hira before he received revelation?
optionsEn: Al-Tahannuth (which Aishah RA explained as al-ta'abbud, devotional worship during the nights of a set number)
Al-I'tikaf al-Madani
Al-Ribat al-Harbi
Al-Siyahah
explanationEn: In the famous narration opening Sahih al-Bukhari, Aishah (RA) stated that seclusion was made beloved to the Prophet ﷺ and he used to go to Cave Hira where he practiced 'al-tahannuth fihi—wa huwa al-ta'abbud—al-layali dhawat al-'adad' (devotional worship for nights of a counted number).

questionEn: Which five verses of the Qur'an were the very first revelation brought down by Angel Jibril (AS) to Prophet Muhammad ﷺ inside Cave Hira on Jabal al-Noor?
optionsEn: The first five verses of Surah Al-Muddaththir (74:1–5)
The first five verses of Surah Al-Alaq (96:1–5): 'Read in the name of your Lord who created...'
The seven verses of Surah Al-Fatihah (1:1–7)
The closing verses of Surah Al-Baqarah (2:285–286)
explanationEn: Inside Cave Hira, Angel Jibril (AS) embraced the Prophet ﷺ three times commanding 'Iqra'' (Read!), and then revealed Surah Al-Alaq 96:1–5: 'Read in the name of your Lord who created—created man from a clinging substance...'
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 3; Sahih Muslim 160; Surah Al-Alaq 96:1-5

questionEn: How is the natural rock opening of Cave Hira near the summit of Jabal al-Noor oriented geographically?
optionsEn: It faces due east toward the Persian Gulf
It faces due south toward Yemen with no view of Makkah
It naturally faces southwest directly toward Al-Masjid al-Haram and the Kaaba
It is an underground shaft with no horizontal opening
explanationEn: Cave Hira is a small fissure-like chamber (about 3.5 meters long and 1.5 meters wide) just below the peak of Jabal al-Noor, whose opening naturally looks directly toward the Sacred Kaaba.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi; Atlas al-Sirah al-Nabawawiyyah

questionEn: Who regularly supported the Prophet ﷺ during his seclusions in Cave Hira, preparing his provisions and even climbing Jabal al-Noor to bring him food and water, earning glad tidings from Allah and Jibril (AS)?
optionsEn: His uncle Abu Lahab
His cousin Aqil ibn Abi Talib
Suhayl ibn Amr
His wife Khadijah bint Khuwaylid (RA)
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Abu Hurayrah (RA) narrated that Jibril (AS) came to the Prophet ﷺ as Khadijah (RA) was approaching with a vessel of stew, food, or drink, and Jibril told him: 'Convey to her greetings of peace (Salam) from her Lord and from me, and give her glad tidings of a house in Paradise made of qasab (hollow pearls) wherein there is neither noise nor fatigue.'

questionEn: In the authentic hadith in Sahih Muslim, when Mount Hira shook beneath the feet of the Prophet ﷺ and several major Companions, what did the Prophet ﷺ say to calm the mountain?
optionsEn: 'Be calm, O Hira! For upon you is none but a Prophet, a Siddiq (truthful one), or a Shahid (martyr)'
'Sink into the earth, O Hira, until the Day of Judgment'
'Split into two halves so a spring of water may flow'
'Rise higher than Mount Uhud in Madinah'
explanationEn: Abu Hurayrah (RA) narrated that the Prophet ﷺ was upon Mount Hira with Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali, Talhah, and Al-Zubayr (RA) when the rock moved; the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Be still, O Hira, for there is none upon you except a Prophet, a Siddiq, or a Martyr.'

questionEn: Is climbing Jabal al-Noor or praying inside Cave Hira considered one of the prescribed rites (manasik) of Hajj or Umrah in Islamic law?
optionsEn: Yes, it is a compulsory pillar (rukn) without which Hajj is invalid

No; scholars agree that climbing Jabal al-Noor or praying in Cave Hira is not part of the rites of Hajj or Umrah, as the Prophet ﷺ never climbed it after prophethood during his Umrahs or Farewell Hajj for worship
Yes, it replaces standing at Arafat for elderly pilgrims
Yes, every pilgrim must collect seven stones from Cave Hira for the Jamarat
explanationEn: Islamic scholars point out that after receiving revelation, the Prophet ﷺ lived in Makkah for 13 years and later returned for Umrah al-Qada, the Conquest, the Umrah of Ji'ranah, and the Farewell Hajj, yet he never prescribed climbing Cave Hira or praying there as an act of worship or pilgrimage rite.
reference: Majmu' Fatawa Ibn Taymiyyah 27/251; Zad al-Ma'ad by Ibn al-Qayyim

questionEn: In which direction from Al-Masjid al-Haram is Jabal Thawr (housing Cave Thawr) located, and why did the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr (RA) head in that direction at the start of the Hijrah to Madinah?
optionsEn: Directly north on the main caravan highway to Madinah
Eastward inside the valley of Mina
Approximately 4 to 5 km south of Al-Masjid al-Haram—opposite the northern road to Madinah—as a strategic measure to evade the Quraysh search parties
Westward on the seashore of Jeddah
explanationEn: Jabal Thawr (~750 m high) lies south of Makkah toward the Yemen direction; by heading south instead of north toward Madinah and hiding in Cave Thawr for three nights, the Prophet ﷺ threw off the Quraysh trackers who scoured the northern Madinah routes first.

questionEn: For how many nights did the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) conceal themselves inside Cave Thawr (Ghar Thawr) before departing along the coastal route toward Madinah?
optionsEn: One single hour at midday
Fourteen consecutive nights
Forty days and forty nights
Three nights (Friday, Saturday, and Sunday nights)
explanationEn: As narrated by Aishah (RA) in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr (RA) hid in the cave of Jabal Thawr for three nights until the initial fury of the Quraysh search subsided.

questionEn: Which verse of the Qur'an explicitly commemorates the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr (RA) inside Cave Thawr with the words: 'when they were in the cave and he said to his companion, Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us'?
optionsEn: Surah At-Tawbah 9:40
Surah Al-Anfal 8:30
Surah Al-Fath 48:1
Surah Al-Qasas 28:85
explanationEn: Surah At-Tawbah 9:40 states: 'If you do not aid the Prophet—Allah has already aided him when those who disbelieved had driven him out [of Makkah] as one of two, when they were in the cave (idh huma fil-ghar) and he said to his companion, Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us (La tahzan inna Allaha ma'ana).'

questionEn: In the hadith of Anas ibn Malik (RA) in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, when the Quraysh trackers stood right above the entrance of Cave Thawr and Abu Bakr (RA) said, 'If one of them were to look down at his feet, he would see us,' how did the Prophet ﷺ reassure him?
optionsEn: 'Draw your sword and let us fight them all at the mouth of the cave'
'O Abu Bakr! What do you think of two with whom Allah is the Third? (Ma zannuka ya Aba Bakr bi-ithnayni Allahu thalithuhuma)'
'Dig a tunnel through the back wall of the mountain'
'Call out to them so they may take us back to Makkah'
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Abu Bakr (RA) looked at the feet of the polytheists as they stood over the cave and feared for the Prophet's ﷺ safety, whereupon the Prophet ﷺ calmly said: 'O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two with whom Allah is the Third?'

questionEn: During the three nights in Cave Thawr, what critical intelligence role did young Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr (RA) perform?
optionsEn: He rode ahead to Madinah to gather an army of 1,000 horsemen
He stood guard with a spear at the gate of Dar al-Nadwah
He spent the day in Makkah listening to the plans and plots of Quraysh, visited the cave under cover of darkness to brief the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr, and returned to Makkah before dawn
He sailed to Abyssinia to inform King Najashi
explanationEn: Aishah (RA) narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari that her brother Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr—an intelligent, perceptive youth—stayed among Quraysh by day to hear their schemes, went to Cave Thawr at nightfall with the news, and slipped back into Makkah before morning as though he had spent the whole night in the city.

questionEn: What vital logistical and counter-tracking role did Amir ibn Fuhayrah (RA), the freedman of Abu Bakr, play at Cave Thawr during the Hijrah?
optionsEn: He built a stone wall across the road to Ta'if
He forged coins in Makkah to pay off Abu Jahl
He carried the Prophet's ﷺ armor to Yemen
He grazed his flock of sheep up to the cave in the evening to provide them with fresh milk and meat, and drove the sheep over Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr's footprints to erase their tracks
explanationEn: As recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, Amir ibn Fuhayrah (RA) tended a flock of sheep, bringing them to Cave Thawr after dark so the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr could drink fresh milk, and then herding the sheep along the path behind Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr in the morning so the hooves obliterated his footsteps.

questionEn: Why was Asma bint Abi Bakr (RA) honored with the title 'Dhat al-Nitaqayn' (She of the Two Waistbands) during the preparations for the departure to Cave Thawr?
optionsEn: When she found nothing with which to tie the food bag (sufrah) and waterskin for the Prophet's ﷺ Hijrah journey, she tore her waistband (nitaq) into two pieces, tying the provisions with one and wearing the other
Because she wove two silk belts for the Kiswah of the Kaaba
Because she carried two swords during the Battle of Badr
Because she owned two palm groves in Khaybar
explanationEn: When the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr (RA) prepared to set out for Cave Thawr, Asma bint Abi Bakr (RA) split her waistband (nitaq) in two to fasten their food bag and waterskin; the Prophet ﷺ gave her glad tidings that Allah had replaced it for her with two waistbands in Paradise, so she was called Dhat al-Nitaqayn.

questionEn: Who was the skilled, trustworthy desert guide hired by the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr (RA) to meet them with their two camels at the foot of Jabal Thawr after three nights and guide them along the uncommonly traveled coastal route?
optionsEn: Suraqah ibn Malik al-Mudlaji
Abdullah ibn Urayqit al-Laythi (from Banu al-Dil)
Buraidah ibn al-Husayb al-Aslami
Kurz ibn Jabir al-Fihri
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari, Aishah (RA) narrated that the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hired a man from Banu al-Dil (from Banu Abd ibn Adi)—Abdullah ibn Urayqit—who was an expert desert guide (khrrit); although he was still on the religion of Quraysh at the time, they trusted him, handed him their two mounts, and he brought them to Cave Thawr on the morning after the third night.

questionEn: Which two prominent mountains immediately flanking the central valley of Makkah (on the eastern side over Safa and the western/northwestern side over Marwah) are known together in the hadith literature as 'Al-Akhshaban'?
optionsEn: Jabal al-Noor and Jabal Thawr
Jabal Uhud and Jabal 'Ayr
Jabal Abi Qubays and Jabal Qu'ayqi'an
Jabal al-Rahmah and Jabal Thabir
explanationEn: In classical Arabic and hadith commentaries (such as Al-Nawawi and Ibn Hajar), 'Al-Akhshaban' (the two great rugged mountains enclosing Makkah) are Jabal Abi Qubays on the east and Jabal Qu'ayqi'an (also called Jabal Hindi) on the west/northwest.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 3231; Sahih Muslim 1795; Fath al-Bari 6/316

questionEn: In the famous hadith narrated by Aishah (RA) in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, after the Prophet ﷺ returned from his painful rejection at Ta'if, what did the Angel of the Mountains (Malak al-Jibal) offer to do with the two Akhshaban mountains, and how did the Prophet ﷺ reply?
optionsEn: The Angel offered to turn the two mountains into solid gold, and the Prophet ﷺ accepted half of it
The Angel offered to move the two mountains to Madinah, and the Prophet ﷺ agreed
The Angel offered to flatten the mountains into a plain for horses, and the Prophet ﷺ consented

The Angel offered to crush them between the two Akhshaban mountains if he wished, and the Prophet ﷺ replied: 'Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins people who will worship Allah alone and associate nothing with Him'
explanationEn: When Aishah (RA) asked the Prophet ﷺ if any day had been harder on him than the Day of Uhud, he recounted his return from Ta'if when Jibril and the Angel of the Mountains greeted him at Qarn al-Tha'alib. The Angel of the Mountains offered to bring the two Akhshaban mountains crashing together upon them, but out of mercy the Prophet ﷺ declined, praying that Allah would bring forth monotheistic believers from their offspring.

questionEn: Where is Jabal Abi Qubays located in relation to Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Immediately to the east of Al-Masjid al-Haram, rising directly behind Mount Safa
Twelve kilometers west of Makkah on the road to Jeddah
Inside the plain of Arafat next to Masjid Namirah
At the Miqat of Dhul-Hulayfah near Madinah
explanationEn: Jabal Abi Qubays rises directly on the eastern side of Al-Masjid al-Haram overlooking Mount Safa (the origin of the rock of Safa is at the foot of Jabal Abi Qubays).
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi; Mu'jam al-Buldan 1/82

questionEn: Where is Jabal Qu'ayqi'an (also known as Jabal Hindi) located in relation to Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: In the far south of Makkah behind Jabal Thawr
On the western and northwestern side of Al-Masjid al-Haram, opposite Jabal Abi Qubays and overlooking Al-Marwah
In the eastern end of Mina near Jamarat al-Aqabah
In the center of Wadi Nakhlah
explanationEn: Jabal Qu'ayqi'an rises on the western/northwestern side of Al-Masjid al-Haram opposite Jabal Abi Qubays; the rock of Al-Marwah sits at the lower spur of Jabal Qu'ayqi'an.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi; Fath al-Bari 6/316

questionEn: Which mountain ridge to the east/southeast of Al-Masjid al-Haram (behind Jabal Abi Qubays) was the site of the brief skirmish on the Day of the Conquest of Makkah where Khalid ibn al-Walid's (RA) column encountered armed resistance from Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl and Safwan ibn Umayyah's group?
optionsEn: Jabal Thawr
Jabal al-Noor
Jabal Khandamah
Jabal al-Rahmah
explanationEn: During the Conquest of Makkah in Ramadan 8 AH, while the other three Muslim columns entered peacefully without bloodshed, a group led by Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, Safwan ibn Umayyah, and Suhayl ibn Amr gathered at Jabal Khandamah and shot arrows at Khalid ibn al-Walid's column before being swiftly dispersed.
reference: Sahih Muslim 1780; Zad al-Ma'ad 3/400; Al-Rahiq al-Makhtum

questionEn: What is the historical name of Makkah's main cemetery located north of Al-Masjid al-Haram, also known in classical sources as 'Al-Hajun'?
optionsEn: Jannat al-Baqi' (Baqi' al-Gharqad)
Maqbarat Shuhada' Uhud
Maqbarat Bab al-Saghir
Jannat al-Mu'alla (Maqbarat al-Ma'la)
explanationEn: Jannat al-Mu'alla (Maqbarat al-Ma'la), situated in the valley of Al-Hajun slightly north of Al-Masjid al-Haram in upper Makkah (al-Ma'la), is the ancient burial ground of Makkah.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/209; Mu'jam al-Buldan 2/225

questionEn: Which beloved wife of the Prophet ﷺ—the Mother of the Believers and the very first person to believe in him—is buried in Jannat al-Mu'alla (Al-Hajun) in Makkah?
optionsEn: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid (RA)
Aishah bint Abi Bakr (RA)
Hafsah bint Umar (RA)
Maymunah bint al-Harith (RA)
explanationEn: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid (RA) passed away in Makkah in Ramadan of the 10th year of prophethood (three years before the Hijrah) at the age of 65 and was buried at Al-Hajun (Jannat al-Mu'alla), with the Prophet ﷺ himself descending into her grave to place her inside.

questionEn: Why was the formal Funeral Prayer (Salat al-Janazah) not performed over Khadijah bint Khuwaylid (RA) when she was buried at Al-Hajun (Jannat al-Mu'alla) in Makkah?
optionsEn: Because funeral prayers are forbidden inside the city of Makkah
Because the formal Funeral Prayer (Salat al-Janazah) had not yet been legislated at the time of her passing prior to the Isra wal-Mi'raj and Hijrah
Because the Prophet ﷺ was away on a military campaign in Tabuk
Because she passed away in Abyssinia
explanationEn: Biographers and hadith scholars (such as Al-Suhayli, Ibn Hajar, and Al-Zurqani) note that Khadijah (RA) passed away in Makkah before the five daily prayers and the formal Salat al-Janazah were prescribed, so the Prophet ﷺ personally descended into her grave at Al-Hajun and supplicated for her.
reference: Fath al-Bari by Ibn Hajar 7/134; Al-Rawd al-Unuf by Al-Suhayli

questionEn: Besides Khadijah (RA), which members of the Prophet's ﷺ family and notable Companions are buried in Jannat al-Mu'alla in Makkah?
optionsEn: His son Ibrahim, his uncle Hamzah, and Uthman ibn Affan (RA)
His daughters Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, and Fatimah (RA)
His sons Al-Qasim and Abdullah, his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and ancestors, and Companions such as Asma bint Abi Bakr and Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr (RA)
Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Al-Hasan ibn Ali (RA)
explanationEn: Jannat al-Mu'alla contains the graves of the Prophet's ﷺ two sons born in Makkah (Al-Qasim and Abdullah), his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib, his great-grandfather Abd Manaf, his uncle Abu Talib, and later Companions who died in Makkah such as Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr and Asma bint Abi Bakr (RA) (whereas Ibrahim, Fatimah, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Uthman, and Al-Hasan are buried in Al-Baqi' in Madinah).
reference: Al-Isabah by Ibn Hajar; Siyar A'lam al-Nubala'

questionEn: What major trial did the Prophet ﷺ, the believers, and the clans of Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib endure for three years in 'Shi'b Abi Talib' (the ravine of Abu Talib near Jabal Abi Qubays) from the 7th to the 10th year of prophethood?
optionsEn: A three-year flood that submerged the ravine under ten meters of water
An invasion by the Roman legions from Syria
A plague of locusts that destroyed all stone houses in Makkah
A harsh social and economic boycott imposed by the Quraysh, who hung a written pact inside the Kaaba forbidding marriage, trade, food sales, or sitting with them
explanationEn: When Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib refused to hand the Prophet ﷺ over to be killed, the Quraysh signed a boycott parchment and hung it inside the Kaaba. Besieged in Shi'b Abi Talib for three years, the Muslims suffered such severe hunger that they ate tree leaves and dried leather until Allah caused a termite (aradah) to eat every unjust word of the pact except 'Bismika Allahumma.'

questionEn: When the Prophet ﷺ mentioned the valley of Banu Kinanah (Al-Muhassab / Khayf Bani Kinanah) before entering Makkah during the Conquest and the Farewell Hajj, what historical memory of that spot did Abu Hurayrah (RA) recount?
optionsEn: It was the place where the Quraysh and Banu Kinanah had sworn their pagan oath against Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib not to marry with them or trade with them until they surrendered the Prophet ﷺ
It was the place where Prophet Ibrahim (AS) sacrificed the ram
It was the place where the first marketplace of Makkah was built
It was the place where the well of Zamzam was originally dug
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, when the Prophet ﷺ announced before entering Makkah: 'Tomorrow, if Allah wills, our encamping place will be at the Khayf of Banu Kinanah, where they swore their oath upon disbelief,' Abu Hurayrah (RA) explained that this referred to the boycott pact sworn by Quraysh and Kinanah against Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib.

questionEn: Where was 'Dar al-Arqam' (the house of the young Companion Al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam al-Makhzumi RA) located in Makkah, and what historic role did it serve in early Islam?
optionsEn: Inside the valley of Mina; it served as a granary for the pilgrims

At the foot of Mount Safa; it served as the secret center where the Prophet ﷺ taught the Qur'an and trained the early Companions during the first three years of the mission until Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) embraced Islam there
At the summit of Jabal Thawr; it served as a watchtower during the Hijrah
At the port of Shu'aybah; it served as a shipyard for the migration to Abyssinia
explanationEn: Dar al-Arqam was situated at the base of Mount Safa (later known as Dar al-Khayzuran). Because Al-Arqam was from Banu Makhzum and his conversion was not initially suspected, his house became the first school of Islam where the early Companions gathered privately with the Prophet ﷺ until Umar (RA) accepted Islam there and the Muslims came out to pray openly at the Kaaba.
reference: Al-Mustadrak by Al-Hakim 6171; Tabaqat Ibn Sa'd 3/242

questionEn: Where is 'Masjid al-Jinn' located in Makkah, and what Qur'anic and prophetic event does its site commemorate?
optionsEn: South of Makkah at Adat Libn; it commemorates Solomon's temple
West of Makkah at Hudaybiyyah; it commemorates the Pledge of the Tree
North of Al-Masjid al-Haram along the route toward Jannat al-Mu'alla; it commemorates the night a delegation of Jinn listened to the Prophet's ﷺ Qur'an recitation and believed in him
East of Makkah in Arafat; it commemorates the Farewell Sermon
explanationEn: Masjid al-Jinn (also historically known as Masjid al-Haras) stands in the Al-Ghazzah / Al-Mu'alla area north of Al-Masjid al-Haram, associated with the night the Jinn listened to the Prophet ﷺ reciting the Qur'an (Surah Al-Jinn 72:1–2 and Surah Al-Ahqaf 46:29) and where the Prophet ﷺ drew a line for Ibn Mas'ud (RA) while speaking to the Jinn.
reference: Sahih Muslim 450; Jami' al-Tirmidhi 2861; Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/201

questionEn: Where is 'Masjid al-Bay'ah' (the Mosque of the Pledge, also called Masjid al-'Aqabah) located, and what pivotal Seerah event took place there?
optionsEn: On the plain of Hudaybiyyah; it marks where Bay'at al-Ridwan took place
At the foot of Mount Safa; it marks where the women of Makkah pledged allegiance after the Conquest
In the center of Muzdalifah; it marks where the tribes of Ta'if surrendered
In a small mountain ravine at Al-'Aqabah in western Mina; it marks the spot where the Ansar of Madinah secretly pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ in the First and Second Pledges of 'Aqabah
explanationEn: Masjid al-Bay'ah sits in the sheltered ravine (shi'b) just off Jamarat al-'Aqabah in Mina where the Prophet ﷺ met the delegation from Yathrib (Madinah) by night during the pilgrimage seasons of the 12th and 13th years of prophethood, receiving the First and Second Pledges of 'Aqabah that paved the way for the Hijrah.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 3892; Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/199

questionEn: Which Abbasid Caliph constructed Masjid al-Bay'ah at the site of the Pledge of 'Aqabah in Mina in the year 144 AH (761 CE), as attested by its preserved foundation inscriptions?
optionsEn: Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur
Caliph Al-Musta'sim
Caliph Al-Qadir
Caliph Al-Nasir li-Din Allah
explanationEn: Two original marble foundation plaques still preserved on the wall of Masjid al-Bay'ah in Mina record that the Abbasid Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur ordered its construction in 144 AH (761 CE) to commemorate the place where the Ansar pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/199; Corpus of Early Arabic Inscriptions

questionEn: In the Second Pledge of 'Aqabah (Bay'at al-'Aqabah al-Kubra) at the site of Masjid al-Bay'ah in Mina, how many men and women of the Ansar pledged to protect the Prophet ﷺ as they protected their own families?
optionsEn: 12 men and no women
73 men and 2 women (Nusaybah bint Ka'b and Asma bint 'Amr RA)
313 men and 10 women
explanationEn: Whereas the First Pledge of 'Aqabah the previous year involved 12 men of the Ansar, the Second Pledge of 'Aqabah at the ravine in Mina was taken by 73 men and 2 women (Umm 'Umarah Nusaybah bint Ka'b and Umm Mani' Asma bint 'Amr RA), from whom the Prophet ﷺ appointed 12 Nuqaba' (leaders).
reference: Musnad Ahmad 15798; Sirat Ibn Hisham 1/442; Zad al-Ma'ad 3/44

questionEn: Where is 'Masjid al-Khayf' located, and why is it called 'al-Khayf' in Arabic?
optionsEn: On the summit of Mount Arafat; 'al-Khayf' means the highest peak
At the coastal port of Jeddah; 'al-Khayf' means the seashore
In the valley of Mina at the foot of the southern mountain (Jabal al-Sabih); 'al-Khayf' in Arabic means the elevated slope above the flood channel and below the steep mountain
At the northern Haram boundary of Tan'eem; 'al-Khayf' means the oasis
explanationEn: Masjid al-Khayf is the main historic mosque in the center of Mina at the foot of the southern mountain. Linguists and geographers explain that 'khayf' means land that rises above the torrent bed (masil al-ma') and slopes down from the thickness of the mountain.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1653; Mu'jam al-Buldan 2/412; Al-Nihayah by Ibn al-Athir

questionEn: What prophetic virtue is reported in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA) regarding Masjid al-Khayf in Mina?
optionsEn: That praying in Masjid al-Khayf equals one million prayers elsewhere
That Masjid al-Khayf was built before the Kaaba
That anyone who sleeps in Masjid al-Khayf does not need to perform Tawaf
That seventy Prophets prayed in Masjid al-Khayf (and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself encamped and prayed there during the Farewell Hajj)
explanationEn: Al-Tabarani in Al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (graded hasan/sahih li-ghayrihi by Al-Mundhiri and Al-Albani) narrated from Ibn Abbas (RA) that seventy prophets prayed in Masjid al-Khayf, and Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim record that the Prophet ﷺ stayed and led prayers at Al-Khayf in Mina during the Farewell Hajj.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1653; Al-Mu'jam al-Kabir by Al-Tabarani 12283; Al-Targhib wa al-Tarhib 2/178

questionEn: Which Qur'anic verse commands pilgrims after departing from Arafat on the evening of the 9th of Dhul-Hijjah: 'Then when you pour forth from Arafat, remember Allah at Al-Mash'ar al-Haram'?
optionsEn: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:198
Surah Al-Hajj 22:27
Surah Al-Imran 3:97
Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:3
explanationEn: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:198 states: 'There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord [during Hajj]. But when you depart from Arafat, remember Allah at Al-Mash'ar al-Haram (Muzdalifah).'

questionEn: What was the specific hill in Muzdalifah at the foot of which the Prophet ﷺ stood after praying Fajr on the 10th of Dhul-Hijjah to face the Qiblah and make prolonged du'a until it became very bright before sunrise, where the Mosque of Al-Mash'ar al-Haram stands today?
optionsEn: The hill of Jabal al-Rahmah
The hill of Quzah
The hill of Mount Safa
The hill of Jabal Abi Qubays
explanationEn: In the long hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah (RA) in Sahih Muslim describing the Farewell Pilgrimage, after praying Fajr at early dawn in Muzdalifah, the Prophet ﷺ rode Al-Qaswa until he came to Al-Mash'ar al-Haram (at the hill of Quzah), faced the Qiblah, supplicated, proclaimed Allah's greatness (Takbir) and oneness (Tahlil), and remained standing until the morning light shone brightly before sunrise.
reference: Sahih Muslim 1218; Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi 2/188

questionEn: In the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah (RA) in Sahih Muslim, how did the Prophet ﷺ broaden the valid standing and overnight area for pilgrims in Muzdalifah so they would not crowd exclusively around the hill of Quzah?
optionsEn: He declared that only the inside of the mosque building is valid
He declared that pilgrims must climb to the highest mountain peak above Muzdalifah
He declared: 'I have stood here, and all of Muzdalifah (Jam') is a standing place (waqaftu hahuna wa Jam'un kulluha mawqif)'
He declared that women and children must spend the night in Wadi Muhassir
explanationEn: Just as he did at Arafat and at the slaughter place in Mina, the Prophet ﷺ removed hardship from the Ummah by declaring: 'I have stood here, and all of Jam' (Muzdalifah) is a place of standing.'

questionEn: What is Another classical name for Muzdalifah used in the Hadith literature, derived from the fact that pilgrims gather there and combine (yajma'un) the Maghrib and Isha prayers there?
optionsEn: Bakkah
Al-Hajun
Al-Abtah
Jam' (Al-Jam')
explanationEn: In authentic hadiths (including Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim), Muzdalifah is frequently called 'Jam'' because people gather (yajtami'un) there on the night of the 10th of Dhul-Hijjah and combine (yajma'un) Maghrib and Isha prayers there.

questionEn: Where is 'Wadi Muhassir' located, and what is the Sunnah for pilgrims when passing through it on the morning of the 10th of Dhul-Hijjah on their way from Muzdalifah to Mina?
optionsEn: It is the narrow valley separating Muzdalifah from Mina; the Sunnah is to hasten one's pace (harwalah / idah') through it without stopping
It is the valley between Safa and Marwah; the Sunnah is to sleep there for two hours
It is the valley east of Arafat; the Sunnah is to pray Dhuhr and Asr there
It is the valley north of Madinah; the Sunnah is to enter Ihram there
explanationEn: Wadi Muhassir is a narrow valley (roughly 545 meters wide) lying between Muzdalifah and Mina (and counted as neither part of Muzdalifah nor Mina). In the hadith of Jabir (RA), when the Prophet ﷺ reached Batn Muhassir, he urged his camel to move quickly through it.

questionEn: Why is Wadi Muhassir called 'Muhassir' (the valley that wearies/halts), and why did the Prophet ﷺ hasten through it when moving from Muzdalifah to Mina?
optionsEn: Because the Quraysh horses grew tired there during the Battle of Badr
Because it was the valley where Abraha's elephant (Mahmud) knelt down and was halted (hassara), and where Allah sent the flocks of birds (tayran ababil) to destroy the Army of the Elephant
Because it was the dry riverbed where Queen Zubaydah's canal ended
Because the tribe of Jurhum buried their weapons there
explanationEn: Scholars such as Ibn al-Qayyim and Al-Nawawi explain that Wadi Muhassir was where the elephant of Abraha halted and refused to advance toward the Kaaba, and where Allah's punishment descended upon the People of the Elephant (Surah Al-Fil 105); following the Prophet's ﷺ practice at places where divine punishment fell, pilgrims pass through it briskly.
reference: Sahih Muslim 1218; Sharh Sahih Muslim by Al-Nawawi 8/187; Zad al-Ma'ad 2/247

questionEn: What is 'Jabal al-Rahmah' (the Mount of Mercy, historically called Jabal Ilal), and where is it located?
optionsEn: The mountain south of Makkah containing the Cave of Thawr
The mountain northeast of Makkah containing the Cave of Hira
The small granite hill rising in the eastern plain of Arafat, at the foot of which the Prophet ﷺ stood on his camel Al-Qaswa facing the Qiblah on the Day of Arafat
The mountain in Madinah where the archers stood during the Battle of Uhud
explanationEn: Jabal al-Rahmah (called Ilal in early geographical texts) is the well-known granite hill (~65 meters above the surrounding plain) in Arafat; on the 9th of Dhul-Hijjah during the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Prophet ﷺ stood on his mount at the rocks at the base of the hill facing the Qiblah in supplication until sunset.

questionEn: What did the Prophet ﷺ clarify regarding whether pilgrims on the Day of Arafat must climb onto the hill of Jabal al-Rahmah itself for their standing (Wuquf) to be valid?
optionsEn: He commanded every pilgrim to climb to the very top and touch the white pillar
He ruled that standing anywhere except on the summit invalidates Hajj
He instructed pilgrims to perform seven circuits of Tawaf around the hill

He stood at the rocks at its base and explicitly declared: 'I have stood here, and all of Arafat is a standing place (waqaftu hahuna wa 'Arafatu kulluha mawqif)', so climbing the hill is neither required nor recommended
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ did not climb to the top of Jabal al-Rahmah; he stood on his camel at the large rocks at its base and proclaimed that the entire plain of Arafat is a valid standing place. Scholars emphasize that crowding to climb the hill or wiping its stones/pillar has no basis in the Sunnah.
reference: Sahih Muslim 1218; Majmu' Fatawa Ibn Taymiyyah 26/133; Zad al-Ma'ad 2/237

questionEn: Who commissioned the monumental hydraulic engineering work known as ''Ayn Zubaydah' (the Spring and Water Canal of Zubaydah) in the late 2nd / early 3rd century AH to supply fresh water to pilgrims in Arafat, Muzdalifah, Mina, and Makkah?
optionsEn: Queen Zubaydah bint Ja'far ibn Abi Ja'far al-Mansur, the wife of the Abbasid Caliph Harun al-Rashid
Shajar al-Durr of Cairo
Fatimah al-Fihriyyah of Fez
Hurrem Sultan of Istanbul
explanationEn: When Queen Zubaydah bint Ja'far (granddaughter of Caliph Al-Mansur and wife of Harun al-Rashid, d. 216 AH / 831 CE) performed Hajj and witnessed the extreme thirst and skyrocketing cost of a waterskin in Makkah and Arafat, she summoned the finest engineers of the Islamic world to construct a permanent water canal.
reference: Wafayat al-A'yan by Ibn Khallikan 2/314; Akhbar Makkah by Al-Fakihi

questionEn: From which mountain valleys east of Makkah did the engineers of 'Ayn Zubaydah channel natural spring water across more than 30 km of mountains and underground conduits to reach Arafat, Muzdalifah, Mina, and Makkah?
optionsEn: From the Nile River in Egypt via the Sinai Peninsula
From Wadi Nu'man (Ayn al-Mashash / Hunayn) and Wadi Hunayn east of Makkah and Arafat
From the Euphrates River in Iraq
From the wells of Quba in Madinah
explanationEn: After initial wells inside Makkah proved insufficient, Queen Zubaydah's engineers tapped abundant springs in Wadi Nu'man and Wadi Hunayn (roughly 35–38 km east/southeast of Makkah), carving channels through solid rock, building aqueducts across valleys, and constructing underground inspection shafts (kharazat) all the way to Arafat (wrapping around Jabal al-Rahmah), Muzdalifah, Mina, and Makkah.
reference: Shifa' al-Gharam by Al-Fasi 1/342; Wafayat al-A'yan 2/314

questionEn: When the chief engineer warned Queen Zubaydah bint Ja'far that cutting the 'Ayn Zubaydah water canal through the granite mountains around Makkah would cost an astronomical fortune, what famous reply did she give?
optionsEn: 'Abandon the project and build a palace in Baghdad instead'
'Tax every pilgrim ten gold dinars before allowing them to drink'
'Carry it out, even if every single strike of the pickaxe costs a gold dinar! (I'malha wa-law kanat kullu darbati mi'walin bi-dinar)'
'Build the canal out of reeds and mud so it costs nothing'
explanationEn: Ibn Khallikan and Makkan historians record that Queen Zubaydah spent roughly 1.7 million gold dinars of her personal wealth on the 'Ayn Zubaydah waterworks, telling her chief treasurer and engineer: 'Carry it out, even if every blow of the pickaxe costs a dinar,' and later threw the expense ledgers into the Tigris saying she left the accounting to the Day of Judgment.
reference: Wafayat al-A'yan by Ibn Khallikan 2/314; Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' 10/241

questionEn: For approximately how many centuries did the 'Ayn Zubaydah water canal system—with periodic restorations by Abbasid, Mamluk, Ottoman, and Saudi rulers (including King Abdulaziz's 'Ayn al-'Aziziyyah commission)—continue to supply water to pilgrims in Makkah and the holy sites?
optionsEn: For only two Hajj seasons before drying up completely
For twenty-five years until the reign of Caliph Al-Ma'mun
For fifty years until the Mamluk era
For nearly 1,200 years (over eleven centuries from the early 9th century CE into the mid-20th century CE)
explanationEn: Constructed around 194 AH (809–810 CE), the 'Ayn Zubaydah stone-lined subterranean and surface aqueduct system functioned as the primary lifeline of fresh water for pilgrims in Arafat, Muzdalifah, Mina, and Makkah for nearly twelve centuries until modern desalination networks and pipelines supplemented it in the late 20th century.
reference: Shifa' al-Gharam by Al-Fasi 1/342; Tarikh 'Ayn Zubaydah

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah, what was the very first request Prophet Ibrahim (AS) made when praying for the valley of Makkah?
optionsEn: That Allah make it a city of peace and security (Baladan Aminan)
That Allah make its mountains out of gold and silver
That Allah grant its rulers dominion over Rome and Persia
That Allah surround it with rivers and palm orchards
explanationEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah (2:126), Prophet Ibrahim (AS) prayed: 'My Lord, make this a city of peace and security (Baladan Aminan) and provide its people with fruits—whoever of them believes in Allah and the Last Day.'

questionEn: How did Prophet Ibrahim (AS) describe the physical geography of Makkah when he settled his family there in Surah Ibrahim?
optionsEn: A forested mountain pass watered by seasonal snowmelt
An uncultivated valley without any sown crops (bi-wadin ghayri dhi zar'in)
A coastal plain overlooking the Red Sea trade routes
A fertile plateau of abundant springs and olive groves
explanationEn: In Surah Ibrahim (14:37), Ibrahim (AS) supplicated: 'Our Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in an uncultivated valley (bi-wadin ghayri dhi zar'in) near Your Sacred House.'

questionEn: According to Surah Ibrahim (14:37), for what spiritual purpose did Ibrahim (AS) state that he settled his family near the Sacred House in Makkah?
optionsEn: So that they may build fortresses upon the surrounding hills
So that they may collect tolls from passing trade caravans
So that they may establish regular prayer (li-yuqimu al-salah)
So that they may record the genealogies of the desert tribes
explanationEn: Ibrahim (AS) explicitly linked settling his family near the Sacred House in Makkah to worship: 'Our Lord, so that they may establish prayer (li-yuqimu al-salah); so make the hearts of people incline toward them' (14:37).

questionEn: In Surah Ibrahim (14:35), what specific spiritual danger did Prophet Ibrahim (AS) ask Allah to keep him and his sons away from after praying for Makkah's security?
optionsEn: Leaving the valley of Makkah for agricultural lands
Forgetting the classical poetry of the Arabs
Abandoning trade journeys in winter and summer
Worshipping idols
explanationEn: Prophet Ibrahim (AS) prayed in Surah Ibrahim (14:35): 'My Lord, make this city secure, and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols (wa-jnubni wa-baniyya an na'buda al-asnam).'

questionEn: What supplication did Ibrahim (AS) and Ismail (AS) recite together in Makkah regarding the rites of pilgrimage in Surah Al-Baqarah (2:128)?
optionsEn: 'And show us our rites of pilgrimage (wa-arina manasikana) and accept our repentance'
'And exempt our descendants from fasting and charity'
'And reveal to us the Psalms and the Gospel in this valley'
'And grant us victory over the armies of Abyssinia and Persia'
explanationEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah (2:128), Ibrahim and Ismail (AS) prayed in Makkah: 'Our Lord, make us both submissive (Muslimayn) to You and from our descendants a submissive nation to You, and show us our rites (wa-arina manasikana) and accept our repentance.'

questionEn: Whose mission in Makkah was the direct fulfillment of Ibrahim and Ismail's prayer in Surah Al-Baqarah (2:129) to 'send among them a Messenger from themselves'?
optionsEn: Prophet Musa (AS)
Prophet Muhammad ﷺ
Prophet Zakariyya (AS)
Prophet Dawud (AS)
explanationEn: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, 'I am the answered prayer of my father Ibrahim,' referring to Ibrahim and Ismail's supplication in Makkah (Qur'an 2:129) for Allah to raise a Messenger among their Makkan descendants.

questionEn: Which four duties did Ibrahim and Ismail (AS) ask Allah to give the Messenger raised in Makkah in Surah Al-Baqarah (2:129)?
optionsEn: To unify the tribes through taxation, build city walls, dig canals, and mint coins
To interpret dreams, command the wind, heal the blind, and part the sea
To recite Allah's verses to them, teach them the Book and Wisdom, and purify them
To compile tribal poetry, establish a royal dynasty, and conquer Yemen
explanationEn: Surah Al-Baqarah (2:129) records their prayer: 'Our Lord, and send among them a Messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and Wisdom and purify them.'

questionEn: With whom did Prophet Ibrahim (AS) conclude his supplication in Surah Ibrahim (14:41) after praying for Makkah and his offspring?
optionsEn: Asking that no non-Arab ever enter the valley of Makkah
Requesting that the Sacred Months be reduced from four to two
Seeking worldly wealth solely for the chieftains of Quraysh
Seeking forgiveness for himself, his parents, and the believers on the Day the account is established
explanationEn: Ibrahim (AS) concluded his prayer in Surah Ibrahim (14:41) with universal mercy: 'Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day the account is established.'

questionEn: Which ancient Arab tribe originating from Yemen settled in Makkah with Hajar's permission, taught Ismail (AS) Arabic, and intermarried with him?
optionsEn: Banu Jurhum
Banu Taghlib
Banu Thaqif
Banu Hanifah
explanationEn: A passing caravan of the Yemeni tribe of Jurhum settled in Makkah with Hajar's permission (while acknowledging she and Ismail owned the water rights); Ismail (AS) grew up among them, learned Arabic from them, and married into their tribe.

questionEn: Because Prophet Ismail (AS) learned Arabic from the tribe of Jurhum and married into them in Makkah, what genealogical category do historians give to his Northern Arab descendants?
optionsEn: Al-Anbat al-Sham (the Nabataean settlers of Petra)
Al-Arab al-Musta'ribah (the Arabized Arabs / Adnanites)
Al-Arab al-Ba'idah (the Extinct Arabs of 'Ad and Thamud)
Al-Arab al-'Aribah (the Southern Qahtanite Arabs of Saba')
explanationEn: Islamic genealogists classify the descendants of Ismail (AS) in Makkah and the Hijaz as Al-Arab al-Musta'ribah (the Arabized Arabs, traced through Adnan), who led the lineage to Quraysh and the Prophet ﷺ.

questionEn: When Prophet Ibrahim (AS) visited Makkah while Ismail (AS) was out hunting and Ismail's first wife complained bitterly of hardship without thanking Allah, what veiled message did Ibrahim leave for his son?
optionsEn: To 'raise the roof of his tent,' meaning to migrate north to Syria
To 'seal the well of the valley,' meaning to stop trading with Yemen
To 'change the threshold of his door,' meaning to part ways with that wife
To 'move his flock to Ta'if,' meaning to abandon Makkah during summer
explanationEn: In the long hadith of Ibn Abbas (RA), Ismail's first wife complained of poverty and showed ingratitude, so Ibrahim (AS) told her to convey his salam to Ismail and tell him to 'change the threshold of his door,' which Ismail understood as divorcing her.

questionEn: During a later visit to Makkah, when Ismail's second wife praised Allah, spoke gratefully of their livelihood, and honored Ibrahim (AS) with meat and water, what message did Ibrahim leave for Ismail?
optionsEn: To 'dig three new wells in Wadi Uranah'
To 'build a fortress on Mount Abu Qubays'
To 'journey to Egypt before the winter rains'
To 'keep firm the threshold of his door,' meaning to retain his righteous wife
explanationEn: Because Ismail's second wife praised Allah, expressed contentment, and showed generous hospitality, Ibrahim (AS) instructed her to tell Ismail to 'keep firm the threshold of his door,' and he supplicated for blessing in their meat and water in Makkah.

questionEn: Why did Ibrahim (AS) specifically pray for blessing in meat and water for the people of Makkah rather than grain during that visit?
optionsEn: Because Makkah had no sown grain crops at that time; otherwise he would have prayed for grain as well
Because grain could not be stored in the climate of the Hijaz
Because the people of Jurhum refused to accept bread from travelers
Because eating grain was forbidden in the law of Ibrahim (AS)
explanationEn: Ibn Abbas (RA) narrated that when Ismail's wife offered meat and water, Ibrahim (AS) prayed for blessing in their meat and water; the Prophet ﷺ noted that Makkah had no grain then, for otherwise Ibrahim would have prayed for it too.

questionEn: Which tribe expelled Banu Jurhum from Makkah after Jurhum violated the sanctity of the Haram and wronged visiting pilgrims?
optionsEn: Banu Kindah
Banu Khuza'ah
Banu Asad
Banu Ghatafan
explanationEn: When the later generations of Jurhum corrupted the sanctuary and mistreated visitors in Makkah, Banu Khuza'ah (with the backing of Banu Bakr) drove Jurhum out of Makkah and assumed custodianship of the city for centuries.

questionEn: Which chieftain of Banu Khuza'ah is identified in authentic hadith as the first person to change the pure monotheism of Ibrahim (AS) in Makkah by introducing idol worship?
optionsEn: Hulayl ibn Hubshiyyah
Waraqah ibn Nawfal
Amr ibn Luhayy al-Khuza'i
Qusayy ibn Kilab
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ stated that he saw Amr ibn Luhayy al-Khuza'i dragging his intestines in the Hellfire because he was the first to change the religion of Ismail (AS), introduce idols to Makkah, and institute pagan superstitious practices.

questionEn: From which region did Amr ibn Luhayy bring the idol Hubal to Makkah after seeing its inhabitants venerating idols?
optionsEn: The oasis of Siwa in western Egypt
The Malabar coast of southern India
The city of Ctesiphon in central Iraq
Al-Balqa' in the region of Sham (Greater Syria / Moab)
explanationEn: Historical accounts in Ibn Hisham record that Amr ibn Luhayy traveled to Al-Balqa' in Sham (Syria), where he saw the Amalekites worshipping idols for rain and victory, and brought Hubal back to Makkah.

questionEn: Despite the spread of idol worship in pre-Islamic Makkah, how did the people of Makkah known as the Hanifs (Hunafa'), such as Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl, conduct themselves?
optionsEn: They rejected idolatry, abstained from meat sacrificed to idols, and sought the pure monotheism (Hanifiyyah) of Ibrahim (AS)
They adopted Zoroastrian fire-worship imported from Persia
They abandoned Makkah permanently to become monks in Constantinople
They worshipped the sun and stars atop Mount Hira
explanationEn: In pre-Islamic Makkah, a small group of monotheists known as Hunafa' (including Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl and Waraqah ibn Nawfal) shunned idols and sought the original religion of Ibrahim (AS).

questionEn: Which fifth-generation ancestor of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ united the scattered clans of Quraysh, recovered the custodianship of Makkah from Banu Khuza'ah, and settled Quraysh inside the valley?
optionsEn: Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy
Qusayy ibn Kilab
Kilab ibn Murrah
Fihr ibn Malik
explanationEn: Qusayy ibn Kilab (c. 400 CE) united the dispersed clans of Quraysh, took over leadership of Makkah from Khuza'ah, and settled Quraysh around the Sanctuary.
reference: Sirat Ibn Hisham, Vol. 1; Al-Raheeq Al-Makhtum

questionEn: Why was Qusayy ibn Kilab given the honorific title 'Al-Mujammi'' ('The Unifier / Gatherer') in Makkan history?
optionsEn: Because he merged the four Sacred Months into a single continuous season
Because he collected all pre-Islamic poems into seven hanging scrolls
Because he gathered the scattered clans of Quraysh together and settled them inside the valley of Makkah
Because he combined the Roman and Persian currencies in Makkan markets
explanationEn: Before Qusayy, the clans of Quraysh lived dispersed in the surrounding hills and valleys; Qusayy brought them together inside the valley of Makkah around the Haram, earning the title Al-Mujammi'.
reference: Al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wal-Muluk; Sirat Ibn Hisham

questionEn: What did Qusayy ibn Kilab call the clans of Quraysh whom he settled in the central hollow of the valley immediately surrounding the Sanctuary of Makkah?
optionsEn: Quraysh al-Yaman (Quraysh of the Southern Frontier)
Quraysh al-Sawahil (Quraysh of the Red Sea Coast)
Quraysh al-Badiyah (Quraysh of the Desert Steppe)
Quraysh al-Bitah (Quraysh of the Hollow/Valley Floor)
explanationEn: Qusayy divided Makkah's quarters among Quraysh: the clans closest to the Sanctuary in the valley floor were called Quraysh al-Bitah, while those on the outer ravines and hills were called Quraysh al-Zawahir.

questionEn: What was the name of the council assembly hall established by Qusayy ibn Kilab in Makkah where the elders of Quraysh met to decide matters of war, trade, and civic affairs?
optionsEn: Dar al-Nadwah
Dar al-Imarah
Dar al-Arqam
Dar al-Hikmah
