optionsEn: Amr ibn al-'As (RA)
Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (RA)
'Attab ibn Asid (RA)
Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA)
explanationEn: Recognizing ability and piety over advanced age, the Prophet ﷺ appointed the young companion 'Attab ibn Asid (RA) as governor of Makkah and leader of the Hajj that year (8 AH), and he continued to govern Makkah faithfully throughout the Prophet's ﷺ life and Abu Bakr's caliphate.
reference: Sirat Ibn Hisham, Vol. 2; Al-Isabah by Ibn Hajar

questionEn: Which eminent companion did the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ leave behind in Makkah after the Conquest of 8 AH specifically to teach the people of Makkah the Qur'an and instruct them in the jurisprudence (Fiqh) of Islam?
optionsEn: Salman al-Farisi (RA)
Abu Hurayrah (RA)
Zayd ibn Harithah (RA)
Mu'adh ibn Jabal (RA)
explanationEn: Before departing Makkah in 8 AH, the Prophet ﷺ appointed 'Attab ibn Asid (RA) over its administration and left Mu'adh ibn Jabal (RA)—whom he praised as the most knowledgeable of the Ummah in halal and haram—to teach the people of Makkah the Qur'an and religion.
reference: Sirat Ibn Hisham, Vol. 2; Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3791

questionEn: After the Battle of Hunayn and Siege of Ta'if in Shawwal 8 AH, from which place outside Makkah did the Prophet ﷺ enter into Ihram to perform Umrah by night before returning to Madinah?
optionsEn: Al-Ji'ranah (after distributing the spoils of Hunayn there)
Yalamlam
Dhat 'Irq
Qarn al-Manazil
explanationEn: After dividing the spoils of Hunayn at Al-Ji'ranah, the Prophet ﷺ entered into Ihram from Al-Ji'ranah, entered Makkah at night to perform Umrah, and departed before dawn back to Al-Ji'ranah and then Madinah.

questionEn: In 9 AH (the year before the Farewell Pilgrimage), whom did the Prophet ﷺ appoint to lead the Muslims in Hajj to Makkah, and whom did he send after him to proclaim the opening declarations of Surah At-Tawbah at Mina?
optionsEn: Mu'adh ibn Jabal (RA) led the Hajj, and Bilal ibn Rabah (RA) proclaimed the verses
Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) was appointed Amir of the Hajj, and Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) was sent to proclaim the verses of Surah At-Tawbah
Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (RA) led the Hajj, and Zubayr ibn al-Awwam (RA) proclaimed the verses
Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) led the Hajj, and Uthman ibn Affan (RA) proclaimed the verses
explanationEn: In 9 AH, the Prophet ﷺ sent Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) to lead the Hajj and subsequently dispatched Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) on Al-'Adba' to proclaim Surah At-Tawbah (Bara'ah) on the Day of Sacrifice at Mina—announcing that after that year no polytheist would perform Hajj and no one would perform Tawaf naked around the House.

questionEn: In which Hijri year did the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ perform his only Hajj after the Hijrah—known as Hajjat al-Wada' (the Farewell Pilgrimage)—teaching the Muslims the rites of Makkah and the Mash'ar sites?
optionsEn: 8 AH (630 CE)
6 AH (628 CE)
explanationEn: Although the Prophet ﷺ performed four Umrahs after migrating to Madinah (all in Dhul-Qa'dah except the one with his Hajj), he performed only one Hajj after the Hijrah: the Farewell Pilgrimage in Dhul-Hijjah 10 AH.

questionEn: During the Farewell Pilgrimage in 10 AH, what foundational instruction did the Prophet ﷺ repeat to the Muslim community while performing the rites in Makkah, Arafat, Muzdalifah, and Mina?
optionsEn: 'Only the residents of Makkah and Madinah are obligated to stand at Arafat'
'The rites of pilgrimage shall change once every hundred years'
'Every tribe may perform the pilgrimage according to the customs of its ancestors'
'Learn from me your rites (Li-ta'khudhu 'anni manasikakum), for I do not know whether I will perform Hajj after this Hajj of mine'
explanationEn: Jabir ibn Abdullah (RA) narrated in Sahih Muslim (1297) that the Prophet ﷺ saw the people watching his every step during the Farewell Hajj and told them: 'Take from me your rites, for perhaps I will not perform Hajj after this year of mine.'

questionEn: In his famous sermon during the Farewell Pilgrimage (10 AH), how did the Prophet ﷺ illustrate the inviolable sanctity of every believer's blood, property, and honor?
optionsEn: By comparing their sanctity to the sanctity of that Sacred Day (Day of Sacrifice / Arafat), in that Sacred Month (Dhul-Hijjah), in that Sacred City (Makkah)
By comparing them to the walls of Constantinople and Damascus
By writing them on a bronze plaque hung upon Mount Thawr
By comparing them to the pearls of the Persian Gulf and the gold of Yemen
explanationEn: After asking the assembled multitude what day, month, and city they were in, the Prophet ﷺ proclaimed: 'Indeed, your blood, your property, and your honor are sacred to you, like the sanctity of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this city (Makkah) of yours!'

questionEn: During the Farewell Sermon in 10 AH, which two specific examples from his own clan of Banu Hashim did the Prophet ﷺ use to show that the blood feuds and usury (Riba) of Jahiliyyah were abolished starting with his own family?
optionsEn: The inheritance of Abu Talib and the orchards of Khaybar
The blood feud of Rabi'ah ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib and the usury (Riba) of his uncle Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib
The trade debts of Abu Lahab and the ransom of Aqil ibn Abi Talib
The dowries of Banu Makhzum and the grazing rights of Marr al-Zahran
explanationEn: Leading by personal and familial example before asking others to comply, the Prophet ﷺ declared in his Farewell Sermon that the first blood claim of Jahiliyyah he waived was that of the infant son of Rabi'ah ibn al-Harith, and the first usury (Riba) he abolished was all the Riba of Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib.

questionEn: Which monumental verse of the Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ while he stood at Arafat on the Friday afternoon of his Farewell Pilgrimage (10 AH)?
optionsEn: 'And prepare against them whatever you are able of power' (Surah Al-Anfal 8:60)
'O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites' (Surah At-Tawbah 9:73)
'This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion' (Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:3)
'Read in the Name of your Lord Who created' (Surah Al-Alaq 96:1)
explanationEn: As Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) explained in Sahih al-Bukhari (45), he knew the exact place and day when Surah Al-Ma'idah (5:3) was revealed: while the Prophet ﷺ was standing at Arafat on a Friday during the Farewell Pilgrimage.

questionEn: When Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) met his governor of Makkah, Nafi' ibn Abd al-Harith, at 'Usfan and learned that Nafi' had appointed the freedman (mawla) Ibn Abza over the people of Makkah because he was a reciter of the Qur'an and scholar of inheritance law, what hadith did Umar quote in approval?
optionsEn: 'No freedman may lead prayers outside the city of Madinah'
'Leadership belongs only to the wealthiest merchants of Banu Makhzum'
'Only elders above the age of sixty may judge between the people of the Valley'
'Indeed, Allah raises by this Book (the Qur'an) some peoples and lowers by it others'
explanationEn: Recorded in Sahih Muslim (817), when Nafi' ibn Abd al-Harith explained that he had placed Ibn Abza in charge of Makkah because of his mastery of the Book of Allah and al-Fara'id (inheritance jurisprudence), Umar (RA) praised the decision by quoting the Prophet's ﷺ words: 'Indeed, Allah elevates by this Book some peoples and brings down by it others.'

questionEn: Why did Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) construct stone flood-control embankments and dams in upper Makkah during his caliphate?
optionsEn: To divert violent flash floods (suyul) such as the 'Umm Nahshal' flood that swept down the steep mountain ravines into the valley of Makkah
To create a defensive moat against naval raids from the Red Sea
To power waterwheels for grinding grain near Dar al-Nadwah
To store rainwater for irrigating wheat fields inside the courtyard
explanationEn: Because Makkah sits in a narrow basin surrounded by steep rocky mountains, sudden torrential rains caused flash floods—such as the famous 'Umm Nahshal' flood during Umar's (RA) reign—prompting Umar to build stone diversion embankments in upper Makkah to protect the Sanctuary and homes.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Azraqi; Tarikh al-Tabari

questionEn: In the year 26 AH (646 CE), which Rightly Guided Caliph responded to the petition of the people of Makkah by designating Jeddah as Makkah's official Red Sea port in place of the older port of Al-Shu'aybah?
optionsEn: Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA)
Uthman ibn Affan (RA)
Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA)
Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA)
explanationEn: In 26 AH, the merchants and residents of Makkah asked Caliph Uthman ibn Affan (RA) to move their maritime port from Al-Shu'aybah (south of Makkah) to Jeddah because Jeddah was closer to Makkah and safer for ships; Uthman traveled to Jeddah, inspected it, and officially established it as Makkah's port.
reference: Akhbar Makkah by Al-Fakihi; Mu'jam al-Buldan by Yaqut al-Hamawi

questionEn: Which companion—the cousin of the Prophet ﷺ—settled in Makkah to establish its renowned School of Tafsir and Fiqh, earning the titles 'Hibr al-Ummah' (Scholar of the Ummah) and 'Turjuman al-Qur'an' (Interpreter of the Qur'an)?
optionsEn: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (RA)
Abu al-Darda' (RA)
Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA)
Mu'adh ibn Jabal (RA)
explanationEn: Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA), for whom the Prophet ﷺ prayed 'O Allah, grant him deep understanding in religion and teach him interpretation (ta'wil)' (Sahih al-Bukhari 143, 3756), spent his later years teaching in Makkah, where he founded the great Makkan School of Qur'anic exegesis.

questionEn: How did Mujahid ibn Jabr al-Makki (d. 104 AH), the foremost Tabi'i scholar of the Makkan School of Tafsir, describe his rigorous method of studying the Qur'an under Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA) in Makkah?
optionsEn: 'I attended his circle only during the last ten nights of Ramadan'
'I memorized his poetry anthology without asking about the verses'
'I copied his written commentary once during the three days of Mina'
'I presented the Mushaf to Ibn Abbas three times from its opening to its conclusion, stopping him at every single verse to ask him what it was revealed about and how it came to be'
explanationEn: Mujahid ibn Jabr al-Makki testified: 'I reviewed the Mushaf with Ibn Abbas three times from Al-Fatihah to its end, stopping at every verse to ask him concerning what and how it was revealed'—making Mujahid the most authoritative transmitter of Makkan Tafsir.
reference: Tafsir al-Tabari, Introduction; Siyar A'lam al-Nubala'

questionEn: Which eminent Tabi'i scholar of Makkah (d. 114 AH)—a humble former freedman (mawla) of African descent—rose through piety and sacred knowledge to become the undisputed Mufti of Makkah during the Hajj season?
optionsEn: 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah
Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri
Ibrahim al-Nakha'i
Al-Hasan al-Basri
explanationEn: 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah (d. 114 AH), a student of Ibn Abbas and Aisha (RA), became such an authority on the rites of Hajj and sacred law in Makkah that the Umayyad caliphs instructed their public herald during Hajj to announce: 'Let no one issue fatwa to the people except 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah!'
reference: Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' by Al-Dhahabi; Tahdhib al-Kamal

questionEn: Which student and freedman (mawla) of Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA) became one of the foremost scholars of the Makkan School in both Qur'anic Tafsir and the prophetic biography (Maghazi)?
optionsEn: Makhul al-Shami (scholar of Damascus)
'Ikrimah al-Barbari (mawla of Ibn Abbas)
Qatadah ibn Di'amah (scholar of Basra)
Nafi' (mawla of Ibn Umar in Madinah)
explanationEn: 'Ikrimah (d. 105 AH), the longtime student and freedman of Ibn Abbas (RA), mastered the Qur'anic sciences and Seerah in Makkah, so much so that ash-Sha'bi remarked: 'There remains no one more knowledgeable of the Book of Allah than 'Ikrimah.'
reference: Siyar A'lam al-Nubala'; Tabaqat Ibn Sa'd

questionEn: Which 2nd-century Hijri scholar of Makkah (d. 150 AH), a student of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, is recognized by historians of Hadith as the first scholar in Makkah to systematically classify Hadith into topical chapters (tasnif)?
optionsEn: Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak
Al-Awza'i
Ibn Jurayj (Abd al-Malik ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Jurayj)
Al-Layth ibn Sa'd
explanationEn: Abd al-Malik ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Jurayj (d. 150 AH), the leading scholar of Makkah after 'Ata', was praised by Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others as the pioneer of systematic Hadith compilation (tasnif al-kutub) in Makkah.
reference: Siyar A'lam al-Nubala'; Tahdhib al-Tahdhib by Ibn Hajar

questionEn: Which renowned Muhaddith of the Sanctuary of Makkah (d. 198 AH) performed Hajj seventy times, linked the Tabi'un to the generation of Imam al-Shafi'i and Imam Ahmad, and led Makkah's premier Hadith circle?
optionsEn: Waki' ibn al-Jarrah (of Kufa)
Sufyan al-Thawri (of Kufa)
Shu'bah ibn al-Hajjaj (of Basra)
Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah
explanationEn: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah (107–198 AH) settled in Makkah as the Shaykh al-Islam and Muhaddith of the Haram; Imam al-Shafi'i said of him: 'Were it not for Malik and Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, the knowledge of the Hijaz would have departed.'

questionEn: Which famous 2nd-century ascetic and Hadith scholar settled in Makkah to devote his life to worship near the Sanctuary, earning the title ''Abid al-Haramayn' (The Devout Worshipper of the Two Sacred Mosques)?
optionsEn: Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad (d. 187 AH)
Ma'ruf al-Karkhi
Bishr al-Hafi
Al-Junayd al-Baghdadi
explanationEn: Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad (d. 187 AH), after his sincere repentance in youth, studied Hadith and settled in Makkah, where he became known as 'Abid al-Haramayn for his profound devotion, humility, and wise counsel to scholars and caliphs alike.
reference: Siyar A'lam al-Nubala', Vol. 8; Hilyat al-Awliya'

questionEn: Which of the four great Imams of Sunni jurisprudence—a descendant of Al-Muttalib of Quraysh—was brought by his mother as a toddler from Gaza to grow up in Makkah, where he memorized the Qur'an at age seven and studied under Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah and Muslim ibn Khalid al-Zanji?
optionsEn: Imam Malik ibn Anas (d. 179 AH)
Imam Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i (d. 204 AH)
Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (d. 241 AH)
Imam Abu Hanifah al-Nu'man (d. 150 AH)
explanationEn: Imam al-Shafi'i (150–204 AH) belonged to Banu al-Muttalib of Quraysh; his mother brought him from Gaza to Makkah at age two so he would grow up among his kin, where he mastered pure Arabic among Banu Hudhayl and studied under the Mufti of Makkah, Muslim ibn Khalid al-Zanji, before traveling to study under Imam Malik in Madinah.
reference: Manaqib al-Shafi'i by Al-Bayhaqi; Siyar A'lam al-Nubala'

questionEn: Which 3rd-century Hijri Makkan historian authored the foundational multi-volume chronicle 'Akhbar Makkah' (Reports of Makkah), preserving the earliest topographical and historical accounts of the Sacred City?
optionsEn: Al-Maqrizi al-Misri (d. 845 AH)
Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi (d. 463 AH)
Abu al-Walid Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Azraqi (d. c. 250 AH)
Ibn Khaldun al-Hadrami (d. 808 AH)
explanationEn: Abu al-Walid al-Azraqi (d. c. 250 AH), followed closely by Abu Abdullah al-Fakihi (d. c. 272 AH), compiled the earliest surviving comprehensive history and topography of Makkah, *Akhbar Makkah wa ma ja'a fiha min al-Athar*.

questionEn: What was 'Darb Zubaydah,' the celebrated Abbasid infrastructure project named after Queen Zubaydah bint Ja'far (wife of Caliph Harun al-Rashid)?
optionsEn: A maritime canal dug between the Nile River and the port of Jeddah
A diplomatic courier road between Baghdad and Constantinople
A covered market street connecting Mount Safa to Mount Thawr
An engineered overland pilgrimage route stretching approximately 1,400 km from Kufa in Iraq to Makkah, equipped with stone water reservoirs, wells, rest stations, and beacon towers
explanationEn: Queen Zubaydah bint Ja'far (d. 216 AH / 831 CE) endowed vast sums to upgrade the Kufa–Makkah pilgrimage highway (Darb Zubaydah) with stone-lined rainwater cisterns (biraks), wells, milestones, and rest houses to protect pilgrims crossing the desert to Makkah.
reference: Wafayat al-A'yan by Ibn Khallikan; Mu'jam al-Buldan

questionEn: How did 'Ayn Zubaydah—commissioned by Queen Zubaydah bint Ja'far after she witnessed the acute water shortage suffered by pilgrims in Makkah—supply fresh water to Makkah and the Mash'ar sites for over a millennium?
optionsEn: Through a masterfully engineered stone aqueduct that channeled mountain spring water from Wadi Nu'man and Wadi Hunayn across valleys and tunnels to Arafat, Muzdalifah, Mina, and Makkah
By diverting the underground stream of Khaybar southward across the Hijaz
By towing icebergs from the Mediterranean Sea to the coast of Jeddah
By boiling seawater in copper cauldrons along the shore of Shu'aybah
explanationEn: 'Ayn Zubaydah was one of the greatest hydraulic engineering feats of the pre-modern Islamic world, channeling sweet water from the springs of Wadi Hunayn and Wadi Nu'man through subterranean masonry channels and arched aqueducts to quench the thirst of pilgrims in Arafat, Mina, and Makkah for more than a thousand years.
reference: Wafayat al-A'yan by Ibn Khallikan; Rihlat Ibn Jubayr

questionEn: When the chief engineer of 'Ayn Zubaydah warned Queen Zubaydah bint Ja'far that cutting the water channel through the hard mountain rock to Makkah would cost an astronomical fortune, what famous reply did she give?
optionsEn: 'Stop the excavation at Arafat and let the pilgrims carry water on camels'
'Carry out the work, even if every single strike of the pickaxe costs a dinar of gold!'
'Use wooden troughs instead of stone masonry to reduce the expense'
'Levy a special toll at the gates of Makkah to pay the stonemasons'
explanationEn: When informed of the immense expense required to cut through the rocky terrain around Makkah, Queen Zubaydah famously instructed her treasurer and engineers: 'Do it, even if every blow of the pickaxe (kullu darbat mi'wal) costs a dinar!'—and later burned the financial ledgers to seek reward solely from Allah.
reference: Wafayat al-A'yan by Ibn Khallikan, Vol. 2

questionEn: What major relief did Sultan Salahuddin al-Ayyubi (Saladin) institute for pilgrims visiting Makkah in the 6th century AH (12th century CE), as witnessed and praised by the traveler Ibn Jubayr?
optionsEn: He built a railway bridge across the Red Sea from Sinai to Yanbu
He exempted the people of Egypt from performing Tawaf al-Wada'
He abolished the oppressive custom taxes and tolls (mukus) previously forced upon pilgrims at Jeddah and Makkah, compensating the local Emir annually with grain and funds from Egypt
He relocated the seasonal markets of Mina to the coast of Jeddah
explanationEn: Before Salahuddin al-Ayyubi, poor pilgrims arriving at Jeddah and Makkah were subjected to heavy, extortionate pilgrim taxes (mukus) and detained if unable to pay; Salahuddin abolished those taxes entirely and sent annual shipments of grain and stipends from Egypt to the Emir and people of Makkah in their stead.

questionEn: Which 6th-century AH (12th-century CE) Andalusian scholar and traveler from Valencia spent more than eight months in Makkah (579 AH / 1183 CE) and recorded a detailed eyewitness chronicle of its Ramadan nights, scholarly circles, and markets?
optionsEn: Ibn Fadlan (envoy to the Volga Bulgars)
Evliya Çelebi (Ottoman chronicler)
Al-Idrisi (author of Nuzhat al-Mushtaq)
Ibn Jubayr (Abu al-Husayn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Jubayr)
explanationEn: Ibn Jubayr (540–614 AH / 1145–1217 CE) stayed in Makkah for over eight months in 579 AH (1183–1184 CE) and authored *Rihlat Ibn Jubayr*, one of the richest historical eyewitness descriptions of medieval Makkah.

questionEn: When Ibn Jubayr visited the markets of Makkah in 579 AH and marveled at the remarkable variety of fresh figs, grapes, pomegranates, peaches, and vegetables brought from Ta'if and nearby valleys into an arid basin, which Qur'anic prayer did he note was visibly fulfilled before his eyes?
optionsEn: The prayer of Prophet Ibrahim (AS) in Surah Ibrahim (14:37): 'And provide for them from the fruits so that they may be grateful'
The prayer of Prophet Nuh (AS) for a blessed landing place
The prayer of Prophet Sulayman (AS) for a kingdom unlike any after him
The prayer of Prophet Musa (AS) for twelve springs in the desert
explanationEn: In *Rihlat Ibn Jubayr*, after describing the extraordinary quality of fruits, melons, and honey flowing daily into barren Makkah from Ta'if and surrounding wadis, Ibn Jubayr wrote that anyone witnessing it sees the living miracle of Ibrahim's (AS) supplication for Makkah's provision of fruits (Qur'an 2:126, 14:37).

questionEn: Which renowned 8th-century AH (14th-century CE) Moroccan traveler from Tangier visited Makkah multiple times beginning in 726 AH (1326 CE), stayed there as a resident student (mujawir), and praised the Makkans' generosity, cleanliness, and care for the needy?
optionsEn: Al-Mas'udi (author of Muruj al-Dhahab)
Ibn Battuta (Shams al-Din Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Lawati)
Ahmad ibn Majid (the Arab navigator)
Leo Africanus (Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Wazzan)
explanationEn: In *Tuhfat al-Nuzzar fi Ghara'ib al-Amsar* (*Rihlat Ibn Battuta*), Ibn Battuta recounted his multiple pilgrimages and years of residence (jiwar) in Makkah, praising its inhabitants for their noble character, clean white attire, chivalry, and devotion to weak and stranded pilgrims.

questionEn: In classical Islamic history, what term was used for scholars and pious worshippers who chose to reside in Makkah alongside the Sacred Mosque to dedicate their time to knowledge, worship, and serving pilgrims?
optionsEn: Al-Warrakun (commercial paper merchants)
Al-Murabitun (frontier garrison horsemen)
Al-Mujawirun (practicing 'Al-Jiwar'—pious neighborhood/residence by the Sanctuary)
Al-Muhtasibun (municipal market inspectors)
explanationEn: Throughout Islamic history, scholars and seekers of knowledge who settled in Makkah (or Madinah) to study and worship next to the Sanctuary were known as *Mujawirun* (residents in *jiwar* of the Sacred House).
reference: Rihlat Ibn Battuta; Al-'Iqd al-Thamin fi Tarikh al-Balad al-Amin by Al-Fasi

questionEn: Which 9th-century AH Makkan scholar and judge (d. 832 AH / 1429 CE) authored 'Al-'Iqd al-Thamin fi Tarikh al-Balad al-Amin' and 'Shifa' al-Gharam,' two of the most comprehensive biographical and historical encyclopedias of Makkah?
optionsEn: Ibn 'Asakir al-Dimashqi
Ibn Khallikan al-Irbili
Al-Sakhawi al-Qahiri
Taqi al-Din Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Fasi al-Makki
explanationEn: Taqi al-Din al-Fasi (775–832 AH), the Maliki Qadi and historian of Makkah, authored *Shifa' al-Gharam bi-Akhbar al-Balad al-Haram* and the multi-volume biographical dictionary of Makkah's scholars and notables, *Al-'Iqd al-Thamin fi Tarikh al-Balad al-Amin*.
reference: Shifa' al-Gharam by Taqi al-Din al-Fasi

questionEn: In the medieval Mamluk and Ottoman eras, what were the 'Ribat' and 'Madrasah' endowments constructed around Makkah designed to provide?
optionsEn: Free lodging, stipends, libraries, and teaching halls for indigent pilgrims, widows, students of sacred knowledge, and visiting scholars in Makkah
Military barracks and artillery foundries for coastal warfare
Customs warehouses for taxing silk shipments from China
Private hunting lodges for governors in the Sacred Precinct
explanationEn: Endowed *Ribats* (charitable hospices) and *Madrasahs* (such as Madrasah al-Sawlatiyyah later in the 19th century and earlier Mamluk/Ottoman endowments) provided free accommodation, food, and scholarship for poor pilgrims and students of knowledge in Makkah.
reference: Shifa' al-Gharam by Al-Fasi; Rihlat Ibn Battuta

questionEn: During the Ottoman era, what was the 'Surrah' (Surre-i Hümayun) sent annually with the official pilgrimage caravan to Makkah and Madinah?
optionsEn: A tax register demanding annual tribute from the Bedouin tribes of the Hijaz
An imperial charitable purse of gold coins, waqf revenues, food provisions, and stipends distributed to the scholars, mosque servants, and poor residents of Makkah and Madinah
A military decree conscripting the youth of Makkah into the naval fleet
A collection of astronomical instruments sent to Mount Abu Qubays
explanationEn: The *Surrah* (charitable purse) was an annual endowment convoy dispatched during the Mamluk and Ottoman centuries to distribute stipends, grain, and financial aid from pious endowments (awqaf) across the Muslim world to the scholars, muezzins, caretakers, and needy inhabitants of Makkah and Madinah.
reference: Mir'at al-Haramayn by Ibrahim Rif'at Pasha

questionEn: In the modern era, what did King Abdulaziz Al Saud order in the 1920s (1344–1346 AH) to ensure the safety of pilgrims traveling to Makkah after centuries of desert highway banditry?
optionsEn: He restricted the pilgrimage only to travelers arriving by steamship from India
He required every pilgrim caravan to hire private foreign mercenaries
He established strict security along all pilgrimage routes to Makkah, abolished tribal road tolls (khuwwah), and introduced organized motor transport and public health services for pilgrims
He closed the overland routes from Najd and Iraq for fifty years
explanationEn: One of the most transformative modern developments in Makkah's history was the establishment of complete road security across the Hijaz, ending centuries of Bedouin raids and illegal tribal tolls (*khuwwah*) on pilgrims, alongside establishing public health quarantines and motor transport.
reference: Tarikh Makkah al-Mukarramah; King Abdulaziz Foundation (Darah) Archives

questionEn: What is the primary modern rail system inaugurated in 2018 (1440 AH) that links Makkah and Madinah via Jeddah and King Abdulaziz International Airport at speeds of up to 300 km/h?
optionsEn: The Hijaz Steam Railway of 1908
The Red Sea Coastal Freight Line
The Darb Zubaydah Monorail
The Haramain High-Speed Railway (Qitar al-Haramayn al-Sari')
explanationEn: The Haramain High-Speed Railway is a 450-kilometer electrified double-track rail network connecting Makkah, Jeddah, King Abdulaziz International Airport, King Abdullah Economic City, and Madinah, reducing travel time between the Two Holy Cities to roughly two hours.
reference: Saudi Railways / Haramain High-Speed Railway Official Documentation

questionEn: Which five stations are directly served by the Haramain High-Speed Railway connecting Makkah and Madinah?
optionsEn: Makkah (Al-Rusaifah), Jeddah (Al-Sulaymaniyah), King Abdulaziz International Airport, King Abdullah Economic City (Rabigh), and Madinah
Makkah, Ta'if, Badr, Khaybar, and Tabuk
Makkah, Mina, Muzdalifah, Arafat, and Ji'ranah
Makkah, Yanbu, Duba, Al-'Ula, and Madinah
explanationEn: The Haramain High-Speed Railway operates five passenger stations: Makkah Station (in Al-Rusaifah district), Jeddah Central Station, King Abdulaziz International Airport Station, King Abdullah Economic City Station in Rabigh, and Madinah Station.

questionEn: What is the specialized metro rail system operating inside Makkah's sacred sites during the Hajj season to transport hundreds of thousands of pilgrims between Arafat, Muzdalifah, and Mina?
optionsEn: The Jabal al-Nur Cable Car
Al-Mashaaer Al-Muqaddassah Metro Line (The Sacred Sites Train)
The Tihamah Underground Subway
The Qarn al-Manazil Express
explanationEn: Inaugurated in 2010 (1431 AH), the Al-Mashaaer Al-Muqaddassah Metro Line runs across nine stations linking Arafat 1–3, Muzdalifah 1–3, and Mina 1–3 (Jamarat), replacing tens of thousands of buses and dramatically easing pilgrim movement.
reference: Royal Commission for Makkah City and Holy Sites

questionEn: Under which charitable Islamic endowment (Waqf) was the Makkah Royal Clock Tower complex (Abraj al-Bayt) constructed so that its revenues directly fund the maintenance and operations of the Two Holy Mosques?
optionsEn: The Darb Zubaydah Trust of Baghdad
The Hijaz Agricultural Cooperative
The King Abdulaziz Endowment for the Two Holy Mosques (Waqf al-Malik Abdulaziz li-l-Haramayn al-Sharifayn)
The Suez Maritime Navigation Company
explanationEn: The Abraj al-Bayt / Makkah Royal Clock Tower complex was established as an Islamic charitable endowment—Waqf al-Malik Abdulaziz li-l-Haramayn— dedicating its lease and hospitality revenues to the upkeep and service of the Sacred Mosque.
reference: King Abdulaziz Endowment for the Two Holy Mosques Documentation

questionEn: Beyond serving as a visual timekeeping landmark for pilgrims in Makkah, what educational and scientific institution is housed at the top of the Makkah Royal Clock Tower?
optionsEn: An international stock exchange floor for maritime shipping
A botanical greenhouse for cultivating Mediterranean olive trees
A military radar base for Red Sea naval vessels
The Clock Tower Museum (housing exhibitions on astronomy, lunar crescent observation, Islamic timekeeping instruments, and the architecture of the Two Holy Mosques)
explanationEn: The upper four floors of the Makkah Royal Clock Tower house the Clock Tower Museum, operated by the Misk Foundation, featuring galleries on the cosmos, solar and lunar calculation of prayer times and the Hijri calendar, and the precision engineering of the Makkah Clock.

questionEn: Which iconic terminal at King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah—famous for its award-winning white fiberglass fabric roof modeled on desert pilgrim tents—serves as the primary dedicated air gateway for millions of Hajj and Umrah pilgrims bound for Makkah?
optionsEn: The Hajj Terminal at King Abdulaziz International Airport
The Qarn al-Manazil Airfield
The Rabigh Industrial Cargo Hub
The Al-Shu'aybah Maritime Pier
explanationEn: Designed to shelter vast numbers of arriving pilgrims in natural cross-ventilated shade, the tent-roofed Hajj Terminal at King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah (winner of the Aga Khan Award for Architecture) is the world's largest specialized aviation terminal dedicated to pilgrims traveling to Makkah.
reference: General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA); Aga Khan Award for Architecture Archives

questionEn: What is 'Nusuk,' the official unified digital platform launched to serve visitors traveling to Makkah and Madinah?
optionsEn: An archaeological database cataloguing Nabataean pottery in northern Arabia
The official smart digital portal and mobile application providing Umrah/Hajj permit booking, visa facilitation, multilingual religious guidance, and logistical support for pilgrims
A medieval manuscript dictionary printed in Cairo
A weather satellite monitoring rainfall over the Indian Ocean
explanationEn: Launched by the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah under the Pilgrim Experience Program, Nusuk serves as the official unified digital gateway helping pilgrims worldwide plan their visit to Makkah and Madinah, schedule permits, and access step-by-step multilingual spiritual guidance.
reference: Ministry of Hajj and Umrah, Nusuk Platform

questionEn: How does Makkah's modern pilgrim infrastructure combat extreme heat stress along the pedestrian pathways of Arafat, Mina, and the approaches to Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: By enclosing the entire valley of Arafat inside an airtight glass dome
By restricting all pilgrimage rites exclusively to the winter months regardless of the lunar calendar
Through thousands of high-pressure water-mist cooling columns, shaded canopies, heat-reflective white road surfaces, and chilled water stations
By requiring pilgrims to travel only in armored underground vehicles
explanationEn: Because the Hijri calendar is lunar and Hajj rotates through intense summer months, extensive heat-mitigation technologies—including evaporative water-mist fan columns that lower ambient air temperatures by several degrees, white heat-reflective asphalt coatings, and shaded walkways—are deployed across Makkah and the Mash'ar sites.
reference: Royal Commission for Makkah City and Holy Sites; Ministry of Hajj and Umrah

questionEn: How are emergency and hospital healthcare services provided to Hajj pilgrims who fall ill or require surgery in Makkah, Mina, and Arafat?
optionsEn: By evacuating every patient by ship to hospitals in Alexandria
Only after the completion of the Days of Tashreeq in Muharram
Only through private commercial clinics that require advance gold deposits
Free of charge through a dedicated network of hospitals, intensive-care units, field clinics, and air/ground ambulances operated by the Ministry of Health across Makkah and the sacred sites
explanationEn: During the Hajj season, a comprehensive network of specialized hospitals (such as Al-Noor Specialist Hospital, King Abdullah Medical City in Makkah, and seasonal hospitals in Mina and Arafat) provides emergency, surgical, cardiac, and heat-stroke care free of charge to pilgrims.
reference: Ministry of Health Hajj Medical Services Reports

questionEn: What major multi-level engineering structure in Mina near Makkah was transformed in the 21st century with multiple stories, unidirectional pedestrian ramps, and air-conditioned shading to allow hundreds of thousands of pilgrims per hour to perform the stoning ritual safely?
optionsEn: The Jamarat Bridge facility (Jisr al-Jamarat) in Mina
The Aqueduct of 'Ayn Zubaydah in Wadi Nu'man
The Viaduct of Marr al-Zahran
The Causeway of Al-Shu'aybah on the Red Sea
explanationEn: To prevent crowd bottlenecks during the stoning of the three Jamarat in Mina, the modern multi-story Jamarat Bridge was engineered with elliptical basin pillars, segregated entry/exit levels connected to tent camps and the Mashaaer Metro, and cooling ventilation.
reference: Royal Commission for Makkah City and Holy Sites

questionEn: Which industrial complex established in Makkah is dedicated to manufacturing the Kiswah and providing artisanal maintenance for the textiles of the Sacred Sanctuary?
optionsEn: The Silk Weavers Guild of Damascus
The King Abdulaziz Complex for the Kiswah of the Kaaba (in the Umm al-Jud district of Makkah)
The Dar al-Tiraz Textile Mill of Alexandria
The Quba Loom Workshop of Madinah
explanationEn: Originally established by King Abdulaziz in 1346 AH (1927 CE) in Makkah (when imports from Egypt were disrupted) and later expanded at Umm al-Jud as the King Abdulaziz Complex for the Holy Kaaba Kiswah, it employs skilled Saudi calligraphers and weavers inside Makkah itself.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque

questionEn: According to Surah Al-Hajj (22:25) and the explanation of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (RA), what makes the spiritual accountability of a person inside the Sacred Sanctuary of Makkah unique compared to any other place on earth?
optionsEn: In Makkah, financial debts between merchants are automatically canceled each year
In Makkah, fasting the month of Ramadan is optional for residents

In Makkah, a person is warned of painful punishment even for firmly intending deviation and wrongdoing (man yurid fihi bi-ilhadin bi-zulmin), whereas elsewhere an unacted evil intention is not recorded until acted upon
In Makkah, obligatory prayers are reduced from five daily prayers to two
explanationEn: Commenting on Surah Al-Hajj (22:25)—'And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing, We will make him taste of a painful punishment'—Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (RA) and Ibn Abbas (RA) explained that Makkah is so sacred that if a person even firmly resolves in his heart to commit a major wrong in the Haram, Allah holds him accountable for that resolve even if he is sitting in Aden.
reference: Qur'an 22:25; Musnad Ahmad 3632; Tafsir Ibn Kathir

questionEn: Why did classical scholars and companions such as Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) and Ibn Abbas (RA) express deep awe and caution regarding prolonged residence in Makkah without guarding one's heart and conduct?
optionsEn: Because trade was legally prohibited in Makkah outside the month of Dhul-Hijjah
Because marriage contracts could not be concluded by residents of Makkah
Because reading books of jurisprudence was forbidden inside the city limits
Out of reverence lest over-familiarity dull one's awe of the Sanctuary or cause one to fall into sin in a place where wrongdoing is magnified in gravity
explanationEn: Because sins committed inside the Sacred Land of Makkah carry far greater gravity due to the honor of the place (even if a single sin is still recorded as one sin, its qualitative enormity is magnified), companions like Ibn Abbas (RA) and scholars like Imam Ahmad advised anyone in Makkah to vigilantly guard their heart, tongue, and limbs.
reference: Tafsir Ibn Kathir on Qur'an 22:25; Zad al-Ma'ad by Ibn al-Qayyim

questionEn: Which three behaviors does Surah Al-Baqarah (2:197) strictly prohibit for every pilgrim who enters into the obligation of Hajj on the journey to Makkah?
optionsEn: No marital relations/obscenity (rafath), no transgression/sin (fusuq), and no quarreling/disputing (jidal) during the Hajj
No buying food, no riding mounts, and no resting in the shade
No asking questions of scholars, no carrying water skins, and no travelling at night
No wearing sandals, no drinking milk, and no speaking in one's native language
explanationEn: Allah commands in Surah Al-Baqarah (2:197): 'Hajj is during well-known months, so whoever has made Hajj obligatory upon himself therein—there is to be for him no sexual relations/obscenity (rafath), no disobedience (fusuq), and no disputing (jidal) during Hajj.'

questionEn: In light of Surah Al-Baqarah (2:198)—'There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord'—what ruling did the revelation establish regarding pilgrims engaging in honest trade and earning a livelihood in Makkah during Hajj?
optionsEn: Merchants must donate one hundred percent of their capital before entering Makkah
Honest trade and seeking livelihood during the pilgrimage season in Makkah are completely permissible and do not invalidate one's reward when sincere intention for Allah is maintained
Any pilgrim who buys or sells goods in Makkah must repeat his Hajj the following year
Only non-pilgrims are permitted to sell food or clothing in Makkah
explanationEn: Ibn Abbas (RA) narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari (1770, 2050) that in early Islam some companions felt hesitant to conduct trade during the Hajj markets of 'Ukaz, Majannah, and Dhu al-Majaz around Makkah until Allah revealed: 'There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord' (2:198).

questionEn: According to authentic hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, what is the promised reward for one who performs Hajj to the Sacred House in Makkah for Allah's sake without committing obscenity (rafath) or sin (fusuq)?
optionsEn: He is granted ownership of a palm grove in the valley of Marr al-Zahran
He is no longer required to pray the voluntary night prayers
He returns from his sins as pure as the day his mother gave birth to him
He is exempted from paying Zakat for the remainder of his life
explanationEn: Abu Hurayrah (RA) narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever performs Hajj to this House and does not commit any obscenity (rafath) or transgression (fusuq) will return as on the day his mother bore him.'

questionEn: When crowds are dense in Makkah during Tawaf or at the sacred sites, what priority do Islamic jurists establish regarding a pilgrim pushing or harming fellow Muslims in order to reach a recommended (Sunnah) spot?
optionsEn: A strong pilgrim is encouraged to push through the weak to complete his rounds faster
Harming others in the Sanctuary is excused if done out of religious zeal
Men and women should lock arms in chains to force their way through the crowd
It is strictly forbidden to push, elbow, or harm another Muslim—preserving the safety and inviolability of a believer (which is obligatory) takes precedence over a recommended act
explanationEn: Following the Prophet's ﷺ instruction to Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) not to crowd or harm the weak when seeking to kiss the Stone ('O Umar, you are a strong man; do not crowd the weak, neither harm anyone nor be harmed'), jurists unanimously rule that avoiding harm to fellow Muslims (wajib) always overrides performing a Sunnah act.
reference: Musnad al-Shafi'i; Al-Majmu' by Al-Nawawi, Vol. 8

questionEn: What did the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ identify as the marks of a 'Hajj Mabrur' (an accepted pilgrimage in Makkah whose only reward is Paradise) when asked by his companions how its righteousness is shown?
optionsEn: Feeding others generously (it'am al-ta'am) and spreading peace and gentle speech (ifsha' al-salam / tib al-kalam)
Spending the largest amount of gold on silk tents and ornate mounts
Arguing loudly with ignorant travelers to prove one's scholarly rank
Refusing to speak to anyone from the time of entering Makkah until returning home
explanationEn: When the Prophet ﷺ said, 'An accepted Hajj (Hajj Mabrur) has no reward except Paradise' (Sahih al-Bukhari 1773) and was asked what constitutes the righteousness (birr) of Hajj, he replied in Musnad Ahmad (14482) and Mustadrak al-Hakim: 'Feeding people (it'am al-ta'am) and speaking kindly / spreading peace.'

questionEn: When a pilgrim in Makkah sees elderly, exhausted, or lost visitors from diverse lands and languages around the Sanctuary, what spiritual perspective does Surah Al-Hajj (22:27) and prophetic etiquette call him to adopt?
optionsEn: Looking down on unlettered villagers who make mistakes in pronunciation
Viewing every pilgrim as an honored guest called by Allah from every distant mountain pass (min kulli fajjin 'amiq), treating them with humility, service, and brotherhood
Giving priority only to pilgrims who speak one's own dialect or belong to one's country
Avoiding any assistance to strangers so as not to delay one's own voluntary circuits
explanationEn: In Surah Al-Hajj (22:27) Allah commanded Ibrahim (AS) to proclaim the Hajj so people come from every distant pass, and the Prophet ﷺ described the pilgrims and Umrah performers as 'the delegation/guests of Allah (wafd Allah)—He called them and they answered Him, and they asked of Him and He gave them.'

questionEn: What ethical duty applies to merchants, hosts, and service providers in Makkah when dealing with visiting pilgrims according to the consensus of Islamic scholars?
optionsEn: Concealing defects in goods sold during the final days of Dhul-Hijjah
Charging ten times the market price to foreign travelers who do not know the local currency
Practicing complete honesty, fairness, hospitality, and compassion toward the guests of the Most Merciful, while avoiding price-gouging, deception, or exploitation
Refusing to sell water or bread except in wholesale caravan quantities
explanationEn: The Prophet ﷺ severely prohibited cheating, hoarding, and exploiting travelers ('Whoever cheats us is not one of us,' Sahih Muslim 101), and scholars of Makkah emphasized that honoring pilgrims with fair dealing and generous service is part of honoring the Sacred House of Allah (Qur'an 22:32).

questionEn: What is the enduring spiritual sign that a believer's time and worship in Makkah have been accepted by Allah after departing the Sacred City for home?
optionsEn: That the person boasts constantly in gatherings about how many times he has visited Makkah
That the person ceases giving charity in his hometown because he gave charity in Makkah
That the person considers himself free from the obligation of seeking forgiveness
That the person returns home with a softer heart, greater mindfulness of Allah (Taqwa), steadfastness in daily prayer, and improved character than before visiting Makkah
explanationEn: As al-Hasan al-Basri and classical scholars explained regarding the sign of an accepted Hajj or Umrah in Makkah, the true mark of acceptance (Hajj Mabrur) is that one returns more detached from sin, more eager for the Hereafter, and better in character and obedience than before.
reference: Lata'if al-Ma'arif by Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali

questionEn: Which Surah of the Qur'an is named 'Al-Balad' (The City), referring specifically to the sacred city of Makkah?
optionsEn: Surah 90
Surah 95
Surah 106
Surah 105
explanationEn: Surah Al-Balad is the 90th chapter of the Qur'an and opens with a divine oath by the sacred city of Makkah.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Balad (90:1-2), how does Allah address the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in relation to the city of Makkah?
optionsEn: Wait until you are a resident of this city
And you, [O Muhammad], are free of restriction (halal / lawful resident) in this city
And you will never leave this city
And you are the ruler of this city from birth
explanationEn: Allah says: 'I swear by this city (Makkah)—and you, [O Muhammad], are free of restriction (hillun) in this city'—which commentators explain both as his residing there and as the future lawfulness of its conquest for him for one hour of a day.
reference: Qur'an 90:1-2; Tafsir al-Tabari; Tafsir Ibn Kathir

questionEn: In Surah Al-Tin (95:3), by which phrase does Allah swear an oath referring to Makkah?
optionsEn: Wa Bakkata al-Mubarakah (And by blessed Bakkah)
Wa Ummil-Qura (And by the Mother of Cities)
Wa hadhal-Baladil-Amin (And by this secure city)
Wal-Qaryatil-Muharramah (And by the forbidden town)
explanationEn: In Surah Al-Tin (95:3), after swearing by the fig, the olive, and Mount Sinai, Allah swears: 'Wa hadhal-Baladil-Amin' (And by this secure city), which all commentators identify as Makkah.

questionEn: Which two Surahs of the Qur'an explicitly use the title 'Umm al-Qura' (Mother of Cities/Towns) to refer to Makkah?
optionsEn: Surah Al-Fath (48:24) and Surah Quraysh (106:1)
Surah Al-Baqarah (2:125) and Surah Al-Imran (3:96)
Surah Ibrahim (14:37) and Surah Al-Hajj (22:29)
Surah Al-An'am (6:92) and Surah Ash-Shura (42:7)
explanationEn: Makkah is called 'Umm al-Qura' in Surah Al-An'am (6:92) and Surah Ash-Shura (42:7): 'that you may warn the Mother of Cities (Umm al-Qura) and those around it.'

questionEn: Why did classical scholars explain that Makkah was given the Qur'anic title 'Umm al-Qura' (Mother of Cities)?
optionsEn: Because all believers turn toward it in prayer, pilgrims gather in it, and the earth was spread out (duhiyat) from beneath it
Because it had the largest agricultural markets in Arabia
Because it was the capital of the Roman and Persian trade leagues
Because it was the only walled city in the Hijaz
explanationEn: Exegetes such as Al-Tabari, Al-Qurtubi, and Ibn Kathir state that Makkah is called Umm al-Qura because it is the Qiblah and sanctuary to which all towns turn, the most honored of all cities, and the point from which the earth was spread out.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Imran (3:96), which ancient name of Makkah is used when describing the first House of worship established for mankind?
optionsEn: Yathrib
Bakkah
Taybah
Faran
explanationEn: Allah says in Surah Al-Imran (3:96): 'Indeed, the first House [of worship] established for mankind was that at Bakkah—blessed and a guidance for the worlds.'

questionEn: What linguistic explanation did Companion Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA) and classical lexicographers give for the name 'Bakkah' (from the root b-k-k)?
optionsEn: It comes from 'barakah', meaning abundant date palms
It comes from 'bukaa', meaning a place where rain weeps continuously
It comes from 'yabukku', meaning it crowds people together and humbles the necks of tyrants
It was named after a Nabataean king named Bakka
explanationEn: Scholars explain that 'Bakkah' derives from 'bakk' (crowding together or breaking/humbling pride), because pilgrims crowd closely in Tawaf and because Allah humbles the necks of every tyrant who seeks to violate its sanctity.

questionEn: Among classical scholars who distinguished between 'Bakkah' and 'Makkah', what distinction did they commonly draw?
optionsEn: Bakkah refers to the mountains, while Makkah refers to the wells
Bakkah refers to Mina and Arafah, while Makkah refers to the Kaaba
Bakkah was the name used only after the Hijrah, while Makkah was pre-Islamic
Bakkah refers specifically to the exact site of the Kaaba and Mataf, while Makkah refers to the entire surrounding city and sanctuary
explanationEn: While many linguists treat 'm' and 'b' as interchangeable labials making Bakkah and Makkah synonymous, several scholars stated that Bakkah specifically denotes the spot of the Kaaba and Mataf where pilgrims crowd, whereas Makkah encompasses the whole city.

questionEn: In which single verse of the Qur'an does the exact spelling 'Makkah' (with the letter Mim) appear explicitly?
optionsEn: Surah Al-Fath (48:24): 'in the valley of Makkah (bi-batni Makkata) after He had given you victory over them'
Surah Al-Baqarah (2:125)
Surah Quraysh (106:1)
Surah Al-Fil (105:1)
explanationEn: The exact word 'Makkah' with a Mim occurs once in the Qur'an, in Surah Al-Fath (48:24): 'And it is He who withheld their hands from you and your hands from them within the valley of Makkah (bi-batni Makkata)...'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Qasas (28:85), Allah promises the Prophet ﷺ: 'Indeed, He who imposed upon you the Qur'an will surely take you back to a place of return (Ma'ad).' How did Ibn Abbas (RA) interpret 'Ma'ad'?
optionsEn: Ta'if
Makkah, to which Allah returned the Prophet ﷺ victorious at its Conquest
Jerusalem
Abyssinia
explanationEn: As recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA) explained that 'la-radduka ila Ma'ad' in Surah Al-Qasas (28:85) means: 'He will surely return you to Makkah.'

questionEn: How did Prophet Ibrahim (AS) describe the geography of Makkah in his supplication in Surah Ibrahim (14:37)?
optionsEn: Bi-jabalil-zaytun (Upon the mount of olives)
Bi-jannatin dhati anharin (In a garden of flowing rivers)
Bi-wadin ghayri dhi zar'in (In a valley without cultivation, near Your Sacred House)
Bi-qaryatin kathiratil-ashjar (In a town of abundant orchards)
explanationEn: Ibrahim (AS) prayed: 'Our Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in an uncultivated valley (bi-wadin ghayri dhi zar'in) near Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer.'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Qasas (28:57), how did Allah remind the Quraysh of the unique blessing of living in Makkah while surrounding tribes lived in fear of raids?
optionsEn: Have We not exempted them from all trade journeys?
Have We not given them the largest army in the peninsula?
Have We not built for them high fortress walls of stone?
Have We not established for them a safe sanctuary (Haraman Aminan), to which are brought the fruits of all things as provision from Us?
explanationEn: When some among Quraysh claimed following guidance would cause them to be snatched from their land, Allah replied: 'Have We not established for them a safe sanctuary (Haraman Aminan), to which are brought the fruits of all things as provision from Us?'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Ankabut (29:67), what contrast does Allah draw between the Sanctuary of Makkah and the lands around it?
optionsEn: Have they not seen that We made [Makkah] a safe sanctuary (Haraman Aminan), while people are being taken away (kidnapped/raided) all around them?
Have they not seen that Makkah has colder winters than the lands around it?
Have they not seen that Makkah has more rivers than Yemen?
Have they not seen that nobody ever travels outside Makkah?
explanationEn: Surah Al-Ankabut (29:67) highlights Allah's protection over Makkah: while Arab tribes across the peninsula suffered constant raids and abductions, residents of the Makkan Haram lived in inviolable security.

questionEn: In Surah An-Naml (27:91), how does the Prophet ﷺ describe his divine command regarding the Lord of Makkah?
optionsEn: I have been commanded to tax every caravan entering this city
I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city (Rabb hadhihil-Baldah), who made it sacred and to whom belongs all things
I have been commanded to rebuild the walls of this city
I have been commanded to leave this city forever without looking back
explanationEn: In Surah An-Naml (27:91), Allah instructs the Prophet ﷺ to proclaim: 'I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city (Baldah), who made it sacred (alladhi harramaha) and to whom [belongs] all things.'

questionEn: In Surah Quraysh (106:1-4), what two great blessings connected to the Kaaba does Allah command the Quraysh to be grateful for by worshipping 'the Lord of this House'?
optionsEn: Making them rulers over Persia and Byzantium
Giving them gold mines and silver mines in the Hijaz
Feeding them against hunger (at'amahum min ju') and securing them from fear (wa amanahum min khawf) during their winter and summer trade journeys
Giving them perennial rivers and olive groves
explanationEn: Because the Quraysh were the custodians of Allah's Sacred House in Makkah, tribes respected their winter journey to Yemen and summer journey to Ash-Sham; thus Allah commanded: 'Let them worship the Lord of this House, Who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Ma'idah (5:97), what term does Allah use for the Kaaba to describe how He made it a means of uprightness, maintenance, and stability for mankind?
optionsEn: Qal'atan lil-junud (A citadel for soldiers)
Malja'an lil-muluk (A palace for kings)
Suqan lil-tujjar (A marketplace for merchants)
Qiyaman lil-nas (A means of standing/support/maintenance for mankind)
explanationEn: Allah says in Surah Al-Ma'idah (5:97): 'Allah has made the Kaaba, the Sacred House, a means of standing/stability for mankind (qiyaman lil-nas), and [also] the sacred month and the sacrificial animals and the garlands.'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hajj (22:25), how does Allah describe the legal status of the native resident of Makkah (al-'akif fihi) and the visiting outsider (wal-bad) inside Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Equal therein (sawa'an al-'akifu fihi wal-bad)
The native resident owns the Mosque and may charge visitors rent
The outsider has priority only during Ramadan
Only the tribe of Quraysh may pray near the Kaaba
explanationEn: Surah Al-Hajj (22:25) declares that Allah made Al-Masjid al-Haram for all mankind—'equal therein is the resident and the visitor (sawa'an al-'akifu fihi wal-bad).' Classical jurists deduced from this the universal right of Muslims to worship in Al-Haram and historic discussions on renting Makkan properties.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hajj (22:25), what severe warning does Allah issue concerning anyone who intends deviation and wrongdoing (bi-ilhadin bi-zulmin) inside Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: His wealth will be doubled in this world
We will make him taste of a painful punishment (nudhiqhu min 'adhabin alim)
His intention is overlooked unless he commits murder
He is merely fined one dirham
explanationEn: Surah Al-Hajj (22:25) states: 'And whoever intends therein [a deed] by deviation in religion or by wrongdoing—We will make him taste of a painful punishment.' Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas (RA) noted that Makkah is unique because even a firm resolve to commit evil in the Haram incurs punishment.
reference: Qur'an 22:25; Musannaf Abd al-Razzaq; Tafsir Ibn Kathir

questionEn: According to Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (RA), commenting on Surah Al-Hajj (22:25), what happens if a person firmly resolves in his heart to commit a grave injustice in the Haram of Makkah, even while he is far away in 'Adan Abyan (Aden in Yemen)?
optionsEn: He only loses half of a good deed
Nothing is recorded until he physically crosses the Miqat
Allah will make him taste a painful punishment for that firm intention against the Haram
It only applies to residents of Ta'if
explanationEn: Ibn Mas'ud (RA) explained regarding 22:25 ('wa man yurid fihi bi-ilhadin bi-zulmin'): 'Even if a man intended in 'Adan Abyan (Aden) to commit a wrongful crime in this House, Allah would make him taste a painful punishment.'
reference: Musnad Ahmad 4192; Mustadrak al-Hakim 3482; Tafsir Ibn Kathir 22:25

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah (2:125), what two descriptions does Allah pair together when naming the Kaaba as a sanctuary for humanity?
optionsEn: Masjid al-Taqwa wa Ribat al-Jihad
Dar al-Salam wa Jannat al-Ma'wa
Madinat al-Noor wa Bayt al-Hikmah
Mathabatan lil-nasi wa Amnan (A place of constant return for mankind and a place of security)
explanationEn: Allah says in Surah Al-Baqarah (2:125): 'And [mention] when We made the House a place of return for mankind and a place of security (mathabatan lil-nasi wa amnan).' Scholars explain 'mathabah' as a place people return to repeatedly without ever growing weary of longing for it.

questionEn: What is the meaning of the word 'Mathabah' (from thaba / yathubu) in Surah Al-Baqarah (2:125) regarding the Kaaba?
optionsEn: A place to which people return again and again, never feeling satisfied that they have had enough of visiting it
A stone quarry from which granite is cut
A valley that floods once every century
A fortress with seven iron gates
explanationEn: Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr explained 'mathabatan lil-nas' to mean that visitors return to the Kaaba repeatedly; whenever a believer leaves it, his heart yearns to return again.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hajj (22:29 and 22:33), the Kaaba is called 'Al-Bayt al-'Atiq' (The Ancient / Emancipated House). What two primary meanings did the Salaf give for 'Al-'Atiq'?
optionsEn: (1) The tallest building in Arabia, and (2) the House painted with gold
(1) The most ancient House on earth, and (2) the House emancipated/freed from the domination of tyrants (jababirah)
(1) The House built by the Romans, and (2) the House surrounded by palm trees
(1) The House that moves every year, and (2) the House without a roof
explanationEn: Al-Hasan al-Basri said 'Al-'Atiq' means the Ancient House (first built on earth), while Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and Qatadah explained that Allah emancipated it (a'taqahu) from ever being conquered and owned by arrogant tyrants such as Abraha.
reference: Sunan al-Tirmidhi 3170; Tafsir al-Tabari 22:29; Tafsir Ibn Kathir

questionEn: In Surah At-Tur (52:4), Allah swears by 'Al-Bayt al-Ma'mur' (The Much-Frequented House). What is the relationship between Al-Bayt al-Ma'mur in the seventh heaven and the Kaaba in Makkah?
optionsEn: Al-Bayt al-Ma'mur is located above Mount Sinai
Al-Bayt al-Ma'mur is located beneath the Well of Zamzam
Al-Bayt al-Ma'mur is directly above the earthly Kaaba, and 70,000 angels enter it every day to worship, never returning to it again
Al-Bayt al-Ma'mur is another name for Masjid al-Qiblatayn
explanationEn: During the Mi'raj (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim), the Prophet ﷺ saw Prophet Ibrahim (AS) leaning his back against Al-Bayt al-Ma'mur in the seventh heaven—the heavenly counterpart directly aligned above the Kaaba—which 70,000 angels enter daily for worship.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 3207; Sahih Muslim 162; Tafsir Ibn Kathir 52:4

questionEn: According to authentic narrations from Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Abbas (RA), if a stone were dropped from Al-Bayt al-Ma'mur in the heavens, where would it fall on earth?
optionsEn: Into the Euphrates River
Into the Red Sea at Jeddah
Onto the summit of Mount Uhud
Directly upon the roof of the Kaaba in Makkah
explanationEn: Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Abbas (RA) stated that Al-Bayt al-Ma'mur is in the heaven directly aligned over the Kaaba; its sanctity in heaven is like the sanctity of the Kaaba on earth, such that if it fell, it would fall directly upon the Kaaba.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah (2:126), what were the two things Prophet Ibrahim (AS) asked Allah to grant to Makkah when he prayed: 'Rabbi ij'al hadha baladan aminan...'?
optionsEn: That Allah make it a city of peace/security (baladan aminan) and provide its people with fruits (warzuq ahlahu min al-thamarat)
That Allah surround it with an ocean and high snow-capped mountains
That Allah make its soil fertile enough to grow wheat without rain
That Allah prevent any non-Arab from ever visiting it for Hajj
explanationEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah (2:126), Ibrahim (AS) prayed for Makkah: 'My Lord, make this a secure city (baladan aminan) and provide its people with fruits—whoever of them believes in Allah and the Last Day.'

questionEn: Notice the phrasing differences between Ibrahim's (AS) two prayers for Makkah: in Surah Al-Baqarah (2:126) he said 'make this a city (baladan aminan)', whereas in Surah Ibrahim (14:35) he said 'make this city (hadhal-balada aminan)' with the definite article. How did scholars explain this difference?
optionsEn: The prayer in 2:126 was for Madinah and 14:35 was for Makkah
The prayer in 2:126 ('a city') was made earlier when Makkah was still an uninhabited valley before it became a town, whereas 14:35 ('this city') was made later after Makkah had become a settled town
There is no difference in time; both were said on the day Ismail was born
The first prayer was made by Ismail and the second by Ibrahim
explanationEn: Scholars such as Ibn Kathir and Al-Qurtubi pointed out that in 2:126 Ibrahim (AS) asked Allah to make the barren valley into 'a secure city' (indefinite: baladan), whereas in 14:35—on a later visit after Jurhum had settled there and Ismail and Ishaq (AS) were born—he prayed: 'make this city (hadhal-balad) secure.'

questionEn: In Surah Ibrahim (14:35), immediately after praying for Makkah to be secure, what urgent protection did Ibrahim (AS) ask for himself and his sons?
optionsEn: And grant my sons kingship over Egypt
And protect my sons from poverty and drought
Wa-jnubni wa baniyya an na'budal-asnam (And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols)
And make all my sons live for a thousand years
explanationEn: In Surah Ibrahim (14:35), Ibrahim (AS) prayed: 'My Lord, make this city [Makkah] secure, and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols (an na'budal-asnam).' Ibrahim al-Taymi wept at this verse, saying: 'Who can feel safe from trial after Ibrahim?'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah (2:144), where was the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ praying when the verses commanding the change of the Qiblah toward Al-Masjid al-Haram in Makkah were revealed?
optionsEn: At the Valley of Arafah during the Farewell Hajj
Inside the Cave of Hira in Makkah
In Abyssinia during the first migration
In Madinah, after having prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) for sixteen or seventeen months
explanationEn: As narrated by Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib (RA) in Sahih al-Bukhari, after arriving in Madinah the Prophet ﷺ prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for 16 or 17 months while earnestly longing to face the Kaaba in Makkah, until Allah revealed Surah Al-Baqarah 2:144.

questionEn: What exact phrase does Surah Al-Baqarah (2:144, 149, 150) repeat three times to command Muslims everywhere to face the Kaaba in prayer?
optionsEn: Fa-walli wajhaka shatral-Masjidil-Haram (So turn your face toward the direction of Al-Masjid al-Haram)
Fa-dkhulu Bakkata sajidin (So enter Bakkah prostrating)
Fa-tufu bil-Baytil-'Atiq (So circumambulate the Ancient House)
Fa-qimu inda Maqami Ibrahim (So stand beside the Station of Ibrahim)
explanationEn: Allah repeats the command three times in Surah Al-Baqarah (2:144, 2:149, 2:150): 'Fa-walli wajhaka shatral-Masjidil-Haram; wa haythu ma kuntum fa-wallu wujuhakum shatrahu'—emphasizing the abrogating legislation of facing Makkah from every corner of the earth.

questionEn: How do the four Sunni schools of jurisprudence define the required precision of facing the Qiblah for someone praying inside Al-Masjid al-Haram who can directly see the Kaaba, versus someone praying far away from Makkah?
optionsEn: Both must use astronomical instruments to hit within one millimeter of the Black Stone
Someone seeing the Kaaba must face the actual physical structure of the Kaaba ('Ayn al-Ka'bah), whereas someone far away must face its general direction (Jihat al-Ka'bah)
Someone seeing the Kaaba may face any gate of the mosque, while someone far away must face the exact corner
Neither needs to face the Kaaba during obligatory prayers
explanationEn: Based on the hadith of Ibn Abbas (RA) ('The House is the Qiblah for the people of the Mosque, the Mosque is the Qiblah for the people of the Haram, and the Haram is the Qiblah for the people of the earth in the east and west'), jurists distinguish between 'Ayn al-Ka'bah (for one who sees it) and Jihat al-Ka'bah (for one distant).
reference: Al-Bayhaqi, Al-Sunan al-Kubra 2:9; Al-Nawawi, Al-Majmu' 3:199; Ibn Qudamah, Al-Mughni 1:460

questionEn: In Surah Al-Tawbah (9:28), what historic decree was revealed in the 9th year of Hijrah regarding entry of polytheists (mushrikun) into Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: They may perform Tawaf only at night
They may only enter during the winter months
They shall not approach Al-Masjid al-Haram after this year of theirs (9 AH)
They may enter only if accompanied by ten merchants
explanationEn: In 9 AH, Allah revealed Surah Al-Tawbah (9:28): 'O you who have believed, indeed the polytheists are impure, so let them not approach Al-Masjid al-Haram after this, their [final] year.' The Prophet ﷺ sent Abu Bakr and Ali (RA) to proclaim during Hajj that no polytheist would perform Hajj after that year and no one would circle the House naked.

questionEn: When the believers in Makkah worried that prohibiting idolaters from attending the seasonal fairs at Al-Masjid al-Haram would cause commercial loss, what reassurance did Allah reveal in the second half of Surah Al-Tawbah (9:28)?
optionsEn: You should abandon Makkah and move to Yemen
You may continue trading with idolaters inside the Mataf forever
You will discover gold under Mount Safa tomorrow
And if you fear poverty ('aylah), Allah will enrich you from His bounty if He wills
explanationEn: Allah reassured them in 9:28: 'And if you fear poverty (wa in khiftum 'aylatan), Allah will enrich you from His bounty if He wills. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Wise.' Soon afterward, the whole Arabian Peninsula entered Islam and abundant wealth and delegations flowed into Makkah.

questionEn: Which classical name of Makkah, meaning 'The Crushing / Humbling One' because it crushes tyrants who violate it and because it lacks springs of running water on the surface, is cited by scholars alongside 'Makkah' and 'Bakkah'?
optionsEn: Al-Bassaasah / Al-Naassah
Al-Khadra'
Al-Zawra'
Al-Fayha'
explanationEn: Classical works on the history of Makkah (such as Al-Azraqi's Akhbar Makkah and Al-Fasi's Shifa' al-Gharam) record names of Makkah including Al-Bassaasah (which crushes and destroys anyone who commits tyranny or deviation in it) and Al-Naassah (which drives out tyrants).
reference: Al-Azraqi, Akhbar Makkah; Al-Fasi, Shifa' al-Gharam; Al-Nawawi, Tahdhib al-Asma' wal-Lughat

questionEn: Which name in Surah Al-Hajj (22:25) and seventeen other Qur'anic verses is the primary name of the Grand Mosque surrounding the Kaaba?
optionsEn: Al-Masjid al-Aqsa
Al-Masjid al-Haram (The Sacred / Inviolable Mosque)
Masjid al-Taqwa
Al-Jami' al-Umawi
explanationEn: Al-Masjid al-Haram appears 15 times in the Qur'an (in Surahs Al-Baqarah, Al-Ma'idah, Al-Anfal, Al-Tawbah, Al-Isra', Al-Hajj, and Al-Fath), referring either to the mosque around the Kaaba or to the entire sacred precinct of Makkah.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Isra' (17:1), how is the starting point of the Prophet's ﷺ Night Journey (Al-Isra') described?
optionsEn: From Masjid Quba to Damascus
From Mount Uhud to Mount Sinai
Min al-Masjidil-Harami ilal-Masjidil-Aqsa (From Al-Masjid al-Haram to Al-Masjid al-Aqsa)
From the Cave of Thawr to Abyssinia
explanationEn: Surah Al-Isra' (17:1) begins: 'Exalted is He who took His Servant by night from Al-Masjid al-Haram to Al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, to show him of Our signs.'

questionEn: In authentic hadiths of Sahih al-Bukhari on the Night Journey (Isra'), where specifically at the Kaaba was the Prophet ﷺ lying when the angels came to him before the journey?
optionsEn: At the Miqat of Qarn al-Manazil
Inside the Cave of Thawr south of Makkah
On the summit of Mount Arafah
In the Hatim / Hijr next to the Kaaba, between sleep and wakefulness
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari (3887, 3207), the Prophet ﷺ said: 'While I was lying at the Kaaba in the Hatim (and sometimes he said: in the Hijr), between sleep and wakefulness, someone came to me...'

questionEn: According to these narrations of the Night Journey in Sahih al-Bukhari, with what sacred water was the Prophet's ﷺ heart washed after his chest was opened at Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Water of Zamzam in a golden basin filled with faith and wisdom
Rainwater collected from Ta'if
Water from the Euphrates River
Water from the Well of Badr
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari (3207, 3342), Anas ibn Malik (RA) narrated that Jibril (AS) brought a golden tray full of Wisdom and Faith, washed the Prophet's ﷺ heart with Zamzam water, and filled his chest with wisdom and faith.

questionEn: When the Quraysh disbelieved the Prophet's ﷺ account of the Night Journey and stood in Al-Hijr asking him to describe Bayt al-Maqdis in detail, what miracle occurred for him right there at the Kaaba?
optionsEn: He drew a map of Jerusalem in the sand of the Mataf
Allah raised and displayed Bayt al-Maqdis before his eyes while he stood in Al-Hijr, so he described its features while looking directly at it
A caravan arrived at that exact second carrying photographs of Jerusalem
He told them he had never looked at the buildings of Jerusalem
explanationEn: Jabir ibn Abdullah (RA) narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'When the Quraysh disbelieved me, I stood in Al-Hijr and Allah displayed Bayt al-Maqdis before me, so I began informing them about its signs while I was looking at it.'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Fath (48:27), what true dream (ru'ya) of the Prophet ﷺ did Allah confirm would surely be fulfilled concerning Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: You will never need to put on Ihram again
You will build a golden palace on Mount Abu Qubays
You will surely enter Al-Masjid al-Haram, if Allah wills, in safety, with your heads shaved (muhalliqin) and [hair] shortened (muqassirin), not fearing anyone
You will demolish the Kaaba and move its stones to Madinah
explanationEn: Before the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (6 AH), the Prophet ﷺ saw in a dream that he and his Companions entered Al-Masjid al-Haram safely, shaving and shortening their hair. Allah revealed Surah Al-Fath (48:27) confirming the dream, which was fulfilled in Umrah al-Qada' (7 AH).

questionEn: In Surah Al-Anfal (8:34), why did Allah declare that the polytheists of Quraysh had no rightful claim to be the true guardians (awliya') of Al-Masjid al-Haram despite holding its keys?
optionsEn: Because they never repaired the roof of the Kaaba
Because they lived too far away from the Kaaba
Because they did not speak eloquent Arabic
Because they barred believers from Al-Masjid al-Haram while lacking taqwa: 'Its true guardians are none but the righteous (al-muttaqun)'
explanationEn: Allah says in Surah Al-Anfal (8:34): 'And what plea have they that Allah should not punish them while they bar [people] from Al-Masjid al-Haram, although they are not its [rightful] guardians? Its true guardians (awliya'uhu) are none but the righteous (al-muttaqun), but most of them do not know.'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Anfal (8:35), how did Allah describe the corrupted prayer of the pre-Islamic polytheists around the Kaaba?
optionsEn: Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling (muka'an) and hand-clapping (tasdiyatan)
Their prayer was silent meditation for three days
Their prayer consisted of reading the Torah in Hebrew
Their prayer was performed only on top of Mount Thawr
explanationEn: Surah Al-Anfal (8:35) states: 'And their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling (muka'an) and clapping of hands (tasdiyatan).' Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar (RA) explained that they used to whistle with their fingers and clap their hands while circling the Kaaba, and even used this to disrupt the Prophet's ﷺ recitation.
reference: Qur'an 8:35; Tafsir al-Tabari; Tafsir Ibn Kathir

questionEn: In Surah Al-Anfal (8:30), where had the elders of Quraysh convened to plot one of three things against the Prophet ﷺ—to imprison him (yuthbituka), kill him (yaqtuluka), or expel him (yukhrijuka)?
optionsEn: At the marketplace of Dhu al-Majaz near Arafah
Inside Dar al-Nadwah adjacent to the Kaaba in Makkah
Inside the fortress of Khaybar
At the court of the Negus in Abyssinia
explanationEn: Surah Al-Anfal (8:30) refers to the assembly of Quraysh chiefs in Dar al-Nadwah just before the Hijrah: 'And [remember, O Muhammad], when those who disbelieved plotted against you to restrain you or kill you or evict you [from Makkah]. But they plan, and Allah plans; and Allah is the best of planners.'
reference: Qur'an 8:30; Sirat Ibn Hisham; Tafsir al-Tabari

questionEn: In Surah Al-Anfal (8:33), what two safeguards preserved the people of Makkah from being destroyed by a sweeping heavenly punishment despite asking for stones to rain down on them?
optionsEn: Their alliance with the tribes of Yemen and Syria
Their wealth in gold and their strong horses
The presence of the Prophet ﷺ among them ('while you are among them') and their seeking of forgiveness ('while they seek forgiveness / yastaghfirun')
The height of the mountains around Makkah
explanationEn: After quoting Abu Jahl's arrogant challenge in 8:32 ('rain down upon us stones from the sky'), Allah revealed in 8:33: 'But Allah would not punish them while you, [O Muhammad], are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.'

questionEn: How did Ibn Abbas (RA) explain the phrase 'while they seek forgiveness (wa hum yastaghfirun)' in Surah Al-Anfal (8:33) regarding the people of Makkah?
optionsEn: They fasted every day of the year
They used to pay taxes to the Persian Empire
They never committed any sin in their lives

Both the weak believers remaining in Makkah who prayed for forgiveness, and the fact that even polytheists in Tawaf used to say 'Ghufranaka, Ghufranaka' (Your forgiveness, Your forgiveness), as well as those among them whom Allah knew would later embrace Islam
explanationEn: Exegetes report from Ibn Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and Al-Dahhak that this verse referred to the Muslim believers still in Makkah who sought forgiveness, those predestined to become Muslim after the Conquest, and the remnant Ibrahimic phrase 'Ghufranaka' uttered during Tawaf.

questionEn: In Surah Muhammad (47:13), revealed while the Prophet ﷺ was migrating from Makkah to Madinah, how did Allah console him regarding Makkah?
optionsEn: And how many a city was stronger in might than your city (qaryatika) which drove you out! We destroyed them, and there was no helper for them
You will never see your city again in this life
Your city is the smallest village in Arabia
Only ten people will ever believe in your city
explanationEn: Ibn Abbas (RA) narrated that as the Prophet ﷺ left Makkah on the Hijrah, he looked back toward the Kaaba and expressed his deep love for Makkah, whereupon Allah revealed Surah Muhammad (47:13) referring to Makkah as 'qaryatika allati akhrajatka' (your city which drove you out).
reference: Qur'an 47:13; Tafsir Ibn Kathir; Sunan al-Tirmidhi

questionEn: When entering Al-Masjid al-Haram, which foot and which general Prophetic supplication for entering mosques are recommended according to the Sunnah?
optionsEn: Stepping in with the left foot while saying: 'Allahumma inni as'aluka min fadlik'
Stepping in with the right foot while sending peace upon the Prophet ﷺ and saying: 'Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik' (O Allah, open for me the gates of Your mercy)
Entering backwards while reciting Surah Al-Fil three times
Jumping over the threshold with both feet together in silence
explanationEn: Al-Masjid al-Haram shares the Prophetic etiquette of all mosques: entering with the right foot, invoking blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ, and saying 'Bismillah, Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik' (Sahih Muslim 713), plus the specific supplications reported from the Companions upon seeing the Kaaba.

questionEn: What authentic supplication did Companion Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) recite upon seeing the Kaaba in Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Rabbighfir li warhamni innaka Antal-Ghafurul-Rahim
Subhana Rabbiyal-A'la three times
Allahumma Antas-Salamu wa minkas-salam, fa-hayyina Rabbana bis-salam (O Allah, You are Peace and from You is peace, so keep us alive, our Lord, in peace)
Allahumma barik lana fi Rajaba wa Sha'ban
explanationEn: Imam al-Shafi'i, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and Al-Bayhaqi recorded with a sahih chain from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that when Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) looked at the House (the Kaaba), he said: 'Allahumma Antas-Salam, wa minkas-salam, fa-hayyina Rabbana bis-salam.'
reference: Musannaf Ibn Abi Shaybah 12915; Al-Bayhaqi, Al-Sunan al-Kubra 5:73; Al-Nawawi, Al-Adhkar

questionEn: What is the traditional greeting of the Mosque (Tahiyyat al-Masjid) specifically for a person entering Al-Masjid al-Haram in Ihram to perform Umrah or Hajj?
optionsEn: Sitting silently for an hour before praying
Praying four rak'ahs at the door before looking at the Kaaba
Performing Sa'i between Safa and Marwah first before seeing the Kaaba
Beginning directly with Tawaf around the Kaaba (unless an obligatory congregational prayer is about to begin or time is tight)
explanationEn: As demonstrated by the Prophet ﷺ (who performed ablution upon entering Makkah and went straight to the Black Stone to begin Tawaf without praying two rak'ahs first) and stated by jurists across the four schools, Tawaf serves as Tahiyyat al-Masjid for the pilgrim entering in Ihram, whereas someone not performing Tawaf prays two rak'ahs of Tahiyyat al-Masjid.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1614; Al-Nawawi, Al-Majmu' 8:14; Ibn Qudamah, Al-Mughni 3:335

questionEn: What should a visitor entering Al-Masjid al-Haram do if they do NOT intend to perform Tawaf upon entry (or if the Mataf is too crowded for them to perform Tawaf)?
optionsEn: Pray two rak'ahs of Tahiyyat al-Masjid before sitting down, just as in any other mosque
Stand without praying until they leave the mosque
Perform one lap of Sa'i instead
Leave the mosque immediately because entry without Tawaf is forbidden
explanationEn: Jurists agree that if a person enters Al-Masjid al-Haram without intending immediate Tawaf (e.g., entering only to attend congregational prayer, a lesson, or I'tikaf), they pray the standard two rak'ahs of Tahiyyat al-Masjid before sitting.
reference: Al-Nawawi, Al-Majmu' 4:53; Majmu' Fatawa Ibn Baz

questionEn: What is the Prophetic ruling regarding the times of day or night during which people may perform Tawaf and pray the two rak'ahs of Tawaf in Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Tawaf is forbidden between Asr and Maghrib and between Fajr and sunrise
No one is to be prevented from circumambulating this House and praying at any hour of the night or day he wishes
Tawaf is only permitted between Dhuhr and Isha
The two rak'ahs of Tawaf may only be prayed after midnight
explanationEn: Jubayr ibn Mut'im (RA) narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'O Banu Abd Manaf! Do not prevent anyone from circumambulating this House and praying at any hour he wishes of the night or day.'
reference: Sunan al-Tirmidhi 868; Sunan Abi Dawud 1894; Sunan al-Nasa'i 2924

questionEn: Why did the Prophet ﷺ specifically address 'O Banu Abd Manaf!' in the hadith commanding that no one be prevented from Tawaf or prayer at the Kaaba at any hour?
optionsEn: Because Banu Abd Manaf were the only tribe prohibited from performing Tawaf
Because Banu Abd Manaf lived outside Makkah in Ta'if
Because Banu Abd Manaf (which included Banu Hashim and Banu Umayyah) held leadership and authority in Makkah, so anyone governing Makkah was commanded never to restrict access to worship at the Kaaba
Because Banu Abd Manaf built the city walls of Madinah
