explanationEn: Scholars such as Al-Tirmidhi and Al-Khattabi explained that the Prophet ﷺ addressed Banu Abd Manaf because religious and political leadership in Makkah and the Caliphate rested among them, binding every ruler and custodian to keep the Kaaba accessible day and night.

questionEn: How are congregational prayer rows (sufuf) uniquely arranged inside Al-Masjid al-Haram around the Kaaba compared to every other mosque in the world?
optionsEn: Only on the west side of the Kaaba
In straight lines facing only from south to north
In triangular rows facing the eastern gate
In concentric circular rows completely surrounding the Kaaba from all four directions
explanationEn: Because the Kaaba itself sits at the center of Al-Masjid al-Haram as the focal point of the Qiblah, worshippers form concentric circles around the Kaaba so that every worshipper in the circle faces the Sacred House.

questionEn: In the fiqh of congregational prayer around the Kaaba inside Al-Masjid al-Haram, when is a worshipper's prayer invalidated due to standing ahead of the Imam (taqaddum 'ala al-imam)?
optionsEn: If the worshipper stands closer to the Kaaba than the Imam ON THE SAME SIDE as the Imam (whereas standing closer to the Kaaba on a different side of the Kaaba is valid according to the majority of scholars)
If the worshipper prays on the upper roof level
If the worshipper prays behind Maqam Ibrahim
Every worshipper on all four sides must stand outside the outer wall of the mosque
explanationEn: The majority of jurists (Hanafi, Shafi'i, Hanbali) hold that around the Kaaba, a follower's prayer is invalid if he stands closer to the Kaaba than the Imam on the same side/direction, whereas standing closer on another of the four sides is valid because they are facing different walls of the Kaaba.
reference: Al-Nawawi, Al-Majmu' 4:299; Ibn Qudamah, Al-Mughni 2:31; Radd al-Muhtar 1:569

questionEn: What did the Prophet ﷺ say about someone who picks up a lost item (luqatah) inside the Haram of Makkah?
optionsEn: Whoever finds a lost item in Makkah automatically owns it after three days
Its lost property is not permissible to pick up except for a mudiff (munshid)—one who announces it continuously so its owner can recover it, never taking ownership of it
Whoever finds a lost item in Makkah owns it after one year just like outside Makkah
Lost items in Makkah must be thrown into the sea
explanationEn: In the Khutbah on the Day of the Conquest of Makkah (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim), the Prophet ﷺ declared: 'Its lost item (luqatah) is not lawful except for one who announces it (illa li-munshid).' Unlike outside Makkah where a finder may own an unclaimed item after anunciar for a year, in Makkah it can only be picked up to preserve and announce for its owner forever.

questionEn: In the same sermon on the sanctity of Makkah, what is the ruling on carrying weapons for fighting inside the Haram of Makkah without lawful necessity?
optionsEn: Carrying weapons for fighting is encouraged inside the Mataf
Every visitor is required to carry a drawn sword during Tawaf
The Prophet ﷺ forbade carrying weapons for fighting in Makkah: 'It is not lawful for any of you to carry weapons in Makkah'
There is no ruling on weapons in Makkah
explanationEn: Jabir ibn Abdullah (RA) reported in Sahih Muslim (1356): 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade that any of us should carry weapons in Makkah'—protecting the peace and security of Allah's Sanctuary.

questionEn: What is the ruling on a Muhrim (pilgrim in Ihram) OR a Halal (non-Muhrim resident/visitor) hunting wild land game inside the boundaries of the Makkan Haram?
optionsEn: It is permitted if done with a bow rather than a trap
It is only forbidden for the Muhrim; residents of Makkah not in Ihram may hunt deer inside the Haram
It is only forbidden during the last ten days of Ramadan
Hunting or frightening wild land game inside the Haram boundaries is strictly forbidden for BOTH the Muhrim and the non-Muhrim (Halal)
explanationEn: Unlike Ihram restrictions that apply only while in Ihram, the sanctity of the Makkan Haram (Hurmat al-Haram) makes hunting, aiding a hunter, or even startling wild land game inside the Haram boundaries forbidden for everyone—both Muhrim and non-Muhrim alike.

questionEn: What exception did the Prophet ﷺ clarify regarding dangerous/harmful creatures (al-fawasiq) inside the Haram of Makkah and during Ihram?
optionsEn: Five harmful creatures (al-fawasiq al-khams) may be killed both outside and inside the Haram: the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse/rat, and the rabid/biting dog (and by analogy predatory beasts)
No scorpion or snake may ever be harmed even if it is attacking a child
Only mosquitoes are exempted
Only lions in Africa are exempted
explanationEn: Aishah and Ibn Umar (RA) narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Five animals are harmful (fawasiq) and may be killed in the Haram (and in Ihram): the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse, and the biting/rabid dog ('al-kalb al-'aqur').'

questionEn: What is the ruling on slaughtering domesticated livestock (such as sheep, cattle, camels, and chickens) inside the Haram of Makkah?
optionsEn: Slaughtering sheep and camels is forbidden inside Makkah
Slaughtering domesticated livestock is completely permissible in the Haram (and is required there for Hady sacrifices); the prohibition applies only to wild game (sayd)
Only fish may be eaten inside Makkah
Chickens are considered wild game and require a camel penalty
explanationEn: By scholarly consensus (Ijma'), the prohibition of 'sayd' (hunting game) in the Haram applies to wild, untamed land animals; domesticated animals (an'am and poultry) are lawful to slaughter in the Haram, and Makkah is in fact the prescribed place of slaughter (Manhar) for Hajj Hady.

questionEn: According to Surah Al-Ma'idah (5:95) and Surah Al-Hajj (22:33), where must the sacrificial offerings (Hady) and expiation animals (Dam/Fidyah) for Hajj and Ihram violations be slaughtered and distributed to the poor?
optionsEn: In the valley of Arafah outside the Haram boundary
In the pilgrim's home country after returning from Hajj
Inside the boundaries of the Haram of Makkah (hadya baligha al-Ka'bah) and distributed to the poor of the Haram
At the Miqat where the pilgrim entered Ihram
explanationEn: Surah Al-Ma'idah (5:95) specifies 'hadya baligha al-Ka'bah' (an offering reaching the Kaaba—meaning the Haram of Makkah), and Surah Al-Hajj (22:33) states 'thumma mahilluha ila al-Bayt al-'Atiq.' Thus sacrificial animals for Hajj and fidyah are slaughtered within the Makkan Haram boundaries.

questionEn: What did the Prophet ﷺ say during the Farewell Hajj when he slaughtered his sacrifice at Mina regarding where in Makkah and its sacred precincts a pilgrim may slaughter the Hady?
optionsEn: Slaughter is only valid on Mount Arafah
Every pilgrim must slaughter on the exact same rock at Jamarat al-Aqabah
Slaughter is only valid inside the Hijr Ismail

I have slaughtered here, and all of Mina is a place of slaughter (manhar), so slaughter in your camping places; and all of the mountain passes of Makkah (fijaj Makkah) are a pathway and a place of slaughter
explanationEn: Jabir ibn Abdullah (RA) reported in Sahih Muslim and Sunan Abi Dawud that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'I have slaughtered here, and all of Mina is a place of slaughter, and all the mountain passes/valleys of Makkah (fijaj Makkah) are a pathway and a place of slaughter.'

questionEn: What is the ruling on cutting wild, unplanted thorny trees or fresh wild herbage (khala') inside the Haram of Makkah vs. cultivated crops and vegetables planted by human beings?
optionsEn: Wild trees and fresh wild herbage that grew on their own in the Haram may not be cut, whereas crops, vegetables, and fruit trees planted and cultivated by people may be harvested
People in Makkah are forbidden from harvesting any wheat, dates, or vegetables they plant in their own gardens
Only wild trees may be cut down for firewood, while planted gardens may never be touched
There is no restriction on cutting wild trees in Makkah
explanationEn: The four schools of fiqh agree that agricultural crops, grains, vegetables, and herbs planted and cultivated by human hands in Makkah are lawful to harvest; the prohibition applies to wild trees and uncultivated wild herbage (khala') native to the Haram, except Idhkhir.

questionEn: What is the ruling on picking up fallen dry leaves or broken dead branches (not cut from a living tree) inside the Haram of Makkah, or grazing livestock on Haram grass according to the majority of scholars?
optionsEn: Even a single dry leaf that fell in the wind requires sacrificing a camel

Fallen dry leaves and dead wood may be used, and according to the majority of jurists (Shafi'i, Maliki, Hanbali), grazing livestock on Haram herbage is permissible because pilgrims' camels grazed there during the Prophet's ﷺ time
Camels and sheep entering Makkah must Have their mouths muzzled for ten days
Livestock are forbidden from entering Makkah
explanationEn: The majority of scholars (Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali, and Abu Yusuf among the Hanafis) permit grazing animals on Haram grass because the Prophet ﷺ and Companions entered Makkah with thousands of camels and horses without muzzling them, while prohibiting cutting fresh wild grass with a sickle.

questionEn: What is the ruling on carrying soil, stones, or pebbles out of the Haram of Makkah to other lands?
optionsEn: A pillar of Umrah
Obligatory upon every pilgrim to carry a sack of rocks home
Disliked (makruh) or prohibited by many classical scholars and Companions (such as Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas RA), who discouraged removing the stones and soil of the Haram outside its sacred boundary
Required before performing Tawaf al-Wada'
explanationEn: Reports from Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, and Ata' ibn Abi Rabah (recorded by Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Shaybah), followed by Shafi'i, Hanbali, and Hanafi scholars, state that the stones and soil of the Makkan Haram should not be carried out to non-sacred land (al-Hill), honoring the uniqueness of the sanctuary (unlike Zamzam water, which is explicitly permitted to carry away).

questionEn: In contrast to the soil and stones of the Haram, what is the ruling on carrying Zamzam water away from Makkah to one's homeland?
optionsEn: Only permitted if boiled first
Strictly forbidden to take outside the Haram boundaries
Only permitted for kings and caliphs
Permissible and recommended (mustahabb), as the Prophet ﷺ himself wrote to Suhayl ibn Amr to send him Zamzam water and Aishah (RA) used to carry Zamzam water back from Makkah in bottles
explanationEn: Aishah (RA) narrated in Sunan al-Tirmidhi (963) that she used to carry Zamzam water away in bottles and reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ carried it away in water-skins and flasks, pouring it over the sick and giving it to them to drink.
reference: Sunan al-Tirmidhi 963; Musannaf Ibn Abi Shaybah

questionEn: Where are funeral prayers (Salat al-Janazah) regularly performed inside Al-Masjid al-Haram after obligatory congregational prayers?
optionsEn: Inside the Mosque facing the Kaaba along with the Imam immediately after the fard prayer
Funeral prayers are strictly forbidden inside Al-Masjid al-Haram
Only on the summit of Jabal al-Noor
Only outside the Tan'eem boundary
explanationEn: Salat al-Janazah is regularly performed in congregation inside Al-Masjid al-Haram after the obligatory prayers, as the Prophet ﷺ prayed funeral prayer in the mosque (e.g., for Suhayl ibn Bayda', Sahih Muslim 973) and the Companions prayed over deceased believers at Al-Masjid al-Haram.

questionEn: After the Imam in Al-Masjid al-Haram finishes an obligatory prayer, what concise announcement does the Mu'adhdhin traditionally make when there is a deceased person present for Salat al-Janazah?
optionsEn: Hayya 'alal-falah ten times
As-Salatu 'alal-amwat / 'alal-mayyit, yarhamukumullah (Prayer upon the deceased, may Allah have mercy upon you)
Qad qamatis-salah twice
La ilaha illallah wahdahu la sharika lah
explanationEn: In the Two Holy Mosques, when biers are present after the obligatory prayer, the Mu'adhdhin calls out 'As-Salatu 'alal-mayyit (or 'alal-amwat / 'alal-atfal), yarhamukumullah' so the congregation knows to stand for Salat al-Janazah.
reference: Practice of Al-Haramayn; Fatawa al-Lajnah al-Da'imah

questionEn: According to an authentic hadith in Musnad Ahmad and Sunan Ibn Majah, how does the reward of a prayer in Al-Masjid al-Haram compare to prayers in other mosques?
optionsEn: One prayer in Al-Masjid al-Haram equals 1,000 prayers elsewhere
One prayer in Al-Masjid al-Haram equals 500 prayers elsewhere
One prayer in Al-Masjid al-Haram is better than 100,000 prayers in any other mosque
One prayer in Al-Masjid al-Haram equals 10 prayers elsewhere
explanationEn: Jabir ibn Abdullah (RA) narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'A prayer in this mosque of mine [in Madinah] is better than 1,000 prayers in any other mosque except Al-Masjid al-Haram, and a prayer in Al-Masjid al-Haram is better than 100,000 prayers in any other mosque.'

questionEn: Does the 100,000-fold multiplication of prayer reward in Makkah apply only to the original small courtyard around the Kaaba, or does it extend across the expanded Al-Masjid al-Haram and the sacred Haram precinct?
optionsEn: It expired after the first century of Islam
It applies only within three meters of the Black Stone
It applies only on the roof of the Kaaba

According to the majority of scholars and the Companions (including Ibn Abbas and Ata' RA), the multiplication of reward encompasses the entire expanded Al-Masjid al-Haram—and according to the strongest view of many scholars, prayers throughout the entire Haram boundary of Makkah
explanationEn: Scholars agree that all expansions of Al-Masjid al-Haram share the full 100,000x virtue, and the majority of Hanbali, Shafi'i, and Hanafi scholars—citing Ibn Abbas and Ata' ibn Abi Rabah (RA) and the Qur'anic usage of 'Al-Masjid al-Haram' for the entire Haram sanctuary—hold that the multiplied reward applies throughout the sacred boundaries (Hudud al-Haram) of Makkah, while praying in the congregation at the Kaaba itself has the greatest virtue.
reference: Musannaf Abd al-Razzaq 9157; Al-Nawawi, Al-Majmu' 7:463; Majmu' Fatawa Ibn Taymiyyah 27:15; Fatawa Ibn Baz 17:175

questionEn: What did the Prophet ﷺ say in the famous hadith narrated by Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (RA) about setting out on a special religious journey (شد الرحال / shadd al-rihal) to any mosque?
optionsEn: Mounts are not saddled (no journey is undertaken specifically for worship at a mosque) except to three mosques: Al-Masjid al-Haram, the Mosque of the Messenger ﷺ, and Al-Masjid al-Aqsa
Journeys may only be made to one mosque in each country
No one should ever travel to Makkah outside Dhul-Hijjah
Mounts may be saddled to any shrine or tomb in the world
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari (1189) and Sahih Muslim (1397), the Prophet ﷺ said: 'La tushaddu al-rihalu illa ila thalathati masajida: al-Masjid al-Haram, wa Masjid al-Rasul ﷺ, wa al-Masjid al-Aqsa.'

questionEn: In a hadith narrated by Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (RA) in Sunan al-Tirmidhi and Sunan al-Nasa'i, what did the Prophet ﷺ encourage regarding following up Hajj and Umrah to Makkah?
optionsEn: Perform Umrah only once every fifty years
Follow up between Hajj and Umrah (tabi'u baynal-Hajji wal-'Umrah), for indeed they both remove poverty and sins just as the blacksmith's bellows remove impurities from iron, gold, and silver
Never perform Umrah in the same decade as Hajj
Perform Hajj without ever entering Makkah
explanationEn: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (RA) narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Follow up between Hajj and Umrah, for they remove poverty and sins just as the bellows remove dross from iron, gold, and silver; and an accepted Hajj (Hajj Mabrur) has no reward less than Paradise.'

questionEn: What special virtue did the Prophet ﷺ state for performing Umrah to Makkah during the month of Ramadan?
optionsEn: An Umrah in Ramadan waives the lifelong obligation of Hajj for a wealthy person
An Umrah in Ramadan replaces the obligation of fasting Ramadan
An Umrah in Ramadan equals a Hajj (or a Hajj with me) in reward
An Umrah in Ramadan consists of only three laps of Tawaf
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari (1782, 1863) and Sahih Muslim (1256), the Prophet ﷺ told Umm Sinan al-Ansariyyah (RA): 'When Ramadan comes, perform Umrah, for an Umrah in Ramadan equals a Hajj (and in one narration: a Hajj with me).' Scholars clarify it equals Hajj in reward, though it does not discharge the obligatory pillar of Hajj.

questionEn: According to a hadith in Sahih Muslim narrated by Hudhayfah and Abu Hurayrah (RA), in which three mosques alone did some Companions and scholars hold that I'tikaf (spiritual retreat) has special distinction or exclusivity?
optionsEn: Only mosques built outside Arabia
Masjid al-Khayf, Masjid Namirah, and Masjid al-Mash'ar al-Haram
Masjid Aishah, Masjid al-Jinn, and Masjid al-Rayah
Al-Masjid al-Haram, Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, and Al-Masjid al-Aqsa
explanationEn: While the four schools permit I'tikaf in any congregational mosque, Hudhayfah (RA) narrated the report 'La i'tikafa illa fil-masajid al-thalathah' (Al-Masjid al-Haram, Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, and Al-Masjid al-Aqsa), highlighting their supreme rank as the noblest places on earth for I'tikaf, especially in the last ten nights of Ramadan.

questionEn: When Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) vowed before Islam during the Jahiliyyah to perform I'tikaf for a night (or day) in Al-Masjid al-Haram and asked the Prophet ﷺ about it after embracing Islam, what did the Prophet ﷺ command him to do?
optionsEn: Awfi bi-nadhrika (Fulfill your vow), so Umar performed I'tikaf for a night in Al-Masjid al-Haram
Ignore the vow because Al-Masjid al-Haram was still in Makkah
Fast for two months instead
Pay a hundred dinars and never enter Al-Masjid al-Haram at night
explanationEn: As recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari (2032) and Sahih Muslim (1656), after the Battle of Hunayn/Conquest of Makkah, Umar (RA) said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I vowed in the Jahiliyyah to perform I'tikaf for one night in Al-Masjid al-Haram.' The Prophet ﷺ replied: 'Fulfill your vow, so perform I'tikaf for a night.'

questionEn: According to the consensus of scholars, if a person makes a vow (nadhr) to pray in a distant ordinary mosque, may they fulfill that vow by praying in Al-Masjid al-Haram instead? And what if they vow specifically to pray in Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: A vow to pray in Al-Masjid al-Haram can be fulfilled in any neighborhood prayer room

If one vows to pray in an ordinary mosque or even in Madinah/Al-Aqsa, praying in Al-Masjid al-Haram fulfills it because it is superior; but if one vows specifically to pray in Al-Masjid al-Haram, no other mosque on earth can substitute for it
All vows to pray in Al-Masjid al-Haram are invalid
Only Al-Masjid al-Aqsa is higher than Al-Masjid al-Haram in fulfilling vows
explanationEn: In Sahih Abi Dawud (3305) and Musnad Ahmad, when a man told the Prophet ﷺ on the Day of the Conquest that he had vowed to pray in Bayt al-Maqdis if Allah conquered Makkah for the Prophet ﷺ, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Pray here [in Al-Masjid al-Haram]!' repeating it three times, and added: 'By Him in Whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, a prayer here is better than a thousand prayers in other lands.' Thus jurists rule that Al-Masjid al-Haram substitutes for the lesser two mosques, whereas neither substitutes for a vow to pray in Al-Masjid al-Haram.

questionEn: What is the Prophetic guidance for women attending prayers and Tawaf in Al-Masjid al-Haram regarding crowding with men?
optionsEn: Women must push through the thickest crowd of men to kiss the Black Stone for their Tawaf to be valid
Women are forbidden from ever entering Al-Masjid al-Haram at night

They are permitted to attend and perform Tawaf, while avoiding crowding among men, not wearing perfume, and observing modesty—even gesturing to the Black Stone from afar rather than pushing through crowds of men
Women may only perform Tawaf once in their entire lifetime
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari (1618), Aishah (RA) performed Tawaf separately from the men without mixing in their crowd, and Atiyyah reported that when a woman asked Aishah (RA) about touching the Black Stone, Aishah and Umm Salamah instructed women not to crowd among men, but to touch it only if empty and otherwise make Takbir and pass on.

questionEn: During the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ and the early Rightly Guided Caliphs, how did women perform Tawaf at the Kaaba?
optionsEn: Women performed only three circuits instead of seven
Women were banned from the Mataf until the Ottoman era
Women performed Tawaf only on top of Mount Abu Qubays
Behind/outside the circle of men without intermingling in their crowd, until Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) and later Umayyad governors formally forbade men from mingling with women's Tawaf circles
explanationEn: Ibn Jurayj narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari (1618) from Ata' that women during the Prophet's ﷺ time did not mix with men during Tawaf; Aishah (RA) circumambulated on the outer perimeter away from the men, and Umar (RA) enforced strict separation so men would not crowd women in the Mataf.

questionEn: What did the Prophet ﷺ say to Umm Salamah (RA) during the Farewell Hajj when she complained of illness and inability to walk around the Kaaba among the crowd?
optionsEn: Circumambulate behind the people while riding your mount (tufi min wara'il-nasi wa anti rakibah)
Skip Tawaf completely and return to Madinah without it
Pay someone else to perform your obligatory Tawaf while you are alive and present
Wait in Makkah for three years until everyone leaves
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari (1619) and Sahih Muslim (1276), Umm Salamah (RA) complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that she was unwell; he told her: 'Perform Tawaf behind the people while you are riding,' so she circumambulated on her camel at the outer edge while the Prophet ﷺ was leading Fajr prayer reciting Surah At-Tur.

questionEn: What legal ruling did jurists derive from the hadith of Umm Salamah (RA) performing Tawaf while riding her mount at the outer edge of the mosque?
optionsEn: Riding is obligatory for every healthy young man during Tawaf

It is permissible for the sick, elderly, or disabled to perform Tawaf and Sa'i while riding (including modern wheelchairs and mobility scooters) on the designated outer/upper paths so as not to harm walking pilgrims
Anyone who uses a wheelchair in Tawaf must sacrifice two camels
Tawaf on an upper floor is invalid
explanationEn: From both the Prophet ﷺ riding his camel in Tawaf so people could see him and ask questions (Sahih Muslim 1273) and his instructing Umm Salamah (RA) to ride behind the crowd (Sahih al-Bukhari 1619), scholars unanimously permit the sick, elderly, and infirm to use wheelchairs or mounts without any expiation (fidyah).

questionEn: Are Tawaf and Sa'i valid when performed on the upper floors or roof of the expanded Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Upper-floor Tawaf requires fourteen circuits instead of seven
No, Tawaf is invalid if one's feet are more than one meter above the ground

Yes, as long as the pilgrim circumambulates completely outside the perimeter of the Kaaba and Hijr Ismail inside the Mosque's space, because the airspace of the Mosque (hawa' al-masjid) shares the ruling of its ground floor
Upper-floor Tawaf is valid only for children under ten
explanationEn: Contemporary scholarly councils (including the Council of Senior Scholars and the Islamic Fiqh Academy) and classical jurists affirm that the airspace above Al-Masjid al-Haram and Al-Mas'a takes the legal ruling of its floor, so Tawaf and Sa'i on the upper levels and roof are completely valid.
reference: Al-Mughni 3:348; Decisions of the Council of Senior Scholars; Fatawa Ibn Baz 17:224

questionEn: Because the circular radius on the upper floors and roof of Al-Masjid al-Haram is much wider than on the ground-floor Mataf right next to the Kaaba, approximately how long is a full seven-lap Tawaf on the upper floors compared to close to the Kaaba?
optionsEn: Over 50 kilometers on the ground floor
Exactly 100 meters on both levels
Shorter on the roof than on the ground floor
Around 1.5 to 2 kilometers near the Kaaba on the Mataf floor, compared to roughly 5 to 7 kilometers on the upper floors and outer roof ring
explanationEn: Near the Kaaba on the ground-floor Mataf, each lap is roughly 200–250 meters (~1.5–1.8 km for 7 laps), whereas on the wide outer upper rings of the Mosque each lap can approach 700–900+ meters (~5–6+ km for 7 laps), though the upper levels are much less congested and accommodate wheelchairs.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Two Holy Mosques Engineering Data

questionEn: What is the ruling if the Iqamah for an obligatory congregational prayer is called in Al-Masjid al-Haram while a pilgrim is in the middle of performing Tawaf or Sa'i?
optionsEn: The pilgrim stops walking, joins the congregational obligatory prayer where they are, and after the prayer ends, resumes their Tawaf or Sa'i from the exact point and lap where they paused
The pilgrim must ignore the obligatory congregational prayer and keep walking through the praying rows
The pilgrim's previous laps are completely nullified and they must restart from lap 1
The pilgrim must leave the mosque and redo their Ihram from the Miqat
explanationEn: Based on the Prophet's ﷺ statement 'When the prayer is established (uqimat al-salah), there is no prayer except the obligatory prayer' (Sahih Muslim 710) and reports from Ibn Umar and Ata' (RA), a pilgrim interrupts Tawaf or Sa'i to join the obligatory congregation, then resumes building upon the completed circuits from the spot where they stopped.
reference: Sahih Muslim 710; Musannaf Abd al-Razzaq 9015; Al-Mughni 3:351; Fatawa Ibn Baz 17:222

questionEn: What is the ruling if a pilgrim loses their Wudu (minor ritual purity) while in the middle of performing Tawaf vs. while in the middle of performing Sa'i between Safa and Marwah?
optionsEn: Neither Tawaf nor Sa'i ever requires Wudu

For Tawaf, the pilgrim must pause, go renew Wudu, and then complete/restart according to the school's rule because Wudu is required for Tawaf; whereas for Sa'i, although Wudu is strongly recommended (Sunnah), if Wudu breaks during Sa'i the pilgrim may complete Sa'i and it remains valid
Sa'i requires Ghusl if Wudu breaks, while Tawaf does not require Wudu
Breaking Wudu in Makkah invalidates one's Islam
explanationEn: The majority of scholars require Wudu as a condition for the validity of Tawaf (based on the Prophet ﷺ performing Wudu before Tawaf and forbidding a menstruating woman from Tawaf until purified), whereas Wudu is recommended (mustahabb) for Sa'i but not a strict condition of its validity.

questionEn: What did Aishah (RA) say in Sahih al-Bukhari when a woman asked if a menstruating pilgrim could perform the rites of Hajj in Makkah?
optionsEn: She should perform Tawaf around the Kaaba without any restriction
A menstruating woman must immediately cancel her Hajj and return home
Do everything that the pilgrim does, except do not circumambulate the House (la tatufi bil-Bayt) until you become pure (even performing Sa'i and all other rites outside the Mosque)
She is forbidden from reciting any dhikr or du'a on the Day of Arafah
explanationEn: When Aishah (RA) experienced menstruation at Sarif before entering Makkah during the Farewell Hajj, the Prophet ﷺ comforted her and said: 'Do everything that the pilgrim does, except do not circumambulate the House until you become pure.'

questionEn: If a woman who has already performed her obligatory Tawaf al-Ifadah (or Umrah Tawaf) experiences menstruation right before her group's departure from Makkah, what is the Prophetic ruling regarding her Farewell Tawaf (Tawaf al-Wada')?
optionsEn: Her entire Hajj becomes invalid
She must pay the price of a camel before leaving Makkah
She must enter Al-Masjid al-Haram and perform Tawaf anyway
Tawaf al-Wada' is waived/dropped from her as a mercy, and she may depart Makkah with her group without any penalty (dam)
explanationEn: Ibn Abbas (RA) narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari (1755) and Sahih Muslim (1328): 'The people were commanded that their last engagement be with the House (Tawaf al-Wada'), except that this was lightened/waived for the menstruating woman.' When Safiyyah bint Huyayy (RA) menstruated after already completing Tawaf al-Ifadah, the Prophet ﷺ permitted immediate departure.

questionEn: What was the practice of the Prophet ﷺ after completing Tawaf al-Wada' (the Farewell Circumambulation) upon departing Makkah?
optionsEn: Making Tawaf al-Wada' the very last rite in Makkah and departing shortly thereafter without staying behind for leisure or residence (though buying travel provisions on the way out is permitted)
Walking backwards all the way from the Kaaba to the city gates
Staying in Makkah for another two weeks of shopping after Tawaf al-Wada'
Climbing Mount Thawr after Tawaf al-Wada'
explanationEn: Based on Ibn Abbas's (RA) hadith ('Let none of you depart until his last engagement is with the House', Sahih Muslim 1327), a departing pilgrim performs Tawaf al-Wada' right before leaving Makkah. Note also that Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) explicitly forbade the innovated practice of walking backwards out of the Mosque after Tawaf al-Wada'.

questionEn: During the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and Caliph Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA), what surrounded the open Mataf courtyard around the Kaaba?
optionsEn: A marble colonnade with seven tall minarets and three gilded domes
There was no enclosure wall around the Mosque; the houses of the Quraysh directly bordered the open Mataf courtyard with narrow lanes (fijaj/abwab) between the houses leading to the Kaaba
A forty-meter stone fortress wall built by King Solomon
A deep water moat crossed by drawbridges
explanationEn: Historical accounts by Al-Azraqi (Akhbar Makkah) and Ibn Kathir confirm that during the era of the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr (RA), Al-Masjid al-Haram had no outer boundary wall; residential houses surrounded the open courtyard around the Kaaba until the population grew under Umar (RA).
reference: Al-Azraqi, Akhbar Makkah 2:64; Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari

questionEn: Why did Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) undertake the very first physical expansion of Al-Masjid al-Haram in 17 AH (638 CE)?
optionsEn: He wanted to convert the Mataf into an agricultural orchard
The Kaaba had been moved to another valley
The number of Muslims and pilgrims grew so rapidly that the small courtyard around the Kaaba became too tight, and also a flash flood (Sayl Umm Nahshal) swept down From upper Makkah into the Mataf
The Byzantine emperor requested a larger courtyard
explanationEn: In 17 AH, as waves of new Muslims crowded the small Mataf and after the heavy flash flood known as Sayl Umm Nahshal swept Maqam Ibrahim down the valley, Umar (RA) purchased surrounding houses, demolished them to widen the courtyard, built the first low perimeter wall (less than a man's height) with lamps mounted on it, and constructed a protective dam against floods in upper Makkah.

questionEn: What fair legal procedure did Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA)—and later Uthman ibn Affan (RA)—use when some Makkan homeowners initially refused to sell their houses adjacent to the Kaaba for the expansion of Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: He built the Mosque on top of the roofs of the houses
He confiscated the houses without paying a single dirham
He abandoned the expansion and moved the Mosque to Ta'if

He had the houses fairly appraised at full value, deposited their compensation money locked inside the treasury of the Kaaba until the owners eventually came and took their payment, and included the land in the Mosque
explanationEn: As recorded by Al-Azraqi and Ibn Sa'd, Umar (RA) told reluctant homeowners: 'Wait—it is you who settled inside the courtyard of the Kaaba, not the Kaaba that settled in your courtyard!' Yet out of justice, he had their properties fairly valued and placed their full price inside the Kaaba until they willingly accepted it; Uthman (RA) followed the same precedent in 26 AH.
reference: Al-Azraqi, Akhbar Makkah 2:65-67; Ibn Sa'd, Al-Tabaqat al-Kubra

questionEn: What architectural innovation did Caliph Uthman ibn Affan (RA) introduce to Al-Masjid al-Haram during the second expansion in 26 AH (646 CE)?
optionsEn: He constructed the first covered porticos / roofed arcades (arwiqah / saqa'if) inside Al-Masjid al-Haram to shade worshippers from the sun
He installed electric chandeliers and escalators
He built nine minarets in the Andalusian style
He paved the entire floor with glass
explanationEn: In 26 AH, Caliph Uthman ibn Affan (RA) expanded Al-Masjid al-Haram further and was the first to build roofed porticos (arwiqah) around the courtyard so worshippers praying around the Kaaba could have shade.
reference: Al-Azraqi, Akhbar Makkah 2:67; Al-Fasi, Shifa' al-Gharam

questionEn: What was 'Dar al-Nadwah' in pre-Islamic Makkah, who originally built it just north-west of the Kaaba, and what ultimately happened to its site?
optionsEn: It was a fortress on Mount Arafah that still stands outside Makkah today

It was the assembly council hall of Quraysh built by Qusayy ibn Kilab; after Islam it passed through Umayyad/Abbasid hands until Abbasid Caliph Al-Mu'tadid incorporated its exact site into Al-Masjid al-Haram in 284 AH (897 CE)
It was the well from which Zamzam flowed
It was a marketplace in Yemen
explanationEn: Qusayy ibn Kilab built Dar al-Nadwah just northwest of the Kaaba with its door facing the Sacred House as Quraysh's civic council chamber. In 284 AH (897 CE), the Abbasid Caliph Al-Mu'tadid Billah demolished Dar al-Nadwah and annexed its land into the northern/western portico of Al-Masjid al-Haram (known as Ziyadat Dar al-Nadwah).
reference: Al-Azraqi, Akhbar Makkah; Al-Fasi, Shifa' al-Gharam 1:238

questionEn: Which Abbasid Caliph carried out two monumental expansions of Al-Masjid al-Haram in 160 AH and 164 AH (777–781 CE), bringing carved marble columns by sea from Egypt and Syria to Jeddah and placing the Kaaba centrally within the Mosque courtyard?
optionsEn: Caliph Al-Radi
Caliph Al-Musta'sim
Caliph Muhammad al-Mahdi
Caliph Al-Qadir
explanationEn: During his pilgrimages in 160 AH and 164 AH, the Abbasid Caliph Al-Mahdi spent vast sums to nearly double the area of Al-Masjid al-Haram, importing hundreds of white marble columns via the Red Sea port of Jeddah and realigning the eastern/southern wings so the Kaaba stood near the center of the courtyard.

questionEn: Which Abbasid Caliph added the 'Bab Ibrahim' (Ibrahim Gate) extension on the western side of Al-Masjid al-Haram in 306 AH (918 CE)?
optionsEn: Caliph Al-Mansur
Caliph Harun al-Rashid
Caliph Al-Ma'mun
Caliph Al-Muqtadir Billah
explanationEn: In 306 AH (918 CE), the Abbasid Caliph Al-Muqtadir Billah annexed a courtyard between two houses of Lady Zubaydah on the western side of Al-Masjid al-Haram, creating the Bab Ibrahim extension. After 306 AH, the overall outer footprint of Al-Masjid al-Haram remained virtually unchanged for over a thousand years until the First Saudi Expansion in 1375 AH (1955 CE).

questionEn: For roughly how many centuries did the total floor area of Al-Masjid al-Haram remain practically unchanged between the Abbasid expansion of Al-Muqtadir in 306 AH (918 CE) and the First Saudi Expansion in 1375 AH (1955 CE)?
optionsEn: More than ten centuries (over 1,000 years, during which rulers restored, rebuilt arcades, domes, and minarets within the existing Abbasid footprint)
Only twenty years
Only one century
Fifty years
explanationEn: Historians of Makkah (including Al-Fasi and modern architectural historians) note that from 306 AH (918 CE) until 1375 AH (1955 CE)—over a millennium—Mamluk and Ottoman sultans extensively rebuilt the roofs, columns, domes, and minarets of Al-Masjid al-Haram, but its outer perimeter remained that set by the Abbasids.
reference: Al-Fasi, Shifa' al-Gharam; Al-Kurdi, Al-Tarikh al-Qawim li-Makkah wa Bayt Allah al-Karim

questionEn: Which Mamluk Sultan built a famous four-madhhab Islamic college and complex (Madrasat al-Ashraf Qaitbay) right beside Al-Masjid al-Haram in 882–884 AH (1477–1479 CE) and carried out major restorations after a fire in the Mosque?
optionsEn: Sultan Baybars I
Sultan Al-Ashraf Qaitbay
Sultan Qutuz
Sultan Al-Adil
explanationEn: The Mamluk Sultan Al-Ashraf Qaitbay visited Makkah for Hajj in 884 AH (1479 CE), restored Al-Masjid al-Haram, and endowed a renowned madrasah complex with a library and ribat for the four Sunni schools of law along the eastern side of the Mosque.
reference: Al-Sakhawi, Al-Daw' al-Lami'; Al-Kurdi, Al-Tarikh al-Qawim

questionEn: In the late 10th century AH (1570s CE), why did the Ottoman Sultans Selim II and Murad III commission the chief imperial architect Mimar Sinan to replace the flat wooden ceilings of Al-Masjid al-Haram's arcades?
optionsEn: They wanted to build a steel suspension bridge over the Kaaba
They wanted to turn the Mosque into an open stadium with no shade at all
The aging wooden beams had deteriorated and sagged, so Sinan replaced them with hundreds of fire-resistant brick-and-stone masonry domes supported by marble and Shumaysi-stone columns
They replaced the stone walls with canvas tents
explanationEn: Beginning under Sultan Selim II in 979 AH (1571 CE) and completed under Sultan Murad III in 984 AH (1576 CE), Mimar Sinan designed the replacement of the old wooden flat roofs of the Abbasid porticos with over 500 whitewashed masonry domes resting on marble and yellow Shumaysi-stone columns—known today as the historic Ottoman Portico (Al-Riwaq al-Uthmani).
reference: Qutb al-Din al-Nahrawali, Al-I'lam bi-A'lam Bayt Allah al-Haram

questionEn: What local stone quarried between Makkah and Jeddah was extensively used alongside white marble in the historic Ottoman columns and arches of Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: White chalk from Dover
Green jade from China
Blue lapis lazuli from Badakhshan
Yellowish-brown Shumaysi stone (Hajar al-Shumaysi)
explanationEn: Quarried from the Wadi al-Shumaysi area (where the Hudaybiyyah boundary lies between Makkah and Jeddah), durable yellow-ochre Shumaysi sandstone was carved into columns, capitals, and arches throughout the historic Ottoman portico of Al-Masjid al-Haram.
reference: Al-Nahrawali, Al-I'lam bi-A'lam Bayt Allah al-Haram; Al-Kurdi, Al-Tarikh al-Qawim

questionEn: How were the historic columns and arches of the Ottoman Portico (Al-Riwaq al-Uthmani) preserved during the modern 21st-century expansion of the Mataf in Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Each historic column, capital, and dome element was carefully documented, numbered, dismantled, restored by specialists, and re-erected along the new wider Mataf perimeter in alignment with the modern levels
Every single historic column was crushed into gravel for highway paving
They were all shipped to a museum in London
They were buried beneath the Red Sea
explanationEn: During the Mataf expansion project under King Abdullah and King Salman, engineers and heritage conservationists laser-scanned, numbered, restored, and re-assembled the historic Abbasid and Ottoman columns and domes along the expanded Mataf arcades.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Two Holy Mosques Engineering Reports

questionEn: Historically, how did the scholars of the four Sunni schools of jurisprudence (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali) conduct prayers in Al-Masjid al-Haram during the late Mamluk and Ottoman eras before they were unified behind a single Imam?
optionsEn: Only one madhhab was ever allowed inside Makkah while the other three prayed in Jeddah

Four separate architectural pavilions (al-Maqamat al-Arba'ah) stood around the Mataf for each of the four madhhabs, until King Abdulaziz unified all congregational prayers behind a single Imam at a time in 1345 AH (1926 CE)
Prayers were held without any Imam at all for four hundred years
Each madhhab prayed on a different day of the week
explanationEn: For several centuries during the Mamluk and Ottoman eras, four separate Maqams (prayer pavilions: Maqam al-Shafi'i above Zamzam, Maqam al-Hanafi on the north/west, Maqam al-Maliki on the west, and Maqam al-Hanbali on the south/east) held sequential or separate congregations around the Kaaba. In 1345 AH (1926 CE), following a scholarly assembly in Makkah, King Abdulaziz unified the congregation of Al-Masjid al-Haram behind one Imam at a time, removing the multiple pavilions later during the Mataf widening to clear space for Tawaf.
reference: Al-Kurdi, Al-Tarikh al-Qawim; Umm al-Qura Official Gazette (1345 AH)

questionEn: Before the introduction of electricity to Al-Masjid al-Haram in the early 20th century, how was the Mataf and Mosque illuminated at night for over a thousand years?
optionsEn: By mirrors reflecting moonlight from Mount Arafah
By burning coal heaps inside the Hijr Ismail
By glass oil lamps (qanadil) fuelled with olive oil or sesame oil suspended from arches and colonnades around the Mataf
The Mosque was kept pitch-black and locked every night at sunset
explanationEn: From the time Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) first mounted oil lamps on the wall around the Mataf and Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan (RA) supplied oil and lamps from Ash-Sham, hundreds of suspended glass oil lamps (qanadil) lit the Mataf and porticos at night until electric lighting was first introduced in the late Ottoman / early Saudi era.
reference: Al-Azraqi, Akhbar Makkah 2:65; Al-Fasi, Shifa' al-Gharam

questionEn: In what year AH/CE did the First Saudi Expansion of Al-Masjid al-Haram officially begin under King Saud bin Abdulaziz (executing the plan initiated by King Abdulaziz)?
explanationEn: King Abdulaziz ordered preparations for a massive expansion of Al-Masjid al-Haram before his passing in 1953, and actual construction of the First Saudi Expansion began in Rabi' al-Akhir 1375 AH (November 1955 CE) under King Saud and continued under King Faisal and King Khalid.
reference: Al-Kurdi, Al-Tarikh al-Qawim; General Presidency for the Affairs of the Two Holy Mosques

questionEn: Which major engineering achievement was part of the First Saudi Expansion of Al-Masjid al-Haram (starting in 1375 AH / 1955 CE) to permanently protect the Kaaba and Mataf from the flash floods of Wadi Ibrahim?
optionsEn: Constructing massive underground concrete flood-diversion tunnels (Majra al-Sayl) that redirected torrential rainwater around and away from Al-Masjid al-Haram, and rerouting the vehicular street that previously cut behind Mount Safa
Moving the Kaaba to the top of a hill
Building a glass dome over the entire city of Makkah
Draining the Red Sea
explanationEn: Historically, Wadi Ibrahim channeled torrential flash floods directly into the depressed basin of the Mataf. As one of the very first steps of the 1955 expansion, engineers diverted the old street that ran behind Safa and constructed a deep underground flood-diversion culvert system to protect the Kaaba from flash floods.
reference: Al-Kurdi, Al-Tarikh al-Qawim; Architecture of the Two Holy Mosques

questionEn: Before the First Saudi Expansion in 1375 AH (1955 CE), what existed directly along the path between Mount Safa and Mount Marwah where pilgrims performed Sa'i?
optionsEn: An underground subway tunnel built by the Abbasids

An open public street lined with shops and houses sitting OUTSIDE the walls of Al-Masjid al-Haram, which pilgrims had to walk through amidst market traffic until the 1955 expansion enclosed and roofed Al-Mas'a as a two-story gallery joined directly to the Mosque
A closed marble hall built by Caliph Umar
A lake crossed by wooden boats
explanationEn: For centuries before 1955, the Mas'a between Safa and Marwah was an unpaved/cobbled public thoroughfare outside the eastern wall of Al-Masjid al-Haram, flanked by shops and residences. The First Saudi Expansion cleared the shops, diverted street traffic, and constructed a dedicated two-story roofed Mas'a building integrated into Al-Masjid al-Haram.
reference: Al-Kurdi, Al-Tarikh al-Qawim; General Presidency for the Affairs of the Two Holy Mosques

questionEn: By approximately how much did the First Saudi Expansion (begun in 1955) increase the total area of Al-Masjid al-Haram compared to its historic Abbasid/Ottoman footprint?
optionsEn: It reduced the size of the Mosque by half
By only 500 square meters
From roughly 28,000–30,000 square meters to over 160,000–190,000 square meters (an increase of more than fivefold)
From 1,000 square meters to 2,000 square meters
explanationEn: Prior to 1955, the entire area of Al-Masjid al-Haram was approximately 28,000–30,000 square meters. The First Saudi Expansion added two stories of arcades, the enclosed two-story Mas'a, widened the Mataf, and expanded the total area to roughly 160,000–193,000 square meters.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Two Holy Mosques

questionEn: Which Saudi monarch laid the foundation stone for the Second Saudi Expansion on the western side of Al-Masjid al-Haram (featuring the monumental King Fahd Gate and twin minarets) in Muharram 1409 AH (September 1988 CE)?
optionsEn: King Faisal bin Abdulaziz
King Khalid bin Abdulaziz
King Saud bin Abdulaziz
King Fahd bin Abdulaziz
explanationEn: In Muharram 1409 AH (September 1988 CE), King Fahd bin Abdulaziz laid the foundation stone for the major western expansion of Al-Masjid al-Haram on the site of the old Little Market (Al-Suwayqah / Al-Souq al-Saghir), adding a vast two-story prayer building with a roof prayer deck, three large domes, escalators, central air-conditioning plant, and the twin-minaret King Fahd Gate (#79).
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Two Holy Mosques

questionEn: Where is the massive central cooling and air-conditioning plant that supplies chilled water through underground tunnels to cool Al-Masjid al-Haram located?
optionsEn: In the Ajyad / Shamiyah utility complexes located a considerable distance outside the Mosque and connected via deep underground service tunnels so noise and exhaust stay away from worshippers
On top of the roof of the Kaaba
Inside the Hijr Ismail
Inside the Cave of Hira
explanationEn: To prevent mechanical noise, vibrations, and heat dissipation near the Sacred Mosque, giant chiller plants were constructed at a distance in Ajyad and Shamiyah (one of the largest district cooling systems in the world), pumping chilled water through underground utility tunnels into Al-Masjid al-Haram.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Two Holy Mosques Engineering Reports

questionEn: Which Saudi monarch launched the Third Saudi Expansion (the largest expansion in the history of Al-Masjid al-Haram, extending across the northern Shamiyah district) in 1428–1432 AH (2008–2011 CE), later continued and inaugurated phases under King Salman?
optionsEn: King Saud bin Abdulaziz
King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz
King Faisal bin Abdulaziz
King Khalid bin Abdulaziz
explanationEn: King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz initiated the historic Third Saudi Expansion on the northern (Shamiyah) side of Al-Masjid al-Haram, along with the widening of Al-Mas'a to four floors and the reconstruction of the multi-level Mataf, raising total capacity across the Mosque, Mas'a, Mataf, and surrounding plazas to over two million worshippers.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Two Holy Mosques

questionEn: How does the modern widening of Al-Mas'a (completed during 2007–2009 under King Abdullah) double the horizontal width and multiply the floors of the Sa'i corridor between Safa and Marwah?
optionsEn: It moved Mount Safa to the western side of the Kaaba
It shortened the distance between Safa and Marwah from 394 meters to 50 meters

It doubled the width of Al-Mas'a from 20 meters to 40 meters and increased it to four primary stories (plus basement and roof levels), raising Sa'i capacity from ~44,000 to over 118,000 pilgrims per hour
It replaced the floor with sand dunes
explanationEn: While preserving the exact 394.5-meter longitudinal distance between the rocks of Safa and Marwah, the Mas'a expansion widened the corridor laterally eastward from 20 m to 40 m and added multiple stories with dedicated wheelchair lanes, tripling hourly pilgrim throughput.
reference: General Presidency for the Affairs of the Two Holy Mosques

questionEn: Why did Islamic jurists carefully examine and approve the 2007–2009 lateral widening of Al-Mas'a from 20 meters to 40 meters before and during its construction?
optionsEn: Because the Qur'an does not mention Safa and Marwah
Because jurists ruled that Sa'i can be performed anywhere in Jeddah
Because Mount Safa and Mount Marwah are artificial hills built in 1955

By verifying through geological surveys and historical records that the eastern rock formations of Mount Safa and Mount Marwah (al-mash'arayn) naturally extended across the full 40-meter width, ensuring every pilgrim walks strictly between the two sacred mounts
explanationEn: Because Sa'i is valid only within the span between the actual geological mounts of Safa and Marwah (bayna al-jabalayn), engineering and geological committees alongside scholars verified the subterranean rock extensions of both mounts across the widened corridor.
reference: Decisions of the Council of Senior Scholars on Al-Mas'a Expansion

questionEn: What is the name of the monumental 601-meter endowment tower complex standing immediately south of Al-Masjid al-Haram (on the site of the former Ottoman Ajyad Fortress), whose revenues are dedicated as a Waqf (endowment) for the service and maintenance of the Two Holy Mosques?
optionsEn: Waqf al-Malik Abdulaziz / Abraj al-Bayt (Makkah Royal Clock Tower)
Burj Khalifa
Kingdom Centre Tower
Al-Faisaliah Tower
explanationEn: The King Abdulaziz Endowment (Waqf al-Malik Abdulaziz li-l-Haramayn al-Sharifayn), commonly known as Abraj al-Bayt or the Makkah Royal Clock Tower (601 meters tall, surmounted by a four-faced clock and golden crescent), was built as a charitable Waqf whose income funds the upkeep of Al-Masjid al-Haram.
reference: King Abdulaziz Endowment for the Two Holy Mosques Documentation

questionEn: What famous Islamic calligrapher of Makkah (d. 1418 AH / 1997 CE), who served for decades as the chief calligrapher of the Kiswah of the Kaaba, designed the monumental Thuluth script used on the Kaaba's Kiswah for over thirty years before his student Mukhtar Alam succeeded him?
optionsEn: Ibn Muqlah of Baghdad
Shaykh Abdul-Rahim Amin Bukhari
Yaqut al-Musta'simi
Ibn al-Bawwab
explanationEn: Shaykh Abdul-Rahim Amin Bukhari (1339–1418 AH / 1920–1997 CE) served at the Kiswah Factory in Makkah for over half a century as the master calligrapher of the Kaaba's Kiswah and mentored its subsequent chief calligrapher, Shaykh Mukhtar Alam.
reference: King Abdulaziz Complex for the Kiswah of the Holy Kaaba Records

questionEn: Which noble Companion was the very first person after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to recite the Qur'an aloud publicly before the Quraysh at the Kaaba in Al-Masjid al-Haram, reciting the opening verses of Surah Ar-Rahman (55)?
optionsEn: Amr ibn al-As (RA)
Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA)
Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (RA)
Abu Sufyan ibn Harb (RA)
explanationEn: As recorded by Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Hisham from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, when the Companions said that the Quraysh had never yet heard the Qur'an recited aloud publicly, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (RA) volunteered, went to Maqam Ibrahim at forenoon while Quraysh sat in their circles around the Kaaba, and recited 'Bismillahir-Rahmanir-Rahim, Ar-Rahman, 'allamal-Qur'an...' Even after they struck his face until it bled, he offered to do it again the next day.

questionEn: Which noble Companion built a small private place of prayer (masjid) in the courtyard of his own house in Makkah during the period of persecution, where he would weep while reciting the Qur'an aloud as the women and youths of Quraysh gathered to listen in amazement?
optionsEn: Salman al-Farisi (RA)
Abu Hurayrah (RA)
Mu'adh ibn Jabal (RA)
Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA)
explanationEn: As narrated by Aishah (RA) in Sahih al-Bukhari (476, 3905), when Abu Bakr (RA) received Ibn al-Daghinnah's protection to remain in Makkah, he built a masjid in the courtyard of his house in Makkah and prayed and recited the Qur'an there while weeping, drawing the wives and children of the polytheists until the chiefs of Quraysh grew alarmed.

questionEn: When the chiefs of Quraysh complained to Ibn al-Daghinnah that Abu Bakr's (RA) tearful Qur'an recitation in his Makkan courtyard was captivating their women and youth, how did Abu Bakr (RA) respond?
optionsEn: He returned Ibn al-Daghinnah's pledge of protection, saying: 'I return to you your protection, and I am content with the protection of Allah (wa arda bi-jiwarillah)'
He agreed never to recite the Qur'an again in Makkah
He moved his house to Ta'if that afternoon
He asked the King of Persia for protection
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari (2297, 3905), rather than conceal his prayer and recitation in Makkah as stipulated by Quraysh, Abu Bakr (RA) nobly renounced Ibn al-Daghinnah's worldly protection and declared: 'I return to you your protection, and I am content with the protection of Allah and His Messenger.'

questionEn: When Companion Tufayl ibn Amr al-Dawsi (RA), an eloquent poet and chief of the tribe of Daws, first arrived in Makkah before his conversion, what did the Quraysh warn him to put in his ears before performing Tawaf around the Kaaba?
optionsEn: Melted wax from Yemen
Fluff of cotton (kursuf) so he would not hear the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ reciting the Qur'an near the Kaaba
Gold earrings from Syria
Water from the Red Sea
explanationEn: The Quraysh frightened Tufayl ibn Amr al-Dawsi (RA) that the Prophet's ﷺ speech was like 'magic' that separated families, so he stuffed cotton (kursuf) into his ears when entering Al-Masjid al-Haram. Yet when he saw the Prophet ﷺ praying at the Kaaba, he thought: 'I am an intelligent poet who can tell good speech from bad—why not listen?' Upon hearing the Qur'an, he embraced Islam and became the caller of the tribe of Daws.
reference: Sirat Ibn Hisham 1:382; Dalail al-Nubuwwah lil-Bayhaqi

questionEn: When Companion Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (RA) first came to Makkah secretly searching for the Prophet ﷺ, where did he stay for days and what was his ONLY food and nourishment before Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) hosted him?
optionsEn: He stayed in the market of Ukaz eating dates and honey
He stayed in the palace of Abu Sufyan and ate roast lamb

He stayed inside Al-Masjid al-Haram and drank nothing but Zamzam water, saying to the Prophet ﷺ: 'I had no food except the water of Zamzam, and I grew plump until the folds of my stomach turned over, and I did not feel any hunger of the stomach'
He stayed on Mount Arafah eating wild game
explanationEn: In Sahih Muslim (2473), Abu Dharr (RA) narrated his famous conversion story in Makkah: he stayed in the Mosque at the Kaaba with no food or drink except Zamzam water until he gained weight and felt no pangs of hunger, whereupon the Prophet ﷺ told him: 'Indeed, it is blessed (innaha mubarakah); it is a food that nourishes (innaha ta'amu tu'm).'

questionEn: When Dimad al-Azdi (RA), a healer from Yemen who treated people for spiritual affliction, came to Makkah and heard the fools of Makkah claim the Prophet ﷺ was possessed, what caused Dimad to embrace Islam on the spot?
optionsEn: Receiving a gift of a hundred camels
Seeing an eclipse of the sun over the Kaaba
Winning a horse race in lower Makkah

Hearing the Prophet's ﷺ opening sermon of praise ('Innal-hamda lillahi nahmaduhu wa nasta'inuhu...'), which moved Dimad so deeply he asked the Prophet ﷺ to repeat it three times, declared it reached the depths of the ocean, and pledged allegiance
explanationEn: Recorded in Sahih Muslim (868), when Dimad al-Azdi offered to perform ruqyah on the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ recited Khutbat al-Hajah ('Indeed, all praise belongs to Allah; we praise Him and seek His help; whomsoever Allah guides, none can misguide...'). Dimad exclaimed: 'I have heard the words of soothsayers, sorcerers, and poets, and I have never heard words like these—they have reached the bottom of the sea (qamusa al-bahr)!' and embraced Islam.

questionEn: Whose protection (jiwar) did the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ enter under when returning to Makkah from his difficult journey to Ta'if in the 10th year of Prophethood, entering Al-Masjid al-Haram surrounded by that chief's armed sons to perform Tawaf around the Kaaba?
optionsEn: Al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi (chief of Banu Nawfal)
Abu Lahab (Abd al-'Uzza)
Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah
Umayyah ibn Khalaf
explanationEn: After returning from Ta'if to Hira, the Prophet ﷺ sent word to Al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi, who armed his sons and nephews, escorted the Prophet ﷺ into Al-Masjid al-Haram to touch the Corner, perform Tawaf, and pray two rak'ahs safely. The Prophet ﷺ never forgot this noble act, saying after Badr: 'Had Al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi been alive and spoken to me on behalf of these foul captives, I would have released them for him.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3139).

questionEn: Who did the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ appoint as the first Governor ('Amil / Amir) over Makkah upon departing after the Conquest of Makkah and the Battle of Hunayn in 8 AH, despite his young age of around twenty-one years?
optionsEn: Mu'adh ibn Jabal (RA)
'Attab ibn Asid (RA)
Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (RA)
Amr ibn Hazm (RA)
explanationEn: When the Prophet ﷺ departed from Ji'ranah after the Conquest of Makkah in 8 AH, he appointed the young Qurayshi Companion 'Attab ibn Asid ibn Abi al-'Is (RA) as Governor of Makkah and leader of the Hajj that year (8 AH), assigning him a daily stipend of one dirham, about which 'Attab famously said: 'May Allah make hungry the liver of anyone who remains hungry on a dirham a day!'
reference: Sirat Ibn Hisham 2:500; Ibn Abd al-Barr, Al-Isti'ab; Usd al-Ghabah

questionEn: Which noble Companion—renowned as the most knowledgeable of the Ummah regarding the lawful and the unlawful (al-halal wal-haram)—did the Prophet ﷺ leave behind in Makkah alongside Governor 'Attab ibn Asid (RA) in 8 AH specifically to teach the people of Makkah the Qur'an and Fiqh of Islam?
optionsEn: Zayd ibn Thabit (RA)
Bilal ibn Rabah (RA)
Mu'adh ibn Jabal (RA)
Anas ibn Malik (RA)
explanationEn: After the Conquest of Makkah in 8 AH, while appointing 'Attab ibn Asid (RA) as administrative governor, the Prophet ﷺ left Mu'adh ibn Jabal (RA) in Makkah to instruct its newly converted residents in the Qur'an and Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh fi al-din).
reference: Sirat Ibn Hisham 2:500; Tabaqat Ibn Sa'd; Al-Isabah

questionEn: Which Companion did the Prophet ﷺ appoint as the official Mu'adhdhin of Al-Masjid al-Haram in Makkah after the Conquest of Makkah, whose descendants inherited the call to prayer in Makkah for centuries?
optionsEn: Salman al-Farisi (RA)
Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum (RA)
Sa'd al-Qaraz (RA)
Abu Mahdhurah (Aws ibn Mi'yar al-Jumahi, RA)
explanationEn: At Ji'ranah after Hunayn (8 AH), when the Prophet ﷺ heard the remarkably resonant voice of the young Makkan Abu Mahdhurah (RA), he personally taught him the words of the Adhan (including Tarji'), wiped his forehead and chest with his blessed hand, prayed for blessing upon him, and appointed him Mu'adhdhin of Al-Masjid al-Haram in Makkah (while Bilal and Ibn Umm Maktum served in Madinah and Sa'd al-Qaraz in Quba).
reference: Sahih Muslim 379; Sunan Abi Dawud 500; Sunan al-Nasa'i 632

questionEn: What is the name of the famous school of Qur'anic exegesis (Tafsir) and Hadith founded in Makkah by Companion Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA), known as 'Habr al-Ummah' (The Scholar of the Ummah) and 'Tarjuman al-Qur'an' (The Interpreter of the Qur'an)?
optionsEn: Madrasat Makkah fi al-Tafsir (The Makkan School of Tafsir), whose foremost students included Mujahid ibn Jabr, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Tawus ibn Kaysan
The Kufan School of Grammar
The Andalusian School of Maliki Fiqh
The Basran School of Mu'tazilism
explanationEn: Seated by the Kaaba in Al-Masjid al-Haram during the late Rightly Guided and early Umayyad periods, Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA)—for whom the Prophet ﷺ prayed 'Allahumma faqqihhu fid-din wa 'allimhu al-ta'wil'—established the premier school of Tafsir, Hadith, and Hajj Fiqh in Makkah.
reference: Ibn Taymiyyah, Muqaddimah fi Usul al-Tafsir; Al-Dhahabi, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala'

questionEn: Which student of Ibn Abbas (RA) and leading Tabi'i scholar of Makkah (d. 104 AH) reviewed the entire Qur'an with Ibn Abbas (RA) three times, stopping at every single verse to ask about what it was revealed concerning and how it came about?
optionsEn: Al-Zuhri of Madinah
Mujahid ibn Jabr al-Makki
Ibrahim al-Nakha'i of Kufa
Al-Layth ibn Sa'd of Egypt
explanationEn: Mujahid ibn Jabr al-Makki (21–104 AH) stated: 'I presented the Mushaf to Ibn Abbas three times from its opening to its conclusion, stopping him at every verse of it and asking him about it.' Sufyan al-Thawri famously said: 'If the Tafsir comes to you from Mujahid, it is sufficient for you.' According to historians, Mujahid passed away in Makkah while in prostration (sujud).
reference: Tafsir al-Tabari 1:90; Al-Dhahabi, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' 4:449

questionEn: Which great Tabi'i jurist and Mufti of Makkah (d. 114 AH)—a freedman of black skin who was physically frail yet unmatched in knowledge of Hajj rites and piety—made Al-Masjid al-Haram his home and bed for twenty years and was proclaimed by the Umayyad herald during Hajj: 'No one shall issue fatwa to the people except him'?
optionsEn: Qatadah ibn Di'amah
Al-Sha'bi
'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah
Rabi'ah al-Ra'y
explanationEn: 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah (27–114 AH) was the undisputed Mufti of Makkah and master of Manasik al-Hajj after Ibn Abbas (RA). Even the Umayyad Caliph Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik and his sons came to sit humbly on their knees before 'Ata' in Al-Masjid al-Haram to ask him questions on the rites of Hajj.
reference: Al-Dhahabi, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' 5:78; Ibn Khallikan, Wafayat al-A'yan

questionEn: Which canonical Qari' (Reciter) among the Seven Mutawatir Readers of the Qur'an was the Imam of Recitation for the people of Makkah (d. 120 AH), transmitting his recitation from Mujahid and Ibn Abbas (RA) from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Zayd ibn Thabit (RA)?
optionsEn: Hamzah al-Zayyat
Nafi' al-Madani
'Asim al-Kufi
Abdullah ibn Kathir al-Makki (Ibn Kathir al-Dari, whose two canonical transmitters are Al-Bazzi and Qunbul)
explanationEn: Abdullah ibn Kathir al-Makki (45–120 AH)—not to be confused with the 8th-century AH historian Isma'il ibn Kathir—was a Tabi'i who met Companions such as Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, and Anas ibn Malik (RA) in Makkah and served for decades as the undisputed Imam of Qira'ah in Al-Masjid al-Haram.
reference: Ibn al-Jazari, Ghayat al-Nihayah fi Tabaqat al-Qurra' 1:443; Al-Dhahabi, Ma'rifat al-Qurra' al-Kibar

questionEn: Who are the two canonical Rawis (transmitters) of the Makkan Qira'ah of Imam Abdullah ibn Kathir al-Makki, both of whom resided and taught in Makkah?
optionsEn: Al-Bazzi (Ahmad ibn Muhammad, the Mu'adhdhin and Imam of Al-Masjid al-Haram) and Qunbul (Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Makhzumi)
Hafs and Shu'bah
Warsh and Qalun
Al-Duri and Al-Susi
explanationEn: The two canonical transmitters of Ibn Kathir al-Makki's Qur'anic reading are Al-Bazzi (170–250 AH, who served for forty years as Mu'adhdhin and recitation leader in Al-Masjid al-Haram) and Qunbul (195–291 AH, head of the Qur'an reciters of the Hijaz in Makkah).
reference: Ibn al-Jazari, Al-Nashr fi al-Qira'at al-'Ashr

questionEn: Which great Imam of the four Sunni schools of jurisprudence grew up as a poor orphan in Makkah after his mother brought him there from Gaza at age two, memorized the Qur'an in Makkah by age seven, lived with the eloquent tribe of Hudhayl near Makkah, and received permission to issue fatwa in Al-Masjid al-Haram from the Mufti of Makkah, Muslim ibn Khalid al-Zanji?
optionsEn: Imam Abu Hanifah al-Nu'man (80–150 AH)
Imam Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i (150–204 AH)
Imam Malik ibn Anas (93–179 AH)
Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (164–241 AH)
explanationEn: Imam al-Shafi'i (RA), a descendant of Al-Muttalib ibn Abd Manaf (the brother of Hashim), was raised in Makkah, studied under the Mufti of Makkah Muslim ibn Khalid al-Zanji and the Muhaddith of Makkah Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah at Al-Masjid al-Haram before traveling to study under Imam Malik in Madinah.
reference: Al-Bayhaqi, Manaqib al-Shafi'i; Al-Dhahabi, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' 10:5

questionEn: Which renowned Muhaddith of the Sacred Sanctuary (Muhaddith al-Haram, 107–198 AH) settled in Makkah, performed Hajj seventy times, and made his circle at Al-Masjid al-Haram the destination for scholars from across the Islamic world (including Imam al-Shafi'i and Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal)?
optionsEn: Abd al-Rahman al-Awza'i
Al-Layth ibn Sa'd
Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah
Waki' ibn al-Jarrah
explanationEn: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah (107–198 AH) was the foremost Hadith master and Qur'an commentator in Makkah for half a century; Imam al-Shafi'i said: 'Were it not for Malik and Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, knowledge would have departed from the Hijaz.'

questionEn: Which pious ascetic and Hadith scholar (d. 187 AH)—formerly a feared highwayman in Khurasan before repenting upon hearing a reciter chant Surah Al-Hadid 57:16 ('Has the time not come for those who have believed that their hearts should become humbly submissive at the remembrance of Allah?')—spent the rest of his life as a Mujawir (resident worshipper) in Al-Masjid al-Haram in Makkah and became known as 'Abid al-Haramayn' (The Worshipper of the Two Sanctuaries)?
optionsEn: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz
Al-Hasan al-Basri
Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib
Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad
explanationEn: Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad (d. 187 AH in Makkah) repented sincerely, moved to Makkah to worship at the Kaaba and study Hadith, counselled Caliph Harun al-Rashid in Makkah until the Caliph wept, and was titled 'Abid al-Haramayn' by Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak.
reference: Al-Dhahabi, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' 8:421; Abu Nu'aym, Hilyat al-Awliya'

questionEn: Which 3rd-century AH Makkan historian (d. 250 AH / 865 CE) authored the foundational two-volume history of Makkah, the Kaaba, and Al-Masjid al-Haram titled 'Akhbar Makkah wa ma Ja'a fiha min al-Athar'?
optionsEn: Abu al-Walid Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Azraqi
Ibn Khaldun
Al-Mas'udi
Ibn Battuta
explanationEn: Abu al-Walid al-Azraqi (d. 250 AH)—transmitting largely from his grandfather Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Azraqi—compiled 'Akhbar Makkah', the earliest and most authoritative surviving historical and architectural monograph on the Kaaba, Al-Masjid al-Haram, and the landmarks of Makkah.
reference: Al-Azraqi, Akhbar Makkah; Sezgin, Geschichte des arabischen Schrifttums

questionEn: Which contemporary 3rd-century AH Makkan scholar (d. 272 or 275 AH) also authored a celebrated six-volume history and hadith compilation on Makkah titled 'Akhbar Makkah fi Qadim al-Dahr wa Hadithihi'?
optionsEn: Al-Ya'qubi
Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Fakihi
Ibn Khallikan
Al-Maqrizi
explanationEn: Abu Abdullah al-Fakihi (d. ~275 AH) authored the comprehensive 'Akhbar Makkah fi Qadim al-Dahr wa Hadithihi', preserving thousands of narrations from the Companions and Tabi'un regarding the rulings, etiquettes, houses, valleys, and historical events of Makkah.

questionEn: Which 9th-century AH Maliki scholar and historian of Makkah (775–832 AH / 1373–1429 CE) authored 'Shifa' al-Gharam bi-Akhbar al-Balad al-Haram' and the biographical dictionary of Makkans 'Al-'Iqd al-Thamin fi Tarikh al-Balad al-Amin'?
optionsEn: Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti
Ibn Hajar al-Haytami
Taqi al-Din Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Hasani al-Fasi
Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali
explanationEn: Qadi Taqi al-Din al-Fasi (d. 832 AH), the Maliki judge of Makkah, authored both 'Shifa' al-Gharam bi-Akhbar al-Balad al-Haram' (on the topography, monuments, and history of Makkah) and the multi-volume 'Al-'Iqd al-Thamin' (biographies of notables who lived in or visited Makkah).
reference: Al-Fasi, Shifa' al-Gharam; Al-Sakhawi, Al-Daw' al-Lami'

questionEn: What is the Arabic term 'Mujawir' (plural: Mujawirun) in the historical tradition of Makkah?
optionsEn: A sailor on the Indian Ocean
A camel driver who only travels between Damascus and Baghdad
A stonecutter who builds minarets in Cairo
A believer from outside Makkah who settles in proximity (jiwar) to Al-Masjid al-Haram to devote themselves to worship, Tawaf, and seeking sacred knowledge
explanationEn: Derived from 'jiwar' (neighboring/living beside Allah's Sanctuary), a 'Mujawir' is a scholar, student, or worshipper who takes up residence near the Kaaba in Makkah (or near the Prophet's ﷺ Mosque in Madinah) for devotion and study.
reference: Ibn Manzur, Lisan al-Arab; Al-Fasi, Shifa' al-Gharam

questionEn: What spiritual counsel did Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) and classical scholars such as Imam Abu Hanifah and Ibn Qudamah give regarding residing permanently in Makkah (al-mujawarah) if one fears growing overly accustomed to the Sanctuary and losing reverence?
optionsEn: That one who resides in Makkah must guard their heart carefully against heedlessness or sin (since bad deeds in the Haram are magnified in gravity), and Umar (RA) encouraged pilgrims after finishing their Hajj rites to return to their homelands with longing in their hearts for the House
That it is obligatory for every Muslim on earth to move permanently to Makkah so all other cities become empty
That sins committed in Makkah are never recorded by the angels
That residing in Makkah is forbidden even for a single week
explanationEn: While residing in Makkah with piety and reverence is virtuous, Umar (RA) used to urge visiting delegations after Hajj to return to their lands ('O people of Yemen, return to your Yemen; O people of Sham, return to your Sham') so that people would remain in awe and yearning for the Sacred House rather than becoming heedless of its inviolable sanctity.
reference: Musannaf Ibn Abi Shaybah; Al-Mughni 3:474; Lata'if al-Ma'arif

questionEn: According to Abdullah ibn Abbas and Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (RA), how do good deeds (hasanat) and bad deeds (sayyi'at) committed inside the Sacred Sanctuary (Al-Haram) of Makkah compare to those outside it?
optionsEn: Sins committed in Makkah are rewarded as good deeds

Good deeds are multiplied in reward, while sins committed in the Haram carry far greater gravity and severity (taghliz) in quality because of the honor of the time and the sacred place (though a sin is still recorded as one sin, not multiplied in count)
Good deeds in Makkah are not rewarded outside Ramadan
Neither good deeds nor sins are recorded inside Makkah
explanationEn: Based upon Surah Al-Hajj (22:25) and Surah Al-An'am (6:160: 'Whoever comes with a good deed shall have ten times its like, and whoever comes with an evil deed shall not be recompensed except the like thereof'), scholars such as Ibn Abbas, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Ibn al-Qayyim explain that in the Haram of Makkah, a sin is still counted as one sin in number, but its magnitude, ugliness, and severity (kayfiyyah / 'izam) are far graver before Allah because of violating His Sacred Sanctuary.
reference: Zad al-Ma'ad 1:51; Majmu' Fatawa Ibn Taymiyyah; Al-Mughni

questionEn: What did the Prophet ﷺ say in the authentic hadith of Sahih Muslim about how Islam and faith return to the Two Sacred Sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah)?
optionsEn: No one will perform Hajj after the third century
Faith will leave the Arabian Peninsula forever in the second century
Indeed, faith (Al-Iman) draws back / retreats to the Hijaz (or to Madinah and between the Two Mosques) just as a snake draws back into its hole
The Kaaba will be moved to Khorasan
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari (1876) and Sahih Muslim (147), the Prophet ﷺ described how faith returns and finds refuge in Madinah and between the Two Mosques (Makkah and Madinah) just as a snake returns to its burrow.

questionEn: According to authentic hadiths in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, which two cities on earth will the False Messiah (Al-Masih al-Dajjal) be completely unable to enter because angels stand guard at their mountain passes?
optionsEn: Constantinople and Rome
Damascus and Baghdad
Cairo and Cordoba
Makkah and Madinah
explanationEn: Anas ibn Malik (RA) narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari (1881) and Sahih Muslim (2943) that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'There is no town which the Dajjal will not tread, except Makkah and Madinah; there is no mountain pass (naqb) of their passes except that angels are standing in rows guarding it.'

questionEn: According to authentic hadiths in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, will Hajj and Umrah to the Kaaba in Makkah continue to be performed EVEN AFTER the emergence and destruction of Gog and Magog (Ya'juj wa Ma'juj)?
optionsEn: Yes; the Prophet ﷺ said: 'This House will surely continue to be visited for Hajj and Umrah after the emergence of Gog and Magog'
No; Hajj stops a thousand years before Gog and Magog
No; the Kaaba is lifted up before the Prophet Isa (AS) descends
Only Umrah stops while Hajj moves to Sinai
explanationEn: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (RA) narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari (1593) that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Hajj and Umrah will surely continue to be performed to this House even after the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj (Gog and Magog).' In fact, Isa (AS) himself will perform Hajj and/or Umrah to Makkah after descending.

questionEn: According to Sahih Muslim (1252), when the Prophet Isa ibn Maryam (Jesus, peace be upon him) descends at the end of time, what act of worship will he perform on his way to Makkah through the pass of Al-Rawha'?
optionsEn: He will abolish Hajj and Umrah
He will proclaim the Talbiyah for Hajj, or for Umrah, or for both combined
He will change the Qiblah back to Jerusalem
He will forbid Tawaf around the Kaaba
explanationEn: Abu Hurayrah (RA) narrated in Sahih Muslim (1252) that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'By Him in Whose Hand is my soul, the son of Maryam will certainly pronounce the Talbiyah in the pass of Al-Rawha' as a pilgrim performing Hajj, or performing Umrah, or combining them both.'

questionEn: At the very end of time, near the final Hour when no true faith remains among people on earth, what did the Prophet ﷺ foretell in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim regarding the physical end of the Kaaba?
optionsEn: A volcano will erupt underneath Mount Safa
The Kaaba will turn into solid diamond and float into the clouds
A thin-shinned man from Abyssinia known as 'Dhu al-Suwayqatayn' will demolish the Kaaba, plucking out its stones one by one and stripping its Kiswah
The Red Sea will flood the entire Hijaz plateau
explanationEn: Abu Hurayrah and Ibn Abbas (RA) narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari (1591, 1596) and Sahih Muslim (2909) that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Dhu al-Suwayqatayn (the man with two thin shins) from Abyssinia will demolish the Kaaba,' and 'It is as if I am looking at him: black, bandy-legged, plucking out its stones one by one.' Scholars explain this occurs at the very end of time after the death of Isa (AS), when the Hour is about to be established upon the worst of people.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1591, 1595, 1596; Sahih Muslim 2909; Fath al-Bari 3:461

questionEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari (1593), how did scholars reconcile the verse 'Have they not seen that We made a safe sanctuary' and the continuing Hajj after Gog and Magog with the hadith of Dhu al-Suwayqatayn demolishing the Kaaba at the very end of time?
optionsEn: The two hadiths cannot be reconciled
Dhu al-Suwayqatayn lived before Prophet Ibrahim (AS)
Dhu al-Suwayqatayn is just another name for Abraha in the Year of the Elephant

Allah protects the Kaaba and continues Hajj and Umrah throughout the lifespan of the believing Ummah (even after Gog and Magog), until near the final Hour when faith disappears and the Hour is established when Hajj to the House is abandoned
explanationEn: In Sahih al-Bukhari (1593), appended to the hadith of Hajj continuing after Gog and Magog, Shu'bah reported the Prophet's ﷺ words: 'The Hour will not be established until Hajj is no longer performed to the House.' Ibn Hajar explains in Fath al-Bari that the Kaaba remains protected as long as believers honour it, and its demolition by Dhu al-Suwayqatayn happens at the very end of time when faith is lifted and the Hour is imminent.
reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 1593; Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari 3:460-462
